title: Can Congress Turn Anti-AAP Sentiment Into A Comeback in Punjab?
description: Punjab’s 2027 Assembly election could offer the Congress a path to revival as anti-incumbency against AAP grows and the Akali Dal and BJP struggle to regain ground.
author: Zaid Bin Shabir
content:
On November 4, Rahul Gandhi returned to Punjab, a State where the Congress party has historically known how to sway voters and win elections. Launching the campaign for the Punjab Assembly elections in Sangrur, an Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stronghold, Rahul attacked the AAP’s record in government and argued that Punjab needed a government that worked for the State rather than being “run from Delhi”.
The rally came at a time when the Congress, the ruling party in only one northern State, Himachal Pradesh, is trying to add momentum to its national-level recovery with a win in a State that had once been its stronghold. Also, after improving its Lok Sabha tally from 44 seats in 2014 to 99 in 2024, the party has increasingly sought to project Rahul as a more assertive opposition leader, taking on the Modi government.
But in Punjab, Rahul’s pitch was not simply an extension of that national campaign. His appeal to sentiments around Punjab’s distinct political identity builds on an older Congress-Punjab relationship.
For much of its post-Independence history, the Congress remained one of the principal political forces in Punjab as its journey intertwined with some of the many consequential changes in the border State. The party’s fortunes declined elsewhere following the BJP’s Modi wave, which swept away many of the Congress’ traditional strongholds after 2014. Yet Punjab, which brought the Congress back to power as recently as 2017, managed to buck the trend.
But voters in this outlier State have always shown little preference for continuity, which often results in the incumbent ruling party’s ouster. This happened in 2022 when the AAP mopped up 92 of Punjab’s 117 Assembly seats. The Congress, with just 18 seats, was roundly defeated. The State’s voters had built a new consensus that created a third political front.
“In 2022, the AAP was the only party that came into the fray without any baggage from the past,” said Sikander Singh, head of Misal Baba Sawan Singh Attari Dharna Dal, a Nihang Sikh group. “The driving force, which persuaded us to vote for it, was the AAP’s Delhi governance model, which had seemingly brought some relief to people there.”
However, with the passage of time, the ground beneath the AAP’s feet shifted. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, it won only 3 seats while the Congress bagged 7 of the State’s 13 parliamentary constituencies. Growing popular disenchantment with the AAP government, which started drawing criticism well before the general election, was perceived to be the cause of this reversal. From governance issues to religious matters, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s government has repeatedly found itself cornered.
Two years after the 2024 election, the AAP is out of power in Delhi and faces strong anti-incumbency in Punjab. Many observers believe that the situation creates a window for the AAP’s political opponents. With the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) struggling to recover its lost credibility and the BJP yet to establish a strong political base, political observers believe Punjab might become the first State to witness a Congress resurgence.
‘Price of power’
The AAP came to power promising a break from the politics of the Congress, the SAD, and the BJP. But its track record on its poll promises is severely contested. “People had very high expectations of the AAP,” said Jagrup Singh Sekhon, former professor of political science at Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar. “They thought the problem of drugs, gangsterism, law and order, unemployment, and mounting fiscal and agrarian crises would be addressed. But the AAP did not live up to those expectations.”
Popular discontent has coalesced around the problem of drug addiction. The government campaign on the issue, “Yudh Nasheyan Virudh”, was launched with much fanfare but has not yielded the desired results. The ruling party is perceived to be responsible for the mess.
“As we would fight to save our crops, so now we fight to save our generations,” said Sikander Singh. “The AAP promised to end the drug menace. Instead, drugs have become more easily available. Drugs and the AAP have devoured Punjab.”
The political damage has also acquired a consequential religious dimension. The acting jathedar of the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority of Sikhs, has declared Mann “Guru Dokhi” (betrayer of the Guru) and “Khalsa Panth Virodhi” (anti-Khalsa Panth).
The State government’s record has also been complicated by the increasingly visceral question of who controls the Punjab’s government. The AAP government has been accused of allowing the ruling party’s central leadership in Delhi to exercise an outsized influence over the State. The impression is that the State’s affairs are being dictated by people with little understanding of, or empathy for, Punjab and its people.
Jagtar Singh, a senior journalist based in Punjab, said: “Immediately after the AAP formed the government, the perception in Punjab was that it was being run by people from Delhi. It was an open secret. Punjabis don’t like Delhi dictating the State, but the interference level keeps rising.”
The extent of that disconnect became apparent when Bhagwant Mann vacated his Lok Sabha seat after becoming Chief Minister in 2022. Barely three months later, the AAP lost the Sangrur bypoll. “It showed that the party’s connection with the people began to take a hit from the very beginning,” Jagtar Singh said.
The AAP, fighting to hold on to its last fort, has attempted to make Mann its Punjab face. Another move has been to drop eight sitting legislators, including Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, in the party’s second list of candidates for the Assembly election, announced on November 12. But the damage, many observers believe, may be hard to reverse.
Sekhon observed: “The damage is already done. Once the Punjab elections are over, I don’t see the AAP continuing as a national party. The AAP may become a marginalised party. That’s the price of power in Punjab.”
The revival bid
Punjab has five principal contenders heading into next year’s election. Each is fighting, in its own way, to recover the political ground it has lost.
The SAD, one of Punjab’s oldest parties, is struggling to reclaim the political space it once occupied almost by default. The Badals’ centralisation of the party weakened its electoral base. Further, its alliance with the BJP—whose centralised model sat uneasily with the SAD’s regional identity—eroded its credibility. By the time the Akalis walked out over the controversial farm laws, they had already ceded much of their Sikh identity or Panthic political space to splinter groups and neo-Panthic forces such as the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De.
The SAD was reduced to three Assembly seats in 2022 and one parliamentary seat in 2024. Other groups filled the vacuum with Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh and independent candidate Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa winning two core SAD strongholds, Khadoor Sahib and Faridkot, in 2024. Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa’s father was one of the assassins of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
Sekhon said: “The BJP has nothing to lose. But if there is any restructuring of the seat-sharing arrangement then the [Shriomani] Akali Dal has a double challenge, and it is already marginalised. People still identify problems [of drugs, corruption, sacrilege, and gangster culture] with its leaders.”
He added: “This accumulation of baggage makes the SAD-BJP reunion as much a risk as a political opportunity.”
The radical political space also appears to be narrowing. “The era of Amritpal [style of politics] has passed,” Sekhon said. “There was a particular momentum in 2024, especially in rural, agrarian constituencies, where voters wanted to teach Arvind Kejriwal and Narendra Modi a lesson and Amritpal became a vehicle for that anger.” His Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De) later contested the Tarn Taran Assembly bypoll but lost.
The BJP has failed to build an independent electoral presence in Punjab, either in seats or in vote share, notwithstanding its 24-year alliance with the SAD. In other States, the BJP has created a record of starting out as a weaker ally to a strong regional party and gradually growing into the dominant force. The did not happen in Punjab.
Ashutosh Kumar, professor of political science at Panjab University, Chandigarh, argued in his study “The 2024 Parliamentary Elections and Punjab Politics: Commonalities, Exceptionalism, and Takeaways” (published in the Journal of Sikh & Punjāb Studies in 2024) that the BJP is likely to remain a force in Punjab despite its electoral setbacks. But its growth, he noted, will depend on whether it can move beyond cultural nationalism and religious mobilisation, take clearer positions on issues concerning Punjab and Sikhs, and shed its anti-farmer image. The party also needs stronger State-level leadership, he argued, as its national leaders have little traction in Punjab and leaders brought in from the Congress, including Captain Amarinder Singh, Sunil Jakhar, and Manpreet Badal, have failed to give it the political momentum it needs.
The Congress, unlike the SAD and the BJP, is not trying to build a new political base. Notwithstanding its crushing 2022 defeat, the party retained a State-wide organisation and a large social coalition. Its seven Lok Sabha seats in 2024 offered enough evidence that voters who abandoned the party in 2022 had not necessarily moved beyond it.
Kumar observed that the Congress has retained a cross-community base that can become electorally decisive if the AAP’s support continues to erode. According to him, the Congress managed to retain its old social base at a time when political loyalties were becoming fragmented in Punjab.
Sekhon explained why the Congress has an advantage: “Today, the AAP is no longer the outsider that promised to disrupt Punjab’s established political order. It is the incumbent defending its record. While others are caught in some major crisis or the other, the Congress has returned to being a principal challenger, its most comfortable role in Punjab.”
The Congress, meanwhile, has sought to contain factionalism by bringing in Sachin Pilot as Punjab in-charge and former Indian hockey team captain and three-time MLA Pargat Singh as State Congress president. “The combination has helped control the strife to a great extent,” Sekhon said.
Harjeshwar Pal Singh, a professor of history, also said that the Congress has a solid base in Punjab. “It has a presence in almost every district, every village, and every mohalla. It has leaders known across the State,” he said. “That is a strength which cannot be created overnight and other parties currently lack it.”
The Punjab edge
This will be the first State election in northern India since the Cockroach Janata Party(CJP) protests forced the Modi government to confront a series of political controversies. The agitation against the former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and then the protests over voter exclusions through the Special Intensive Revision have added to the political goodwill of Rahul Gandhi, as Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, and of the Congress as the major opposition party.
Uttar Pradesh, like Punjab, will also go to the polls next year. But in Uttar Pradesh, the Congress remains one among several political players. The BJP, the Samajwadi Party, and the Bahujan Samaj Party all have considerable influence in the Uttar Pradesh contest. Punjab is different.
Politics in Uttar Pradesh is influenced by politics at the national level. In contrast, Punjab has remained more immune to national developments. “Punjab has never been swayed by the ‘national constituency phenomenon’, attempted earlier by the Congress and now by the BJP, both polity wideparties,” Professor Ashutosh Kumar wrote in his 2024 study. “The latter’s repeated attempts to contest elections on national issues like national security, Article 370, citizenship, exalted status of India on the global stage, has not cut much ice in the State. On the contrary, even in the Lok Sabha elections, local issues like drugs, mafia hold, the farming sector distress, have remained decisive.”
He added: “At a time when there has been a growing perception about a large-scale ideological shift from middle to right-wing conservatism, visible in the ascendance of cultural nationalism in the plains and hills of north, central, and western India, Punjab again seems immune from it, despite having a sizeable Hindu population.”
That distinctiveness, in addition to Punjab’s social composition, has created a natural advantage for the Congress. Unlike other political parties, the Congress has usually drawn support across Sikh, Hindu, and Dalit constituencies.
“Punjab, along with Kerala, is a State that is most productive for the Congress because it is a catch-all party,” explained Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “It does not cater to one particular social group. It has historically brought different identities into the same political coalition.”
No room for complacence
The Congress may have emerged as the principal challenger to the AAP, but the voters who want the AAP out still have to decide which party they believe can replace it. This is where this election differs from the 2022 election, as Sekhon explained: “The 2022 election was altogether different. People had an option then that was relatively free of the political record of the established parties. This time, almost all the parties are sailing in the same waters. It’s not a vote for the best party but a choice of lesser evil.”
That difference could have implications for the Congress’ prospects.
“The biggest advantage of the Congress is that it does not have to convince Punjab to accept it as a political force,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “The question is whether it can convince different social and religious groups that they have a common political interest in bringing the Congress back.”
The calculation could also become particularly important among Punjab’s floating voters who have repeatedly shifted their loyalties. “Punjab’s floating voter is not necessarily looking for the party with the strongest ideology,” said Sekhon. “She is looking at which party can actually form the government. Once the voter starts believing that one party has the capacity to win, the floating vote begins moving in that direction.”
That is where the Congress’ rise as the principal opposition becomes electorally significant. It makes the party a plausible choice for voters who want to punish the AAP but may not be entirely sure of whom they want to reward, said Sekhon.
Yet, there is no room for complacence. “The Congress cannot assume that every voter who is unhappy with the AAP will automatically come to it,” said Jagtar Singh. “Punjab has shown many times that people can reject one party without necessarily choosing the traditional alternative. The Congress has to make itself the obvious alternative. If the voter thinks there is uncertainty about the Congress, the anti-government vote can still be divided.”
There is also a limit to what Rahul Gandhi can do for the party. His confrontation with the Modi government and his association with the farmers’ cause have given the Congress an additional political resonance in Punjab. But the Assembly election will eventually be decided on questions of local relevance.
“Rahul Gandhi can create a political atmosphere, but the Punjab election will be fought by the State leadership,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “People will ask who is going to run Punjab, what they will do about drugs, employment, farming, and law and order. The Congress has to give them an answer that is bigger than simply defeating the AAP.”
Indeed, an anti-incumbency vote many not be easy to consolidate. “People in Punjab defeat a party, they don’t elect a party,” said Jagtar Singh. “They can decide that a government has to go without having already decided which party should replace it.”
Zaid Bin Shabir is a journalist based in Srinagar.

title: O.P. Sharma: Remembering India's last pictorialist
description: Exploring the life, experiments and enduring legacy of O.P. Sharma.
author: Rahaab Allana
content:
The revelation, if it comes at all, will come in a small fraction of a second with an unconscious gesture, a gleam of the eye, a brief lifting of the mask that all humans wear to conceal their innermost selves from the world. In that fleeting interval of opportunity the photographer must act or lose his prize. —Yousuf Karsh
A woman emerging through the surface of a painting as if stepping out of a dream; a shipwreck that seems to etch a moment from W.H. Auden’s elegiac poetry; a black cat fixates on the viewer, apparition-like, in a graveyard, much like a frame lifted from a Murakami novella; angular shards of light create anthropomorphic forms at the Ellora caves; supernatural beams of light emanate from a portrait, like in a 1980s sci-fi film poster; as Bismillah Khan is lost in a rhapsodic trance, a musical instrument materialises like a mirage around him. Such is the ethereal image-making of O.P. Sharma, widely regarded as India’s last pictorialist. He passed away on November 6, at the age of 89, in Delhi.
Just a few weeks ago, while viewing “Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography” at the Tate Modern in London, I stood enraptured, once again, in front of a work by him from the 1960s. It was profoundly moving to see this master artisan, portraitist, and technical wizard in the company of some of the world’s greatest image-makers. The recognition was timely though long overdue—and yet it left me wanting more. More images and a suitable commendation.
My own deep interest in his oeuvre had been initiated through his 1998 solo exhibition catalogue, presented by Art Heritage gallery in Delhi, authored by the prolific critic of his time, K.B. Goel. Later, in 2010, pictorialism as a field became a disciplinary concern, while I was co-curating “The Artful Pose: Early Studio Photography in Mumbai (c. 1855–1940),” which included atmospheric images from the 19th and early 20th centuries, at the city’s Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Museum. And finally, in 2020, after persistent efforts, and some absurd coincidences (there was another younger artist of the same name at Triveni Kala Sangam whom I had mistakenly scheduled to meet), I was extremely privileged to have, finally and formally, encountered “O.P.” at his home in Bharati Artists’ Colony in Delhi’s trans-Yamuna area.
Interestingly, the colony came into being some decades after artists resettled in Delhi post-Partition; among them were B.C. Sanyal, Kanwal and Devayani Krishna, Dhanraj Bhagat, and P.N. Mago, who in 1949 founded the Delhi Silpi Chakra, a mutual-aid society and salon for artists (Satish Gujral and Richard Bartholomew would join it later). Born from a desire to retreat from the city centre, the colony paired homes with attached studios to give artists an ideal environment for creative productivity.
Nervously excited at the prospect of an engagement with the genius, I arrived for our meeting accompanied by my friend, Srinivas Kuruganti, former photo editor of TheCaravan. O.P. ji sat at one end of the living room, lamplight illuminating his profile; on the wall next to him was a garlanded photograph of his late wife/creative partner, Chitrangada, daughter of the very same noted modernist artists, Kanwal and Devyani Krishna. Surrounded by black-and-white prints, photo catalogues and books, he was peering intently at a newspaper article. He looked up at us from under those distinctive bushy eyebrows, smiled a welcome. Srinivas soon started filming. O.P. spoke about photography as the bedrock of his personal and professional life, ending almost every sentence with a mild ironic “samjhe?” (do you understand?) For many months, Srinivas and I contemplated whether he had endearingly named us “Sanjay”.
What attracted me most to O.P.’s thought and ethic was his unwavering conviction that photography as a craft and profession was most intensively developed by the passionate, dedicated, largely self-taught practitioner. As he remarked in a 2020 interview (to Diva Gujral), “Pictorial photography is the mother of all branches of photography”; and its biggest contributors are amateurs “who spend their time, money, energy and their life to discover new things”. And he was absolutely firm on how images should be “made”—not just “taken”—and developed: as analogue prints, with each frame pictorially conceptualised before the shot, and with desired effects created in the darkroom.
****
Over the years, it was clear that O.P. ji needed to be adequately recognised. And so, immersive discussions began in connection with the Alkazi Foundation’s planned tribute (in partnership with Art Heritage gallery) to his work at Shridharani Gallery in Delhi, in an exhibition titled “O.P. Sharma and the Fine Art of Photography: 1950s-1990s” (2024). This moment brought us—Sukanya Baskar (the assigned lead curator) and me (her collaborator)—into close contact with O.P. time and again, and to those nearest to him, his son and daughter-in-law, Aseem Sharma and Mohita Junnarkar, dedicated and loving caregivers.
After each session we were treated to delicious cutlets and samosas from a Nathu’s outlet in the neighbourhood. It was very rewarding to eventually open his show on Teacher’s Day, in the very same gallery which had hosted his first exhibition in 1963. O.P. eventually spent days at the exhibition, interacting with former students and conducting walkthroughs. We observed how he had touched the lives of so many in the city. They all came to pay their respects and absorb his astute observations on image-making.
Fascinating insights
Discussions with O.P. ji yielded fascinating insights. O.P.’s engagement with the medium began in 1954, inspired by the work of Armenian-Canadian photographer Yousuf Karsh (opening quote) at an international exhibition hosted by the UP Amateur Photographic Association in Lucknow. During his university studies there, a physics professor taught him to develop black-and-white film, triggering his lifelong obsession with the darkroom and technical experimentation; he gave up fine arts and committed himself to photography. “My interest grew, and eventually, my naani [maternal grandmother] presented me with a twin-lens reflex German camera but she also told me she could not spend any more money on this. Therefore, I used to walk from my home to the college, to save four annas to buy film and paper,” O.P. recalled in a 2018 interview. He learnt aspects of the craft from senior members of the Lucknow Camera Club.
Arriving in Delhi in 1958, O.P. ji joined Modern School as a teacher; he set up its photography unit and darkroom, and began a four-decade career during which he trained generations of students and furthered his own professional excellence. His future father-in-law, Kanwal Krishna, taught art at the school; its director, the prolific M.N. Kapur, himself an enthusiastic lensman, was an anchor. The Kapur daughters, Geeta (later a renowned art critic) and Anuradha (later a renowned theatre director) posed for O.P., who spent endless hours in his studio and the school darkroom, absorbed in technical experiments. Modern School is just down the road from Mandi House, Delhi’s hub of cultural venues where greats from every discipline—theatre, classical music and dance, literature, visual arts—regularly performed; concerts were also frequently held on the school campus. O.P. photographed many virtuosos on stage and invited them to his studio to sit for portraits—portraiture was a genre in which his skills found sublime expression.
O.P.’s Rasa Bhava Darshan project—an extended collaboration with the veteran Bombay theatre/film actor Sajjan Lal Purohit, completed in phases between 1960 and the mid-1970s— drew on Manmohan Ghosh’s translation of Bharat Muni’s Sanskrit treatise Natya Shastra to visualise the eight primary rasas and 49 bhavas of classical Indian aesthetics as a photographic portrait series. Working with scholar/dramaturge Brij Vallabh Mishra, Sajjan posed while O.P. photographed; the massive suite of images was entirely shot in the actor’s home.
A selection was exhibited between 1979 and 1980. In the exhibition brochure, O.P. described his use of Miranda and Asahi Pentax 35mm cameras, 500-watt photoflood lamps, and natural light to play with tonal values of grey; the images were finalised in a Kodak D-23 developer, and printed on Agfa-Gevaert paper. This stunning series was published as a book in 1998, and was meant to be rendered as a 25-minute film on 16 mm, incorporating paintings by Ram Kumar. It was through Sajjan that O.P. and Chitrangada found work in the Indian film industry; the couple created publicity stills for Do Boond Pani (1971); Siddhartha (1972); Chhupa Rustam (1973); and Shalimar (1978).
From 1980 onwards, O.P. ji and Chitrangada directed the Camera Art Institute at Triveni Kala Sangam, the holistic arts institution at Mandi House, conceptualised in 1950 by Sundari Shridharani and Uday Shankar. O.P. ji soon joined, and directed his pedagogy towards both theory and practice, especially printing and technical processes. Photographer Chandan Gomes, a former student, recalls “looking up in awe at a quiet, scholarly gentleman” with “immaculately combed hair, a gentle smile and a piercing gaze”, who “spoke with a calm certainty that made you listen to him with complete concentration” (“Remembering the Photographic Legacy of O.P. Sharma” by Chandan Gomes, published in Critical Collective on October 24, 2024).
Echoes of Surrealism
The restrained demeanour belied O.P.’s rigour; he was a perfectionist and formidable taskmaster, and those who could not grasp principles of optics to the required high level failed the course. Sifting one day through the papers in his studio with Sukanya Baskar, we found pages liberally marked in red ballpoint, with words and phrases enthusiastically circled and underlined.
Through the 1980s, he explored camera-less techniques of image production: controlling light or using chemicals to imprint photosensitive paper and create photograms, photomontages, sodium sulphite prints and collages. This radical experimentation echoed Western movements of the 1920s such as Surrealism and New Vision, and O.P. became known for his invention of what he called the “C-effect”, which produced distinct swirl patterns and infused the image with movement. He also wrote do-it-yourself instruction manuals in English and Hindi. And to O.P. goes the credit for having August 19—the day the French government officially announced the invention of the daguerreotype by chemist-artist Louis Daguerre in 1839—declared as World Photography Day in 1991. He had personally written to as many as 200 photographic societies, artists, and institutions around the world to gain support for this cause.
Along with technological innovation and teaching, and in alignment with his belief in his medium as a social and cultural good, O.P. devoted much time and energy to founding photography groups in different cities and promoting their work. These included the Amateur Photographic Society of Agra (1959), the Foto Arte Group (1974), and the India International Photographic Council (IIPC), established in 1983 and active to this day. The IIPC organised educational workshops, published a monthly journal, and created spaces for discussion, critique and documentation, thus ensuring custodianship of pictorialist legacies.
This last-mentioned endeavour acquired great significance in the context of the intense ongoing debate between Indian photographers and photojournalists about the primacy of genre: the value, necessity, and relevance of documentary realism versus those of pictorialism. Jury members of the First Indian Biennale of Photography, organised by the Lalit Kala Akademi in 1989, included O.P.’s close associate T. Kasinath, the then Director of the Photo Division of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, who actively pushed for the recognition of pictorial photography. However, submissions to the Second Indian Biennale of Creative Photography in 1993, in which O.P. participated, clearly indicated that despite methodological and thematic expansion, pictorialism as an aesthetic choice was now on the wane.
O.P. had long considered contemporary photography to be awash with misconceptions—about the digital era, about rules of composition, about the intricate analogue grammar now seemingly lost to point-and-shoot generations. “If a photograph is technically poor, it is only half a photograph. Unless you understand each and every part of the photographic process—from pressing the shutter to producing the final print—you can’t produce a good image,” he declared in a 2018 interview. Kodak founder George Eastman’s famous tagline, “You press the button, we do the rest”, was read by O.P. as an admission that many of us do nothing but mechanically press buttons.
The last few years have been special. I was honoured to guest-edit Aperture magazine’s Delhi issue in 2021, titled Looking Out, Looking In. The master’s dazzling, mesmeric portrait of Geeta Kapur, embodying both his technical virtuosity and creative philosophy, was selected by the Aperture editors for the cover. “A photograph on its own is like an uncut diamond,” he remarked as we reviewed captions for his 2024 tribute show. “Only when you understand every part of the photographic process—as Ansel Adams and Edward Weston did—and refine and polish the stone, does it become a Kohinoor!”
Rahaab Allana is Curator/Publisher, Alkazi Foundation for the Arts, New Delhi.

title: Thiruparankundram Deepam Row: 1923 court decree declared Hill temple property, dargah had rights over three specific areas, Deepathoon outside its land
description: A century of judicial rulings, from the 1923 civil court decree to the 2025 Madras High Court order, clarified the temple's ownership of Thiruparankundram hill, the Dargah's limited property rights and the Deepathoon's location outside Dargah land. | OpIndia News
author: Jinit Jain
content:
A controversy erupted earlier today after the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government defied the Supreme Court-mandated order to light the Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai and instead lighted the traditional lamp at its usual spot, triggering outrage among the Hindu population. The Hindu outfits slammed the Vijay government, criticizing it for what they called a brazen display of Muslim appeasement.
The issue has, nevertheless, brought renewed attention to a century-old legal dispute between the Subramaniya Swamy Temple and the Sikkandar Badusha Dargah. Historical court records reveal that a civil court declared the temple the owner of Thiruparankundram hill in 1923, while recognising the Dargah’s ownership and possession of certain specific areas and structures. The original decree was subsequently restored by the Privy Council in 1931.
The legal history has assumed significance amid the latest dispute over the traditional lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar situated on the upper reaches of the hill.
A detailed account of the century-old litigation was reproduced in the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court’s June 24, 2025 judgment in a batch of petitions concerning Thiruparankundram hill.
How the dispute between the temple and Dargah began
The dispute dates back to 1917, when the Sikkandar Badusha Dargah proposed constructing a mandapam on Thiruparankundram hill. The Subramaniya Swamy Temple objected to the construction, asserting that the entire hill belonged to the temple.
The temple subsequently instituted a civil suit, initially numbered O.S. No. 101 of 1917, which was later renumbered as O.S. No. 4 of 1920 before the First Additional Subordinate Judge, Madurai.
The temple sought a declaration of ownership over the entire hill, an injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with its possession and recovery of possession of certain portions of the property. The Dargah and the government were among the defendants in the proceedings.
After examining the rival claims, the civil court delivered its decree on August 25, 1923, recognising the temple’s ownership and possession of the hill, subject to specific exceptions.
What the 1923 civil court decree said about ownership
The decree made an important distinction between the temple’s ownership of the hill and the rights of the Muslim defendants over particular portions.
The court declared the Subramaniya Swamy Temple the owner and possessor of the whole of Thiruparankundram hill and the Giri Veedhi, except certain assessed and occupied lands, Nellithope, the new mandapam, the flight of steps leading from Nellithope to the mosque and the top rock on which the mosque and the Muslim flagstaff stood.
The court separately recognised the Muslim defendants as owners and in possession of Nellithope, everything situated within it, the flight of steps, the new mandapam and the entire top of the hillock on which the mosque and flagstaff stood.
The decree also recognised the Kasi Viswanathaswamy Temple and its sacred water body as belonging to the Hindu temple.
Thus, the civil court recognised the temple’s ownership over the hill while protecting the Dargah’s rights over specifically identified properties and structures. It did not declare the Dargah the owner of the entire hill.
How the Privy Council restored the temple’s ownership decree in 1931
The Dargah challenged the civil court’s decision by filing First Appeal No. 34 of 1924 before the Madras High Court. On May 4, 1926, the High Court dismissed the Dargah’s appeal while allowing a cross-appeal filed by the government.
The Subramaniya Swamy Temple subsequently approached the Privy Council in Appeal No. 5 of 1930.
On May 12, 1931, the Privy Council allowed the temple’s appeal and restored the original decree passed by the Subordinate Judge on August 25, 1923.
The Privy Council observed that the temple had established its possession over the unoccupied portions of the hill from time immemorial and that its authorities had consistently treated the property as belonging to the temple.
It concluded that the original Subordinate Judge had arrived at the correct decision and that there was no sufficient ground to disturb the decree.
The Privy Council consequently set aside the Madras High Court’s decree and restored the original civil court judgment.
Subsequent disputes over the hill
The litigation did not end with the Privy Council’s decision.
In 1958, the temple instituted another civil suit, O.S. No. 111 of 1958, seeking an injunction against the removal of stones from portions of the hill outside Nellithope and the assessed and occupied areas.
The trial court passed a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from cutting stones from the specified portions. It also directed that the exact location and extent of Nellithope and the assessed and occupied areas be determined through further proceedings.
The decree was modified by the District Court in 1961, which directed that the boundaries be identified through a survey commission.
Further proceedings followed in subsequent years, reflecting continuing disagreements over the precise extent of the properties and the respective rights of the parties.
What is the present dispute over Thiruparankundram Deepathoon?
The historical ownership dispute has acquired renewed significance because of the controversy over the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon.
The Subramaniya Swamy Temple, situated at the foothills of Thiruparankundram, is one of the six sacred abodes of Lord Murugan. The Sikkandar Badusha Dargah is situated on the hilltop, while a Shiva temple and Jain religious remains are also found on the hill.
The present controversy centres on the demand by Hindu organisations and devotees to light the traditional Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar situated near the Dargah.
Hindu organisations maintain that the pillar is situated on temple-owned land and that lighting the ceremonial lamp there is part of the religious tradition associated with the hill. They cite historical civil court decrees and the Privy Council’s decision to support their position.
The Dargah and Muslim organisations have opposed the proposed lighting at the location, citing its proximity to their place of worship. The dispute has consequently involved questions concerning property boundaries, access, religious practices and the respective rights of the temple and the Dargah.
The controversy reached the courts again in 2025. In its June 24 judgment, the Madras High Court’s Madurai Bench examined several petitions concerning religious practices at the Dargah, including animal sacrifice, prayers and gatherings.
The two-judge bench delivered separate opinions on the issues, resulting in a split verdict and a reference to the Chief Justice for further proceedings. The judgment also discussed the historical civil court decrees recognising the rights of both parties over specified portions of the hill.
December 2025 Madras High Court order: Deepathoon does not fall within Dargah property
Then in December 2025, Justice G.R. Swaminathan of the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court allowed a batch of petitions seeking permission to light the ceremonial lamp at the ancient Deepathoon on Thiruparankundram hill.
The judge extensively examined the 1923 civil court decree and the Privy Council’s subsequent decision. He held that the Muslim community’s ownership rights extended to only three specific portions of the hill: Nellithope, the flight of steps leading to the mosque and the actual site on which the mosque stands.
The rest of the hill, including its unoccupied portions, belonged to the temple’s Devasthanam.
Rejecting the argument that the petitioners should approach a civil court again for fresh demarcation of the property, Justice Swaminathan observed that the boundaries of Nellithope had already been determined through earlier proceedings. Since the Deepathoon was not situated within Nellithope, there was no requirement to reopen the ownership dispute.
The judge also made an important observation about the geographical location of the Deepathoon.
Thiruparankundram hill has two peaks. The Sikkandar Badusha Dargah and mosque are situated on the higher peak, while the Deepathoon is located on the lower peak, at a distance of at least 50 metres from the mosque.
Justice Swaminathan noted that the Dargah had a compound wall and that the Deepathoon was situated outside it, on an unoccupied portion of the hill. He concluded that the pillar belonged exclusively to the temple.
The judge observed that the entire upper portion of the hill did not belong to the Dargah and that the earlier judgments had already settled the ownership question.
He further noted that the Devasthanam could reach the Deepathoon by climbing steps from the Nellithope area, with the temple having the benefit of an earlier injunction protecting its access.
Court says lighting the Deepam is necessary to protect temple property
Justice Swaminathan went beyond examining the historical ownership dispute and addressed the temple administration’s responsibility to protect its property.
He observed that refusing to light the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon could undermine the temple’s ability to assert its ownership over the unoccupied portions of the hill.
The judge noted that despite the 1923 decree and the subsequent Privy Council ruling clarifying the ownership rights, there had been attempts by the mosque trustees to disturb the existing status quo. He said the temple administration had a responsibility to remain vigilant against any attempts to encroach upon its property.
The court also rejected the argument that lighting the lamp at the Deepathoon would interfere with the religious rights of the Dargah or the Muslim community. It observed that the ceremonial lighting would not affect the Dargah’s structure, which was situated at a safe distance.
Justice Swaminathan held that the temple had a legal duty to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon in addition to the customary location near the Uchipillaiyar Temple.
The court quashed the decision taken by the temple’s Executive Officer to conduct the ritual only at the usual Deepa Mandapam, observing that a decision of such importance should have been taken by the temple’s Trust Board rather than the Executive Officer.
It directed the temple administration to conduct the ritual at the Deepathoon from 2025 onwards and ordered police protection to ensure that it could be performed peacefully.

title: 250-400 Muslims stormed Hindu family’s house, tore women’s clothes, pelted stones: Victims reveal pre-planned attack in Gujarat’s Vadgam, share daily torment – Exclusive Ground Report
description: A Muslim mob attacked a Hindu Rajput family in Vadgam, Gujarat. They assaulted women, and pelted stones at their house. | OpIndia News
author: લિંકન સોખડિયા
content:
A series of attacks on members of the Hindu community in villages falling under the Vadgam Assembly constituency of Gujarat’s Banaskantha district shows no signs of stopping. Notably, Congress leader Jignesh Mevani is an MLA from the constituency.
The recent incident of an attack on young Hindu Dalits for bursting Diwali crackers in Bhagal village of Palanpur taluka is still fresh. Now, another shocking incident has come to light from Teywada village in Vadgam taluka, where a Muslim mob entered the house of a Hindu Rajput family and attempted to assault its members. The attackers also pelted stones and tore the clothes of the women in the house.
The OpIndia Gujarati team reached Tewari village and spoke to the affected women, residents and an injured man undergoing treatment at a private hospital in Palanpur.
The mob entered the house when there were only women and a child sleeping in a crib
When the OpIndia team visited the victim’s house, they found broken windowpanes and signs of damage caused by stone-pelting. Stones were also seen lying around the cradle in which a small child had been sleeping when the incident took place. Fortunately, one of the girls in the family quickly picked up the child, fortunately preventing any injury.
Speaking exclusively to OpIndia, the victim women narrated their ordeal; the family had gone to the fields or were away for work when the attackers arrived. Only women and children were at home at the time.
The victim said: “Initially, five Muslim men came and directly attacked, making provocative remarks like ‘entering the houses of Hindus-Rajputs and robbing them of their girls and women.’ Women who were alone in the house were pushed down, their sarees and blouses were torn off, and attempts were made to strangle them. The T-shirts and clothes of the daughters who were trying to save them were also torn off.”
Another victim said that the incident left her so traumatised that she could not speak for two days.
Victims reveal attack was planned, name two local Muslim men
During the ground report, the affected women and villagers called the attack a planned attack and informed about the role of two local Muslim men: ‘Imran Doctor’ and former village sarpanch ‘Ilyasbhai’.
The victim women further said: “First five people came and attacked, then Imran Doctor and former Sarpanch Ilyasbhai came there. They first turned the people away on the pretext of making peace and removed their four-wheelers parked in the square and put them in a safe place so that their vehicles would not be damaged in the stone pelting. Then a crowd of 250 to 400 people gathered and climbed on the roof and pelted our houses with stones, and Imran Doctor himself incited the crowd to rob the honour of women.”
‘Hindus are being forced to leave their villages due to the lack of houses’
Another victim woman from Teywada village told OpIndia that Hindu families are often harassed because they are fewer in number compared to Muslims living in the village. The villagers said that they are being harassed by throwing garbage on the road, making fun of the Hindu daughters coming and going, and psychologically pressuring them to flee by saying, “You should leave this village and run away.”
Injured man says attackers broke his hand; underwent surgery
The men of the Hindu family have sustained serious injuries in this attack. The elders of the family are admitted to the hospital in serious condition. The OpIndia team also spoke to the injured Hindu man Sureshbhai, who is undergoing treatment at a private hospital in Palanpur.
Sureshbhai said: “While I was outside, my brother called me and said that we had been attacked. As soon as I reached there on my bike, I was attacked with weapons like a hatchet and a spade. I have a fracture in my hand and had to undergo an operation to have a plate inserted, which cost around Rs 1.5 lakh to Rs 1.75 lakh. This attack was not sudden, but was carried out with complete planning.”
Police register complaints from both sides, detain 19 people
OpIndia Gujarati team also contacted the PI of the Chaphi police station to get official details about the entire attack. As per the information given by him over the phone, as he was busy with court proceedings, the police have registered a complaint against both parties in this incident, and so far a total of 19 people from both sides have been detained. Currently, police are deployed in the village, and the situation is peaceful.
Meanwhile, villagers also said that some Hindu youths who were victims of the attack had also been falsely implicated through counter-complaints. They demanded strict action against those seen pelting stones in videos of the incident.
Why are Hindus unsafe in MLA Jignesh Mevani’s constituency?
The incident has also brought attention to the recent cases of violence against Hindus reported from villages in the Vadgam Assembly constituency of Gujarat, represented by Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani.
On the one hand, in Bhagal village, where the Gujarat ATS arrested Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) terrorists in July 2026, Hindu Dalit youths were attacked for bursting firecrackers during Diwali. On the other hand, in Teywada village, a Muslim mob attempted to force its way into the house of a Hindu Rajput family and assaulted the women.
The question arises as to why Jignesh Mevani, the Congress-backed MLA from Vadgam, who delivers speeches across the country invoking the Constitution and advocating Dalit and women’s rights, has remained silent over these attacks on Hindu families and Dalit youths in his own constituency. Are extremist elements in the area receiving political protection to appease a particular vote bank?
While people have confidence in Gujarat’s law and order machinery, there is an urgent need for exemplary and strict action against those accused of assaulting women and carrying out premeditated stone-pelting in Teywada village. The viral video of the incident should also be examined as part of the investigation.
(Note: This article is a translation of the original article published on OpIndia Gujarati. The complete ground report of Teywada village can be viewed on OpIndia Gujarati’s YouTube channel.)

title: From ‘Rainbow Warriors’ to Cockroach Janta Party: How a 1962 Christian tract reached Goa’s land fight in 2026
description: The ideological journey from the 1962 *Warriors of the Rainbow* publication to Greenpeace and Goa’s activist networks has found a new political expression in the Cockroach Janta Party’s campaign against Section 39A. | OpIndia News
category: Featured, News Reports, OpIndia Explains, Opinions
author: आशीष नौटियाल
content:
You’ve probably gotten used to reading a certain kind of news on your phone and in the newspapers — where every time there’s a new face, a new slogan, and a new “environment” or “people’s movement” story. Sometimes someone says the trees and rivers must be saved, sometimes someone stands up to stop development in the name of heritage, and sometimes suddenly some strange-sounding NGOs and political parties hit the streets over Goa’s land and Section 39A.
You smile and say, “Arre, this is democracy. Such protests keep happening in every state.”
But just stop for a moment and flip through the pages of history and geopolitics. Whenever in any country, any society, or any sensitive geography the script of a “movement” is written from outside, and it is brought down to the ground wearing the mask of “local people’s concerns,” it doesn’t remain just a protest. It becomes the next episode of a long game. And today we will examine that entire ideological chain, that network, and that blueprint which starts from a book in 1962, goes through Greenpeace, some faces of the Church, civil society NGOs, and stops at the ‘Cockroach Janta Party’ that reached Goa in November 2026.
And yes, before we land on Goa’s soil, it is very important to remind you of an old point. In the context of the Cockroach Janta Party, i.e. CJP, we have talked about this earlier — how Gene Sharp’s book From Dictatorship to Democracy became the blueprint for regime change operations from the Arab Spring to many places around the world. How the so-called non-violence, civil resistance, and “people’s voice” vocabulary is used to bring about a change of power, which we call the regime-change blueprint. The same model was also adopted by CJP when they came down to Jantar Mantar… Now another aspect appears to be getting added to the same chain — a book that was painted in the colours of Christian faith and spiritual enlightenment, and which later gave climate activism such an ideological and spiritual cloak that asking questions in front of it is considered “unethical” or “anti-people.”
Let’s begin from America in 1962. That year a small book is published — Warriors of the Rainbow. The writers are William Willoya and Vinson Brown. Willoya was a Christian preacher, and Brown was the owner of Naturegraph Publishers. The biggest story sold about this book was that it was some “ancient Native American prophecy.” Whereas the reality is that it was not any ancient tribal tradition, but an evangelical Christian tract. Meaning, it was simply a small book for Christian preaching.
What was written in the book? That when the earth will be in crisis, trees will start drying up, rivers will turn black, then people of different colours — red, white, yellow and black — will unite and become ‘Rainbow Warriors’ and save the earth. It sounds very poetic and cute. But its real purpose was not to save tribal traditions, but was linked to Christian spiritual awakening.
Many scholars call it a “fake folklore.” In the real traditions of tribes like the Hopi, Cree or Lakota, there is no solid basis for it. Still, it was promoted as “ancient knowledge.” Some people honestly believed it to be true, and some carried it forward as a notion and an idea.
Now look at the 1970s. This idea reaches Greenpeace. One of the early and influential members of Greenpeace was Bob Hunter. He read this book and made it the spiritual foundation of his movement. The slogan “We are Rainbow Warriors” gave climate activism a global identity, and that identity was “We are all one.”
This is where a big change came. Protecting the environment was no longer just a matter of policy, science or economy. A mysterious, biblical and spiritual claim got attached to it. When any issue takes the form of a ‘mission’ or ‘faith’, its methods also change. Now a whole chain starts becoming visible — an idea that came out of a Christian tract, global climate activism built from it, and then the same language and framing descends into local movements.
Now the same language reaches Goa. Around 2014, the name of Abhijit Prabhudesai and the ‘Federation of Rainbow Warriors’ comes to the fore in Goa. In an interview given to Civil Society magazine, he himself said that this name was taken from the vision of the American natives. His roots were linked to the organisation of Goa’s farmers, but the framing was global. He said that “the circle of life has broken. People will unite and protest. They will be called Rainbow Warriors.”
Prabhudesai and his team ran several big campaigns in Goa — against mining, against coal transportation and double tracking, the Amche Mollem movement, against the Coastal Zone Plan, against the Tamnar power line and highway expansion. Names like Diana Tavares, Siddharth Karapurkar, Jose Coutinho, Leah Gomes, Vilma Dias kept appearing repeatedly. The argument was that development should not happen without the consent of the people, and gram sabhas should be heard.
During this period, some priests of the Church also appeared active. Father Bolmax Fidelis Pereira, parish priest of Chicalim. He was a botanist, a teacher, and also an environmental activist. His range did not seem limited to just one issue. About five months ago he was seen promoting CJP, expressing anger against the central government, and remember, this was the same period when many activists, along with the Church, were registering their anger against the FCRA bill and language like fatwas was also coming out.
He remained one of the prominent faces who connected the youth in the ‘Amche Mollem’ movement. He remained active in the opposition to coal and double tracking. In 2026, he stood with the people of Palem-Siridao at Azad Maidan in opposition to Section 39A. He said “Enough is Enough” and called land conversion a threat to ecology.
In May 2026, at the age of 50, this eco-father’s Ram Naam Satya happened. Goa’s environmental movements themselves called him the ‘eco-priest’. Orville Dourado Rodrigues of Goyancho Ekvott had called him the ‘driving force’ who raised the youth, and Abhijit Prabhudesai also often mentioned his absence. Father Albano Fernandes also participated in the protests at Azad Maidan. Of course, no official statement comes from the Church institutionally, but the continuous activity of some priests at the personal level points towards a pattern. The question is that whenever a big movement happens in Goa regarding land, mining or ecology, why do some faces connected to the Church keep appearing in the centre again and again?
Is this only personal sentiment, or is it part of a larger network that becomes active on every sensitive issue with a fixed script?
In the same chronology, an organisation named ‘Enough is Enough’ also comes forward. Former Chief Justice of Allahabad High Court Ferdino Rebello is its leader. In a way, these are the angry uncles of the Prashant Bhushan type of this organisation. Names like Claude Alvares and Norma Alvares (founders of Goa Foundation), Devidas Amonkar, Elvis Gomes, Govind Shirodkar, Swapnesh Sherlekar are connected to it. The demand was made that Section 39A and 17(2) be abolished. A ten-point charter was made, and proposals were passed in several gram sabhas including Palem-Siridao, Tivim, Aldona, Assagao.
Now understand a subtlety here. In some villages of Goa, some Hindu names also appear standing in opposition. In Aldona and Assagao there is a large Catholic population, while in Tivim there is a Hindu majority. Meaning, the same community is not everywhere on the ground. But the organisational structure and ideological leadership of the movement appears to come out of those same civil society networks that have already been active in climate activism. Goa Foundation, Rainbow Warriors, Goyancho Ekvott — these names keep circling in the same circle again and again.
Now it is also necessary to know what the real debate regarding Section 39A is. It is part of the Goa Town and Country Planning Act. The government says that this is a step to permanently protect eco-sensitive areas. Those opposing say that this will benefit the builders and put Goa’s identity in danger. Both sides have their arguments. The problem arises when the same network, the same language and the same framework is applied to every new project.
And then comes November 2026… ‘Cockroach Janta Party’ enters Goa. The founder is Abhijit Dipke, from Aurangabad in Maharashtra, Dalit background, supposedly studied from Boston University, earlier worked in the social media team of the Aam Aadmi Party. On CJI’s statement, the post “What if all cockroaches come together?” went viral, CJP was formed, the ‘Kya Bolti Public’ campaign started, and as soon as they reached Goa the first priority was declared — and that is to abolish Section 39A.
Dipke says that “If 39A remains, Goa will not remain. Goenkars will not remain.” He raises questions on the Karapur project, talks about the nexus of builders and leaders, and says that “Goa is Goa because of its people, not because of builders.” Names like Saurabh Das and Ashutosh Ranka are associated with him, who call themselves ‘watchdogs’ and say that changing the government is not the goal.
But just think! A person whose political journey has been linked to the Aam Aadmi Party, Delhi and Maharashtra, whose launching happens directly from abroad to Delhi, who are a direct part of the regime-change mould of Gene Sharp’s book’s CANVAS… why does he suddenly make Goa’s land and Section 39A the biggest issue of his campaign? Is this the own voice of Goa’s youth, or a new political form of the already running civil society and activist network?
Here the entire story of the changing of the idea and its execution becomes visible. The fakelore of ‘Rainbow Warriors’ that came out of the 1962 Christian book, then Greenpeace’s global climate activism, then Abhijit Prabhudesai’s local version in Goa, the participation of some priests connected to the Church, the organised opposition of organisations like Goa Foundation and ‘Enough is Enough’, and now the same issue being adopted by a new political group with Aam Aadmi Party background.
This is a complete ecosystem. In it there is the framing of “Save the Earth,” the language of calling development “loot,” and the art of connecting external ideas and new political faces in the name of protecting local identity. People of Congress and AAP are also seen in the protests, CJP calls itself independent, but the way of choosing issues shows the same old network.
Now another important question, which is often ignored. When accusations of “looting the land” are being levelled against the government and builders in opposition to Section 39A, then one must also remember those cases related to land in Goa where serious allegations were made against the Church or officials connected to it. Some time ago the ED filed a chargesheet against two former procurators of the Archdiocese of Goa and Daman — Father Arlino de Melo and Father Victor Conceicao Rodrigues.
According to the investigating agency, on a tenanted land of about 2,479 square metres in Caranzalem, the name of the Archdiocese was registered through forged documents, and in 2007 that land was sold to Models Real Estate Developers for just 61.97 lakh rupees, from which later allegedly more than 27 crore rupees of ‘proceeds of crime’ were generated and properties were attached. Before this, the case of Vanxim Island had also come forward, where there was local opposition on the allegations of selling tenanted land to a resort developer, although the Church rejected the allegations.
These examples show that the story of land deals and irregularities is actually completely opposite to the image that these Church fathers are planting along with CJP. When a special narrative is created in the name of ‘saving Goa’s land’, then it is necessary to also put these old cases and facts forward so that the picture does not remain incomplete.
Now look at this entire pattern a little bigger, in the national context. This is not an isolated incident. Lift the timeline and see — in Nicobar attempts are made to stop big projects in the name of saving turtles, at the time of Vizhinjam port fatwa-like things come out from the Church’s side, in Lakshadweep Muslims did opposition, and now the same pattern is being repeated around Section 39A in Goa.
Why is this a matter of concern? Why is this a warning bell for India? Because when in strategic, coastal and sensitive areas the same kind of opposition keeps rising again and again regarding development, infrastructure and laws, its impact does not remain limited to just one project or one state. The capacity of the state starts looking weak, the possibilities of investment and employment get affected, and most of all, an artificial polarisation and distrust is created within the local society.
Goa’s identity is not just mountains, fields and sea. The livelihood, education, health and better opportunities of the people there are equally important. If every development is rejected by calling it “builders’ loot,” then where will the opportunities for the youth come from?
The story is the same, from ‘Rainbow Warriors’ to ‘Cockroach’. Only the faces change, the names change, and the issue changes. But the framework remains the same… the umbilical cord of the ecosystem remains the same…
Let the people of Goa themselves decide what kind of future they want. But before taking the decision it is necessary to understand where this idea came from, why this name was chosen, and which network is working behind it. Because until we recognise the ideological frameworks and strategies hidden behind words and slogans, until then some new ‘warrior’ or new ‘watchdog’ will keep coming and deciding the direction of our own story on our own land.

title: Delhi Airport Airside Bus Service Between T1 And T2/T3 May Start In March-April 2027: Report
description: Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA) may have to wait until March or April 2027 for an interim airside bus service connecting Terminal 1
author: Arjun Brij
content:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 01:58 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA) may have to wait until March or April 2027 for an interim airside bus service connecting Terminal 1 with Terminals 2 and 3, prolonging the difficulties faced by passengers transferring between terminals, a Times of India report stated.
The service is awaiting security clearance, while the proposed automated air train connecting the airport’s terminals is not expected to become operational before December 2030.
The proposed bus service is being held up by approval from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), which has been pending since the summer. Although the airport operator has completed the necessary arrangements, winter fog and low visibility could make the launch difficult, officials said.
“The airport operator is hopeful of getting a BCAS nod as all arrangements have been made. Due to low visibility in winter, this may not be the right time to start the bus service inside the airport perimeter,” officials were quoted as saying by TOI.
The buses will operate within the airport's airside perimeter, allowing passengers to avoid city roads when transferring between T1 and T2/T3.
At present, travellers rely on Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) buses running outside the airport, where congestion during peak hours can delay connections.
Passengers transferring between T2 and T3 will continue using the existing city-side walking route or shuttle arrangements, as the two terminals are located close to each other.

title: JLN Stadium Confirmed As Key Transfer Point Between Kochi Metro's Blue And Pink Lines From August 2027
description: Kochi Metro Rail Limited has finalised Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium as the main interchange between its Blue and Pink lines when
author: Arjun Brij
content:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 12:33 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Kochi Metro Rail Ltd (KMRL) has designated Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) Stadium station as the interchange between its existing Blue Line and the upcoming 11.2 km Pink Line, with commuters required to change trains there when Phase 2 opens in August 2027, Times of India reported.
The arrangement will initially mean no direct services between Infopark and Blue Line destinations.
Passengers travelling between Kakkanad, Aluva, Tripunithura and other key locations will be able to use a single ticket for journeys involving both corridors, with JLN Stadium serving as the transfer point.
The Pink Line is expected to cover a km in approximately two minutes. Travel from JLN Stadium to Civil Station is estimated at 12 minutes, while the journey to Infopark will take around 22 minutes.
“As the Pink Line terminates at JLN Stadium, anyone traveling between Phase 1 (Blue Line) and Phase 2 must switch trains there. For example, a passenger going from Infopark to Aluva or Tripunithura will get off at JLN Stadium and board a Blue Line train,” a senior KMRL official was quoted as saying by TOI.
The station's platforms will be arranged to facilitate transfers. Platform 1 will handle departing trains towards Infopark and Aluva, while Platform 2 will accommodate arrivals from both directions.
KMRL may introduce direct Pink Line services to Blue Line destinations in the future by using turnaround tracks at Maharaja’s College or Kadavanthra, depending on passenger demand.
The operator plans to deploy eight of its existing 25 trains on the Pink Line, retaining 17 for the Blue Line. It has also proposed purchasing eight additional trains for Rs 275 crore, expanding its fleet to 33.
The procurement is awaiting funding approvals from the Kerala and Union governments, with possible assistance from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.
Land acquisition near Palarivattom and Padamughal has been completed. The corridor will feature a track arrangement inspired by Chennai Metro, including an elevated crossing near Kurishupally in Palarivattom to allow the Infopark-bound track to cross over the Aluva line.

title: India's Strategic Zojila Tunnel Project 70 Per Cent Complete, Nitin Gadkari Confirms Six To Eight-Month Completion Deadline
description: Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari announced that Asia's longest tunnel project at Zojila will be compl
author: Arjun Brij
content:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 11:45 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari announced that Asia's longest tunnel project at Zojila will be completed within the next six to eight months, with around 70 per cent of the work already finished.
The 13.15 km tunnel achieved a breakthrough on 9 June this year when excavation spanning more than 13 km was completed.
Located on the strategically significant Srinagar-Leh National Highway, the horseshoe-shaped, single-tube, two-lane tunnel measures 9.5 metres wide and 7.57 metres high, constructed at an elevation of around 11,578 feet above sea level.
The entire project, valued at approximately Rs 6,500 crore, spans 31 km, including approach roads and bridges, stretching from Sonmarg to Minimarg.
Once operational, the tunnel will provide year-round, weather-proof connectivity to Ladakh, which remains cut off for several months during winter due to heavy snowfall at the Zojila Pass.
Travel time across the pass will be reduced from between one and 1.5 hours to approximately 15 minutes.
The project, being executed by Hyderabad-based Megha Engineering and Infrastructure Limited using the New Austrian Tunnelling Method, will enhance both civilian and military mobility across the treacherous Zojila Pass, which is typically closed to traffic for nearly three months during winter.

title: Who suggested de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a protest site? Govt gives no answer, cites national security
description: On October 11, the Delhi Police issued a circular which ‘de-notified’ Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
author: Basant Kumar
content:
On October 11, the Delhi Police issued a circular which ‘de-notified’ Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
Amidst protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and various opposition parties demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar last month, the Delhi Police issued a circular.
Dated October 11, the Delhi Police Standing Order, signed by Commissioner Anurag Kumar, de-notified Jantar Mantar as a protest site and designated Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi in its place.
The order said the decision was based on the recommendations of a committee constituted by the Ministry of Home Affairs to examine “alternative proper venues” for citizens to hold protests and demonstrations in place of the existing “designated site”.
The circular contained no details about the committee’s members, the specific recommendations made, or the date the committee was formed, among other details.
On October 13, Newslaundry filed a Right to Information (RTI) application with the Ministry of Home Affairs, posing four questions, including:
- A certified copy of the order constituting the committee tasked with identifying alternative protest sites in Delhi, and the date on which it was formed.
- The names, designations and departments of the committee’s chairperson and all its members, and a certified copy of its Terms of Reference.
- Certified copies of the minutes of all the committee’s meetings, along with its final report or recommendations on the alternative sites.
- Certified copies of all relevant orders, file notings, recorded reasons and official correspondence on the decision to remove Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site and designate alternative venues.
Ravi Kumar Chaudhary, the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) for the Union Territory (UT) Division of the Ministry of Home Affairs, replied to our application. He said that “upon consideration of the nature of the information sought and the potential implications of its disclosure, the information is exempted from disclosure under Section 8(1)(a) of the Right to Information Act, 2005.”
Section 8(1)(a) allows information to be withheld if disclosing it could prejudice India’s sovereignty and integrity, the security of the state, or its strategic, scientific or economic interests. It also covers information that could harm relations with a foreign state or incite an offence.
Expressing displeasure at the government’s response, Nikhil Dey of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS), an organisation that actively campaigned for the enactment of the RTI Act, said, “The idea that an answer to such a question could be withheld on the grounds of 'security' is simply unacceptable. It reveals the government’s attitude. Are the identities of committee members or the designated locations for protests matters of ‘national security’? National security has been turned into a tool to suppress democracy.”
