title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package
description: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
author: Azadeh Moshiri
content:
India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

title: Exclusive: China-Pakistan satellite waltz is watching every inch of India 24×7
description: This is the third exclusive by ThePrint on China's satellite surveillance of India.
author: Soumya Pillai
content:
New Delhi: China and Pakistan are building a coordinated network of satellites that could provide persistent surveillance of Indian territory. This space-based cooperation was consolidated during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, a space surveillance report highlights.
According to a report by Bengaluru-based space surveillance startup Digantara, exclusively accessed by ThePrint, Chinese space capabilities, including satellite data, may have been used to observe Indian military installations and other strategic sites during Operation Sindoor.
One of the most significant findings points to the role of China’s high-resolution optical remote-sensing satellite, Yaogan-41, during the 88-hour military confrontation between India and Pakistan.
“Chinese Satellite Yaogan-41 offers continuous subcontinent coverage. A dual-use satellite, it tracked Indian airbases during Operation Sindoor,” the report read.
While the report pointed to the specific use of Yaogan-41 against India during Operation Sindoor, it also explained how China and Pakistan have been building a complementary network of space surveillance to ensure that not an inch of India is left unmonitored.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, Pakistan placed six satellites in orbit. Five of these—Pakistan Remote Sensing Satellite-Earth Observation 1 (PRSC-EO1), Pakistan Remote Sensing Satellite-2 (PRSS-2), HS-1, PRSC-EO2 and PRSC-EO3—were launched on Chinese rockets, in Chinese launch facilities. While all these satellites are individually placed to focus on Indian territory, they also complement the Chinese network of satellites.
The combined Earth-observation capabilities of the Pakistani and Chinese satellites give a more continuous picture of Indian military infrastructure, troop movements, border installations, airbases, naval facilities and strategic assets.
“China launched five satellites for Pakistan, enhancing ISTAR and observation of Indian assets and space monitoring capabilities,” the report read.
ISTAR is a military system that combines information gathered from satellites, drones, aircraft, radars, ground sensors and intelligence networks to give a military force a detailed picture of its adversary’s activities and capabilities.
Experts suggested that with China sharpening its space ambitions, India will need to work on its capabilities to increase its presence in space.
The Pak satellites
The Digantara report showed that the China-supported Pakistani space launches began much before 2025. Starting in 2018, satellites including PRSC-EO1, PakSat MM1, ICUBE-Q, PRSS-1 and Pak TES 1A were already eyeing Indian territory, placed in orbits complementing the existing Chinese network of satellites.
The meticulously choreographed satellite network waltz, when viewed as a whole, is designed so that as one satellite moves out of range of a particular region, another moves into position to take over, ensuring consistent coverage of the area. These Pakistani satellites are, in a way, filling the small gaps left in the already expansive Chinese satellite network. The orbits for these satellites are also chosen to ensure that regions of interest are monitored from multiple angles, range and clarity.
For instance, the PRSS-1 is Pakistan’s Earth-observation satellite, launched alongside PakTES-1A in July 2018. It is an electro-optical imaging payload, with two principal image products—panchromatic and multispectral.
Panchromatic imagery can distinguish objects or features roughly one metre across under suitable imaging conditions. Multispectral imagery captures information across different portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, helping identify vegetation, land-use patterns, water bodies and other surface features.
According to the Pakistani space agency, Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), PRSS-1 offers a four-day revisit capability anywhere on the globe. For example, if PRSS-1 captures an image of Delhi on Monday, it can capture another image of Delhi approximately four days later. It can do the same for locations elsewhere in the world. This allows scientists and authorities to monitor changes on the ground. PRSS-1 has ground stations in Islamabad and Karachi for receiving, processing, and archiving satellite imagery.
PAKSAT-MM1, launched in 2024, is a communications satellite, developed with Chinese assistance. It is designed to provide telecommunications services across Pakistan and surrounding regions. It carries payloads operating in four frequency bands: C-band for television broadcasting and communications, Ku-band for broadcasting, VSAT (very small aperture terminal) connectivity and mobile backhaul, Ka-band for high-speed broadband and high-throughput internet, and L-band for satellite-based augmentation services (SBAS), which can improve positioning and navigation accuracy.
PRSC-EO1, on the other hand, is a part of Pakistan’s newer remote-sensing satellite programme, which uses optical sensors to acquire images of the Earth’s surface.
All of these satellites received technological and launch support from China.
In 2022, Pakistan’s SUPARCO and the China Great Wall Industry Corporation (CGWIC)—a subsidiary of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC)—signed a multi-launch service agreement to provide Pakistan with a long-term arrangement to launch multiple satellites using China’s rockets and associated technical services.
Also read: Exclusive: 3 Chinese satellites stayed focused on Gujarat coast during Operation Sindoor
Complementing ground support
Digantara’s space surveillance report has also found Pakistan’s growing involvement in the Asia-Pacific Ground-Based Space Object Observation System Project (APOSOS) to be concerning.
APOSOS is a multinational space-surveillance network initiated under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO), in which China plays a central role in its operation and data management. The project uses ground-based optical telescopes to observe and track objects in space, including satellites.
Curiously, Pakistan was one of the three countries where the first three observation nodes or stations of APOSOS were established. Each node is equipped with a 15-cm aperture optical telescope, and observation data from the different nodes is transmitted to a central facility at the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in China’s capital, Beijing. The other two stations are Peru and Iran.
Since Pakistan is not just a member of APOSOS, but the host of one of the facilities, it has gained a geographical advantage of getting access to observations from different parts of the world, which can be used to track satellites in orbit, including India’s space assets.
This is the third article in ThePrint’s exclusive three-part series examining China’s space surveillance moves.
(Edited by Ratan Priya)

title: As Turkey’s Kizilelma enters service after air-to-air kill, where’s India’s ‘loyal wingman’ programme
description: Induction of Turkey’s Kizilelma marks a major step in a worldwide push to build unmanned aircraft that can fly alongside, and eventually take on some missions performed by, traditional fighter jets.
author: Harini Ts
content:
New Delhi: Turkey has commissioned the first three Bayraktar Kizilelma unmanned fighter aircraft into its defence forces, which its maker described as the first instance of any country’s armed forces commissioning an autonomous fighter jet.
Turkish manufacturer Baykar said the aircraft passed its qualification trials and has been commissioned into active service. Kizilelma is not a traditional armed drone. It has been designed to carry out fighter-type missions, including sky-to-sky combat.
According to a report by the defence news portal TWZ (previously The War Zone), the aircraft showcased this performance in November 2025, firing a domestically developed Gökdoğan beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile (BVRAAM) to strike a jet-powered target drone. The target was detected using Turkish defence electronics firm ASELSAN’s MURAD active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, showing the integration of onboard radar and beyond-visual-range missile capabilities on an unmanned aircraft.
The aircraft has also showcased self-piloted formation flying. Yet, the extent to which it can independently spot, follow and engage hostile aircraft in a real-world combat environment remains unclear.
However, this marks a major step in a worldwide push to build unmanned aircraft that can fly alongside, and eventually take on some missions performed by, traditional fighter jets. While China’s GJ-11 stealth unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) is believed to have entered active service, there has been no public demonstration of its combat capabilities.
The US is also pushing ahead with its Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) programme.
In July, American defence manufacturer Anduril said that its YFQ-44A drone had completed a full beyond-line-of-sight strike on a simulated target, terming the trial test a major step towards making CCAs active.
Boeing Australia, meanwhile, is building its MQ-28 Ghost Bat—uncrewed CCA—for the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF), which has likewise showcased air-to-air combat capabilities.
The developments are particularly significant for India as New Delhi is looking to expedite its indigenous ‘loyal wingman’ programme before 2030.
In May, when he was Chief of Integrated Defence Staff, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit urged for the homegrown Ghatak UCAV programme to progress fast. He said India should aim to achieve initial operational clearance for a ‘loyal wingman’ capability by 2030, pointing to similar initiatives in the US and Australia as examples. Ghatak is not a direct rival to the Turkish drone since its primary function is striking ground targets.
Dixit noted that the Indian Air Force (IAF) could eventually one day pair Tejas fighters alongside Ghatak aircraft carrying specialised mission payloads, including electronic warfare equipment, targeting sensors and precision-guided weapons. Pilots would be able to direct these pilotless aircraft while remaining outside hostile airspace, he had said.
He also stressed for a clear operational requirement from the IAF and a committed joint programme bringing together the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and private-sector partners. In March, The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) had cleared Acceptance of Necessity to acquire 60 RPSAs—four squadrons—at an estimated cost of close to Rs 40,000 crore.
Ghatak, A Remotely Piloted Strike Aircraft (RPSA) is intended as a stealthy, jet-powered, tailless flying-wing unmanned combat aircraft for surveillance, identification, precision strike and offensive air operations. Its internal weapons bay is designed to carry roughly 1.5 tonnes of precision-guided munitions while preserving a low radar signature.
It is expected to fly at about Mach 0.8, with a service ceiling near 13,000 metres, powered by a Kaveri-derived engine producing about 49–51 kN.
Ghatak is being developed by DRDO specifically its Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE) under the Remotely Piloted Strike Aircraft (RPSA) programme. The programme goes back to the Autonomous Unmanned Research Aircraft (AURA) feasibility study, which begun in May 2016.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

title: Animal cruelty notice against horse race at Anant Singh’s daughter’s wedding
description: The horse race will take place in Anant Singh’s village, Nadwan, as part of his daughter’s big fat wedding. The winner will take home a Thar SUV.
author: Krishan Murari
content:
Barh (Bihar): Ahead of a horse race scheduled at Bihar MLA Anant Singh’s daughter’s wedding, the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed the state’s animal husbandry department to inspect and verify welfare arrangements for the participating horses at Singh’s village, Nadwan.
Animal rights activist Naresh Kadiyan filed a complaint with the AWBI, raising concerns over the registration of the participating horses and compliance with animal welfare rules.
“Rules are not being followed for the horse race. There is no veterinary fitness or compliance with the animal welfare provisions,” Kadiyan told ThePrint.
Kadiyan said he would file an FIR against Mokama MLA Anant Singh if action was not taken.
“The district administration is intimidated by this MLA and is taking no action. But I will not let this go,” he said.
However, the organisers said the race would go ahead regardless of any objections.
“This is Anant Singh’s daughter’s wedding. Who has the guts to put a stop to this?” an organiser said.
AWBI seeks inspection, verification of horses
In a letter to Arun Kumar, the district animal husbandry officer for Patna, the AWBI directed obtaining a list of participating horses from the organisers and verify their registration, veterinary fitness and compliance with animal welfare rules.
“Verify Turf Club registration of each horse and whether the Turf Club is registered with AWBI. Verify veterinary fitness certificates and compliance with the Transport of Animals Rules, including rest before racing,” reads the letter dated 23 November, accessed by ThePrint.
The letter further directs officials to ensure that no sick, injured, exhausted or unfit horse participates in the race. It also asks them to verify permissions obtained from the police and district administration.
“If the organisers cannot produce the required documents or cruelty or unfitness is found, the matter should be reported at once to the District Magistrate and the Senior Superintendent of Police, Patna, so that action under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 and other applicable law, including postponement or stoppage of the event where justified, can be considered,” the letter states.
The AWBI has also sought an action-taken report detailing the inspection findings and the provisions or exemptions relied upon by the organisers.
“We are assigning numbers to the horses and collecting data on all of them. We are also assessing the health of the horses before the race starts,” Arun Kumar told ThePrint.
The horse race is scheduled to take place in Anant Singh’s village, Nadwan, where horses from different states have arrived. The horses are named Sikandar, Thar, Rocket, Lal Badshah, Babar, and Khagaria Express.
Around 200 horses are expected to participate, with the winner set to be awarded a Thar SUV.
Activist raises concerns over welfare, minors
In his complaint, Kadiyan said the proposed event raises serious questions about the legal status of the participating horses, their registration, transportation, veterinary fitness, welfare conditions, and the AWBI’s regulatory jurisdiction.
He also called for officials to check whether minors were involved in the event and ensure appropriate child-safety measures.
“Verify the involvement of minors and ensure appropriate child-safety measures. Depute an appropriately qualified veterinary inspection team, in coordination with Bihar’s competent authorities, to inspect the temporary stables and racing ground,” reads Kadiyan’s complaint.
(Edited by Maryam Hassan)

title: Fact-Check: Does This Video Show BJP Demolishing Muslim Homes in Tripura? No!
description: Fact-Check: A video is going viral on social media, falsely claiming to show Muslim homes being demolished during eviction drives conducted by the BJP in Tripura.
author: Anika K
content:
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show Muslim homes being demolished during eviction drives conducted by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in Tripura.
- One of the posts sharing the video has captioned, "BJP’s bulldozer politics is spreading, with Muslim homes now being demolished in Tripura. Around 19,000 families have faced eviction drives in Assam under BJP rule, with Muslims disproportionately affected."
(An archived version of a similar claim can be found here.)
Is it true?: No, the claim is false.
- The video shows an eviction drive carried out in Dhaka's Mirpur, Bangladesh.
How did we find out?: We ran a reverse image search on the video using Google Lens and found a video from May 2026 with similar visuals.
- The video was uploaded by a Bangladesh-based digital news portal, rajneete.com, on 21 May 2026.
- This indicates that the video is not recent.
- The video's caption reads, "Slum eviction drive in Mirpur; illegal structures are being demolished using excavators. Yesterday, Wednesday (May 21), the eviction drive in the Mirpur area led to tension and clashes. During the operation, police personnel on duty faced a sudden attack by the slum dwellers." (translated from Bangla to English)
- Bangla news portal Times Today Digital also shared the video, stating that it shows an eviction drive against illegal structures carried out in the Kalshi area of Dhaka, Bangladesh.
- Another video, shared by ATN Bangla News showed the same visuals and was captioned, "Slum dwellers plead through windows to prevent the demolition of their homes." (translated from Bangla to English)
- According to the caption, the video shows Mirpur, Dhaka.
- We were able to geolocate the area on Google Maps and confirm that it matches the visuals in the video.
Conclusion: The video doesn't show Tripura; it shows an eviction drive carried out in Mirpur, Bangladesh.

title: Do You Need a Credit Card? Here’s How to Decide
description: Learn how to decide if a credit card suits your income, spending habits and repayment discipline, including fees, benefits and credit score impact.
author: Partner
content:
What a Credit Card Helps You Do
A credit card can be more than a payment option. When used responsibly, it can support convenience, flexibility, and financial planning.
Common benefits of using a credit card
- Cash flow flexibility: Lets you make purchases now and repay later within the billing cycle
- Convenient payments: Useful for online shopping, subscriptions, travel bookings, and large purchases
- Emergency support: Can help cover urgent expenses when immediate cash is not available
- Reward opportunities: Some cards offer cashback, reward points, travel benefits, or discounts
- Credit history building: Responsible use may help strengthen your credit profile over time
- Purchase tracking: Monthly statements make it easier to review where your money is going
When a Credit Card May Make Sense for You
A credit card may be a good fit if you already manage your money with discipline and want a tool that adds flexibility without disrupting your budget.
You may be ready for a credit card if:
- You have a stable source of income
- You can repay the full bill on time every month
- You already track your spending regularly
- You want to build or strengthen your credit score
- You need a reliable payment method for online purchases, travel, or subscriptions
- You understand the difference between using credit and living on credit
A credit card tends to work best for people who see it as a payment tool, not as extra income. If you are likely to use it for planned spending and clear the dues on time, it may support your financial routine well.
Costs and Fees You Should Understand First
Before you apply, bear in mind that a credit card is not free money. There can be costs involved, particularly if you don't pay it off on time or use it without having a full understanding of the terms. Common credit card costs to watch out for:
- Interest charges: Usually apply when the full outstanding amount is not paid by the due date
- Late payment fees: Charged if you miss your payment deadline
- Annual or joining fees: Most card issuers charge these depending on the card type
- Cash withdrawal charges: Using a credit card to withdraw cash often attracts fees and interest
- Over-limit charges: May apply if spending crosses the approved limit
- GST and other applicable taxes: These may be charged on certain fees and finance charges
How a Credit Card Affects Your Credit Score
One of the biggest long-term effects of using a credit card is its impact on your credit score. Used responsibly, a credit card can help establish or improve your credit history.
A credit score may be influenced by factors such as:
- Paying dues on time
- Keeping credit utilisation under control
- Avoiding repeated missed payments
- Not applying for too many credit products too quickly
- Maintaining a healthy repayment history over time
Questions to Ask Yourself Before Applying
Before applying for some of the best credit cards in India. Take a step back and assess your own needs first. The right card for one person may be the wrong card for another. Ask yourself:
- Why do I want a credit card?
- Will I pay the bill in full every month?
- What kind of spending will I use it for?
- Do I need rewards, travel benefits, cashback, or just convenience?
- Am I comfortable managing due dates and statements?
- Do I understand the card’s fees and charges?
- Will this card help my finances, or make them harder to manage?
You should also compare practical factors such as eligibility, annual fees, reward structure, acceptance, and repayment terms before making a decision.
Signs You Are Ready for a Credit Card
Not everyone needs a credit card immediately, but some signs suggest you may be prepared to use one well. You may be ready if:
- You budget consistently
- You avoid unnecessary borrowing
- You pay bills on time
- You understand interest and fees
- You have stable monthly income
- You want to build your credit history carefully
- You can use credit without treating it as extra cash
These signs matter more than simply qualifying for a card. Approval alone does not mean a credit card is the right financial step for you.
Conclusion
A credit card can be a useful tool if it's the right kind of card for you and your spending habits, your ability to pay it off and your long term objectives. It can be of benefit in terms of convenience, rewards, being able to cover an emergency and of course building your credit. Before applying, focus less on finding the best credit card in India in general and more on finding out whether a credit card fits your financial behavior right now.

title: Meet the Young Innovator Using Data to Understand India’s Vanishing Groundwater
description: A Surat schoolboy built JALAAKAR, an AI groundwater prediction tool that uses rainfall, soil and borewell data to estimate underground water availability.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
A borewell can run dry without much warning. For a farmer depending on it to irrigate crops or a family relying on it for everyday water needs, the question that follows is simple: how much water is actually left underground?
Finding an answer is not easy. Unlike rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, groundwater reserves cannot be seen. Their availability depends on several factors, from rainfall and soil conditions to the rate at which water is extracted. Without reliable estimates, planning how much to draw or where to focus conservation efforts becomes difficult.
A school student from Surat, Gujarat, is exploring how technology could make this information easier to access.
Dheyay Shah has developed JALAAKAR, a machine-learning-based tool that estimates groundwater availability across different talukas using historical records and environmental data. His innovation recently won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026, a nationwide challenge that received more than 6,100 project submissions from school students across India.
Making groundwater easier to understand
India depends heavily on groundwater for drinking water, agriculture and other everyday needs. However, excessive extraction, changing rainfall patterns and growing demand have put pressure on these underground reserves.
One of the difficulties in managing this resource is knowing how much water is available in a particular area. Groundwater levels can vary depending on local geography, the amount of rainfall received, and how much water is being extracted.
This is where Dheyay's project comes in. Instead of relying on isolated measurements, JALAAKAR brings together different sources of information to generate estimates that help people better understand groundwater conditions.
How JALAAKAR uses machine learning
At its core, JALAAKAR uses machine learning to identify patterns in historical groundwater and environmental data.
The tool considers information such as past borewell records, rainfall patterns, and soil characteristics. Each of these offers a different piece of information about underground water reserves.
For instance, rainfall influences how much water can seep into the ground and replenish aquifers. Soil characteristics determine how readily this water can percolate, while borewell records provide insights into changes in groundwater levels over time.
JALAAKAR analyses these datasets to identify relationships and recurring patterns. It then uses what it learns from the historical information to estimate groundwater availability at the taluka level.
In simpler terms, the tool attempts to use what has happened in the past to understand what groundwater conditions might look like in a particular area.
Such estimates could eventually help local communities, farmers, and those involved in water management make more informed decisions about extraction and conservation.
However, predictive estimates are not a substitute for actual groundwater measurements. The tool's accuracy, independent field validation, and suitability for different geographical conditions would need to be established before it can be used for wider water-management decisions.
A young innovator looking beneath the surface
Dheyay's project was recognised at vivo Ignite 2026, where he emerged as the national winner. The competition brought together school students working on ideas that apply science and technology to real-world challenges.
With more than 6,100 projects received, the challenge evaluated innovations on parameters such as creativity, scientific application, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and potential social impact.
What makes JALAAKAR interesting is the problem it chooses to address. Groundwater management is often discussed in terms of large-scale infrastructure and policy, but it also begins with something much simpler: understanding how much water is available before using it.
Dheyay's work explores how data can help answer that question. While the tool would need further testing and refinement before wider application, it offers a promising starting point for making groundwater information more accessible.
For a young student, looking beneath the surface has meant looking at a problem that affects millions of people. And if developed further, JALAAKAR could contribute to a future where communities have better information to guide how they use and protect one of their most important natural resources.

title: This 26-YO Pays Weavers Up to 35% More To Keep a 300-YO Tamil Nadu Craft Alive
description: Bhavani’s Jamakkalam weaving has a 300-year history, but its artisan numbers have fallen sharply. Discover how a young entrepreneur is opening new markets for this traditional Tamil Nadu craft.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
Look closely at a Jamakkalam, and you might spot a smile. Hidden in its traditional stripes is a pattern called Pallu Mutham, meaning pearl-like teeth. A 26-year-old entrepreneur recognised its potential.
That entrepreneur is Varsha Sivakumar, who grew up in Bhavani, Tamil Nadu, surrounded by Jamakkalam looms. Today, through House of Jamakkalam, she works with 30 to 35 weavers to bring this traditional textile to new buyers.
Full story
But what exactly is Jamakkalam? This thick, striped cotton weave originated nearly 300 years ago in Bhavani and neighbouring Kumarapalayam. First woven by the Jangamar community, it became a familiar part of Tamil households.
Wedding trousseaus, temple courtyards and everyday homes once made up its market. The craft even received a Geographical Indication tag in 2005–06. Yet, recognition could not prevent its biggest problem: dwindling demand.
History of Jamakkalam
In two decades, Bhavani's active weaver population reportedly fell from 20,000 to around 3,000. Cooperative orders declined, finished pieces piled up unsold, and younger generations began choosing other occupations over weaving.
Varsha saw this differently after a classroom presentation in 2017. At the National Institute of Fashion Technology, a guest lecturer presented Jamakkalam as a craft worth studying. Varsha wondered why she had overlooked it.
She returned to the weaving clusters, documented techniques and listened to artisans. Her biggest discovery? The craft did not need an entirely new design language. Its existing patterns simply needed to reach contemporary buyers.
Read Varsha's story
Take the Smiling Pouch. Its distinctive appearance comes from Pallu Mutham, a traditional arrangement of stripes that already resembles a woven smile. Varsha did not invent the pattern. She recognised what generations had created.
There is another important change. House of Jamakkalam absorbs the higher cost of finer yarn, pays upfront and offers 30–35% premiums on complex orders, without penalising artisans for flawed pieces.
Instagram has also connected the weavers to overseas customers, particularly Sri Lankan Tamils commissioning Jamakkalams for weddings. Varsha's ambition is regular monthly orders for every loom. The 300-year-old weave is finding new homes, one order at a time.
Support the weavers

title: 5 Indian Businesses Creating Social Impact Through Their Business Models
description: Here are five Indian businesses creating social impact through inclusive hiring, affordable healthcare, rural livelihoods and women’s entrepreneurship.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
What comes to mind when you think of a successful business? Crores in revenue, thousands of employees, a presence across the world, or perhaps a celebrated CEO?
Now consider a few other measures of success. How many women earned their first independent income? How many people with disabilities found a workplace where they could build a career? How many families could afford life-saving medical treatment? How many rural artisans could earn a living without leaving their villages?
Recent conversations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s management practices have brought a larger question into focus: what truly makes a good business leader?
Closer to home, these five Indian enterprises offer a different perspective on success. From hospitality and healthcare to waste management and handicrafts, they show how building a profitable business can go hand in hand with creating meaningful opportunities and improving people's lives.
Making room for every ability
At Lemon Tree Hotels, learning Indian Sign Language is part of employee training. It helps colleagues communicate with one another and makes everyday working life more accessible for employees with hearing disabilities.
Patu Keswani, the founder of the hotel group, began hiring people with disabilities in 2007. Over the years, the company has adapted its training programmes to accommodate people with different needs.
Deaf employees receive training with the help of sign language interpreters, while colleagues with low vision are provided accessible learning materials. Some neurodivergent employees undergo internships lasting more than six months to help them settle into their roles.
According to its 2025–26 annual report, Lemon Tree employed 305 people with disabilities and another 635 people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds across its owned, leased and managed hotels.
Much like several inclusive cafés across India, the hotel chain demonstrates how adapting workplaces to people's needs can open up meaningful career opportunities.
Taking village crafts to the world
In 1978, Nand Kishore Chaudhary began Jaipur Rugs with two looms and nine artisans. He wanted to connect rural craftspeople directly with larger markets, helping them earn through skills they had developed over generations.
According to the founder's website, the business has grown to work with around 40,000 artisans across 600 villages in five Indian states. Around 80 percent of them are women.
For many of these women, weaving offers an opportunity to earn from their homes without having to migrate to cities or travel far for work.
As The Better India previously reported, the company delivers raw materials to artisans' homes and collects the finished carpets from them.
Through its Manchaha initiative, artisans also get the freedom to create their own rug designs, drawing inspiration from their surroundings, experiences and imagination.
Their craftsmanship has found customers across the world while creating livelihood opportunities closer to home.
Making life-saving surgeries affordable
For a family struggling to afford heart surgery, the cost of treatment can stand between a loved one and potentially life-saving medical care.
It was this challenge that cardiac surgeon Dr Devi Shetty sought to address when he founded Narayana Health in Bengaluru in 2001.
His hospital model focuses on performing a large number of surgeries, making efficient use of medical equipment and reducing procurement and operational expenses.
The savings help bring down the cost of treatment for patients.
A 2017 case study by The Commonwealth Fund documented that Narayana Health had brought the average cost of open-heart surgery below US$2,000 at the time.
By rethinking how hospitals operate, Dr Shetty built a business model that demonstrates how greater efficiency can help more families access specialised medical care.
Helping waste pickers become entrepreneurs
When Lotfar moved to Bengaluru in 2010, he was struggling to make ends meet as a waste picker.
A 2022 report by Tata Trusts documented how his life changed after he began working with Hasiru Dala. By then, he owned four trucks and employed around 20 other waste pickers.
Founded in 2015 by Shekar Prabhakar, Nalini Shekar and Marwan Abubaker, Hasiru Dala Innovations is a waste management enterprise that helps informal waste workers build more secure livelihoods and run their own businesses.
These entrepreneurs provide waste collection and management services to residential communities, offices and events. They earn through service fees as well as the sale of recyclable materials.
By 2022, the enterprise had supported 24 waste-picker entrepreneurs, who had, in turn, created employment opportunities for around 300 other waste pickers.
The model brings the people who have long helped keep our cities clean into the business of managing their waste, giving them opportunities to grow as entrepreneurs.
From making papads to becoming business owners
In 1959, seven women in Mumbai borrowed Rs 80 and began making papads. Their aim was simple: to earn an income of their own.
What began as a small venture became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, one of India's most recognisable household brands.
According to its official website, the enterprise provides self-employment to around 45,000 women across 83 branches in 16 states.
What makes Lijjat particularly interesting is its shared ownership model. Its women members participate in running the enterprise, and the profits and losses of each branch are shared among its members.
For thousands of women, a skill they already possessed became a means of earning an income and having a stake in the business they helped build.
More than six decades later, the enterprise offers an example of what women can achieve when they have access to economic opportunities and collective ownership.
These five enterprises have taken different paths to growth. Yet, each offers a valuable lesson in how businesses can widen access to opportunities, recognise overlooked talent and help people build better lives for themselves.
Perhaps, alongside asking how much a business earns, we could also ask a question that deserves just as much attention: Who grows when the business grows?

title: How BJP Used State Power to Win Kolhapur’s Gokul Dairy
description: The BJP was helped by a Maharashtra government ordinance and the votes of four government-appointed directors  to win Gokul dairy’s chairmanship in Kolhapur, overriding the panel elected through a democratic process.
author: Amey  Tirodkar
content:
Gokul Zilla Sahakari Dudh Utpadak Sangh (Gokul district cooperative milk-producing federation) in Kolhapur district, known popularly as Gokul, is Maharashtra’s largest dairy cooperative. Around 5.5 lakh farmers of the district are directly linked to this cooperative, established in 1963. Known for the high quality of its milk, Gokul’s provisional turnover for 2025-26 was Rs.4,185 crore.
The election to the post of the cooperative chairman on November 10 pushed Gokul into the news for all the wrong reasons. The election, won by a BJP-led panel (Chhatrapati Shahu Shetkari Aghadi) backed by Maharashtra’s ruling Mahayuti, is widely perceived to have been manipulated, with many alleging subversion of democratic mandate.
On October 19, in well-publicised elections to the board of directors, the BJP-backed panel won 12 of the 25 seats. The panel led by Congress MLC Satej Patil (Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi) won 13 seats. The mandate clearly was in favour of the Congress-led panel.
But then this panel found itself in a fix when it came to electing the board chairman. A Gokul by-law requires a quorum of at least 14 board members for the election to be valid. The panel led by Satej Patil had 13. On the day of the election on October 28, all 12 of the Mahayuti-backed board members absented themselves.
In Mumbai, State Medical Education Minister Hasan Mushrif, whose son Navid Mushrif led the previous board, told the media: “People have voted us [the Mahayuti panel] to oppose their [Satej] panel. Not to elect their chairman. So, our members decided to remain absent.” Father and son belong to the Nationalist Congress Party (Ajit Pawar), which is part of Maharashtra’s ruling coalition.
The group led by Satej Patil moved court, and on November 2, the Bombay High Court directed that the election be held on November 10, with notices to all 25 elected board members to remain present.
But on November 6, an ordinance issued by the State government made provision for five government-appointed directors in cooperatives with an annual turnover over Rs.500 crore; four of them would have voting rights. This ordinance amended a clause in the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, which denied voting rights to nominated and government-designated directors in elections for chairmen or other office-bearers.
The 5 members were duly appointed, and the chairman election of November 10 was held after the High Court refused to impose a stay on the ordinance. The balance of power was now in favour of the Mahayuti, whose candidate, Rajesh Patil, won 16 votes—12 from the elected board, 4 from the government appointees—in the election held on November 10. The Congress-backed panel’s candidate, Shashikant Patil Chuyekar, got 13.
Thus, through executive overreach, the BJP seized control of an institution that wields significant political influence over a vast network of farmers who are attached to it and dependent on it.
What happened before the election
The backstory of how Satej Patil’s group came to win as many as 13 seats on the board reflects the dynamics of district-level politics.
The five-year term of the previous board ended in May. In the last five years, Gokul grew spectacularly, establishing 1,400 new cooperative milk societies, which brought up the total number of such societies to 5,418.
In the last election to the board held in 2021, Hasan Mushrif and Satej Patil were on the same side of the political divide. Hasan Mushrif was then a Minister in Uddhav Thackeray’s government. His party, the as-yet-unbroken NCP, had an alliance with the Congress; this alliance won the board, ending the rule of the Mahadevrao Mahadik family, which by then was with the BJP.
By 2026, the Mushrifs and Satej Patil were political adversaries. Yet, Hasan Mushrif was at first reluctant to have his party cooperate with the BJP’s Rajya Sabha member Munna Mahadik, whose family’s control over Gokul his side had broken in 2021, over the 2026 Gokul election. Frontline learnt from reliable sources that Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis himself stepped in to smooth out the differences and make the Mahayuti alliance work for the election. Apart from Hasan Mushrif and Mahadik, another key person for this alliance was Chandrakant Patil, State Higher and Technical Education Minister, who is originally from Kolhapur.
After the board elections were announced, State Dairy Development Minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil cancelled the voting rights of the 1,400 new milk societies that were added to the cooperative in the last 5 years. This was seen as a move designed to help the Mahayuti-backed panel. But these societies got back their voting rights by first moving the Bombay High Court and then the Supreme Court.
A panel contesting the board elections needs letters of support from member milk societies. When the Gokul elections were announced, 4,500 member societies, out of a total of 5,418, were supportive of the Mahayuti. But the attempt to cancel the voting rights of 1,400 societies created an undercurrent of opposition.
A senior journalist from Kolhapur, Vijay Chormare, said: “This cancellation of membership was nothing but an SIR process in Gokul. The way the ECI [Election Commission of India] is cancelling the voting rights of citizens rampantly—the same strategy was applied in Gokul. Just as anger against the ECI is palpable all over the country, Gokul members were angry with the Mahayuti even before the campaign got started.”
Satej Patil seized his chance. He personally visited the 5,418 member societies in 3 months and promised them that no member of his family would contest the Gokul elections; all candidates on his panel would be ordinary farmers. This was an important pledge because the Mahayuti alliance candidates were mostly relatives of leaders. The strategy worked, and the victory of Satej Patil’s panel got prominent coverage on Marathi news channels and in newspapers.
Why this desperation?
Countering criticism about the manner in which the BJP seized control of Gokul, Fadnavis keeps saying that the November 6 ordinance was necessary to end “the constitutional crisis in Gokul”. The Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has observed that the BJP snatches power in any way it can when it senses that it is losing.
The question to ask is why the BJP-led regime needed to go out on a limb to win Gokul. Cooperative institutions, it is true, have played an important role in Maharashtra’s politics for five decades. Yet, Maharashtra’s political economy has moved beyond the role played by these institutions. The share of agriculture in the State’s economy has fallen from 40 per cent in 1960 to 15 per cent at present. Urban infrastructure, real estate, and mega projects now dominate the political economy. Gokul, in comparison, is small fry.
Neeraj Hatekar, a professor of economics, explained why Gokul nevertheless has political significance for the BJP: “The BJP wanted to win Gokul because it gives it direct control of and connect with 5.5 lakh farmers of an influential district.”
But Gokul is also directly under the Dairy Development Department and Cooperative Department. This makes it easy for the government to influence decision-making in the cooperative. Then why the desperation to control the board? A senior journalist, Deepak Lokhande, said: “The BJP believes in a vindictive kind of politics. Defeating Satej Patil in Gokul was more important for it than handling Gokul through Mantralaya. To earn that pleasure, it took such extreme step.”
The political scientist Suhas Palshikar believes that the BJP is not bothered about the criticism that it subverts democracy: “Wherever there is a whiff of power, the party would go and grab it by hook or by crook. In the process, the criticism about democratic functioning is not even considered.”
In the larger scheme of things, it was perhaps important for the BJP to thwart the rise of Satej Patil, who is emerging as the Congress’ de facto leader in Maharashtra. He has popular appeal and works hard to win elections. He is also a Maratha, which is a highly political community. Vasant Bhosale, editor of Lokmat (Kolhapur edition), said: “Satej Patil could challenge the BJP like Revanth Reddy of Telangana or D.K. Shivakumar of Karnataka. Winning Gokul would have given him a boost. So, he had to be defeated. Misusing government power and creating an issue out of the quorum rule was part of the game to ensure that.”
Satej Patil made a serious allegation while campaigning for the Gokul election. He said that the BJP wanted to finish the Gokul brand to help Amul grow. “The Central government has created Sardar Patel Multistate Milk Federation in which Gokul will be merged. That’s why a hidden power (“adrishya shakti”) is trying to win Gokul,” he said.
Some experts and commentators in Maharashtra believe that the BJP wants to weaken Marathi institutions. “Gokul is Maharashtra’s institution, a powerful brand. The same thing was tried with Nandini of Karnataka. But the Karnataka voters defeated the BJP and saved their Nandini. In Kolhapur also, people have defeated the BJP. The State government is helping the Gujarati lobby to finish Gokul,” said Deepak Pawar of Marathi Abhyas Kendra.
At any rate, the BJP regime’s manoeuvres have made the Gokul election national news. As the veteran journalist S.M. Deshmukh said: “Earlier, even journalists in Mantralaya used to be unaware of the outcome of these elections because these were locally fought polls. It was rare for the Chief Minister to get involved. But this time a small election became big because big people made their hands dirty in a small election. That’s the problem with Maharashtra politics now. Big leaders think with small hearts.”

title: Vinod Kapri's Pyre and Beckett's Godot: Waiting as Love and Loneliness
description: In Vinod Kapri’s Pyre (2024), an octogenarian couple in a ghost village wait for a son who never arrives, realising that even loving companionship cannot shield them from a world that has long moved on.
author: Zainab S. Qazi
content:
If faith were to have another face, it might resemble the hopeful act of waiting. For what is waiting if not to believe, and keep believing, that the light is here and waiting for us to catch it? That the chase will end any day now, and the self will find solace, even when the world outside is veiled in darkness? What is waiting if not love disguised as faith, a quiet conviction that something, someone out there is worth holding on to?
Perhaps it is no coincidence that Vinod Kapri’s Pyre (2024) begins with the octogenarian couple Padam (Padam Singh Kapri) and Tulsi (Hira Devi) invoking the gods while navigating a hilly and lifeless terrain in Kumaon, Uttarakhand. A few minutes in, Padam suggests that Tulsi jump off the cliff, and the scene cuts to black as the title card appears. For the next hour and a half, the audience is trapped in the circular, often futile, spectatorship of waiting, until the film is gradually enveloped by a bleak landscape where death and life linger in uneasy proximity. What emerges is an existential portrait of loneliness in which even their loving companionship cannot protect Padam and Tulsi from a world that has long moved on, forgetting the last two people who still believe and hold on.
In many ways, Pyre can be read alongside the renowned Irish playwright Samuel Beckett’s seminal tragicomedy, Waiting for Godot. The octogenarian couple share the weariness of Estragon and Vladimir, who tirelessly wait for their waiting to end. The Kumaoni village mirrors the play’s existentialist landscape where, to quote Beckett, “nobody comes, nobody goes, it’s awful!”
In both, sanity is lost to the very act of waiting, and the self is recognised only through the other. Pyre’s elusive Godot—the one who never arrives—is Padam and Tulsi’s son Hariya. The hope of his arrival persists even when his physical absence becomes an inescapable reality. Hariya, like Godot, inhabits a world beyond their reach: close enough to be imagined, too far to be reached. In one poignant scene, Tulsi tells Padam: “Hamara beta laapata ho gaya hai” (We’ve lost our son). Padam replies: “Hamara beta laapata nahi hua hai, Tulsi. Hum khud laapata ho gaye hain” (We haven’t lost our son, Tulsi. It is we who are lost).
What emerges is the peculiar inadequacy of companionship in the face of overwhelming loneliness. This tension lies at the heart of the theatre of the absurd, to which Beckett’s play belongs: companionship sits beside abject loneliness, and two individuals are caught in a temporal loop, spinning within the circularity of time, which seems to have stopped for them even as it moves on for the rest of the world. Their banter as a loving couple, their slow moments of tenderness, and even Padam’s occasional humour, do not quite dispel the desolation surrounding them. There is something deeply absurd and unsettling in the way their affection endures in a life overshadowed by despair and mortality.
Unlike the solitary tree in Beckett’s play, which stands silent witness to the dying spirits of Vladimir and Estragon, nature remains indifferent to the couple’s gradual unravelling in Pyre. Landslides, heavy rains, and cloudbursts become a testament to their dying house, exposing its vulnerabilities and making their already precarious conditions even more difficult to endure. Nature offers neither refuge nor consolation; like the rest of the world, it moves on regardless of the lives trapped within it.
The cost of out-migration
The existential, almost ghostly spirit of the Kumaoni village looms large over many villages in the hills of Uttarakhand today. Rural-urban migration is on the rise, driven by push factors like high unemployment, poor pay, and poverty, compelling young people to leave their hometowns for cities. Kapri’s film brings this issue to light: ageing parents are left behind, waiting endlessly for their children to return. While Hariya’s presumed migration becomes a microcosm of the larger out-migration from the region, the film takes an unexpected turn towards the end, when it is revealed that Hariya is long dead and Padam has been writing letters in his son’s name to keep Tulsi’s hope alive. This is where the film grows even more existential, leaving the audience with a set of unsettling realisations that extend beyond the couple’s predicament: the lies we tell ourselves, the fictions we construct, and the stories we keep returning to in order to make sense of an uncertain, bewildering existence.
Death hovers over the film from the very beginning. Padam urges Tulsi to make their own pyres, for he fears no one would come to pay their last respects. For him, their love alone cannot save either of them, and each anticipates the other’s death with dread. In what I would call the year’s most haunting climax, a lone Tulsi mourns the dead Padam, since she must now live not only in a deserted village but also the absence of her only confidant, her best friend, her shield. And then the most telling image of the home comes to life when goats and heavy rains encircle Padam’s pyre. There is life all around him, yet this is the most lifeless scene of them all, set against a broken home that once sheltered two lives and now bears witness to the loneliness of the one left behind.
We return, then, to the central questions. What would remain of Vladimir if Estragon were gone, too? Perhaps it would resemble Tulsi’s world: a profound silence, with the only one who occasionally interrupted it also now gone. How do we make sense of the futile task of waiting if we have no one to wait with? The most tragic form of waiting is that one day you may be left with neither the person you wait for nor the person you waited with.
Zainab S. Qazi is an independent writer and researcher based in New Delhi. She writes at the intersection of film, media, culture, gender, and politics.
