title: We Aren't Begging: Masood Slams SP Over Seat-Sharing, Says Cong Will Decide If Talks Should Continue
description: Congress Uttar Pradesh working committee chief Imran Masood on Wednesday lashed out at the SP, saying, 'We aren't begging,' after the latter announced candidates for five seats ahead of the upcoming assembly polls even as the seat-sharing talks are underway.
author: PTI
content:
We Aren't Begging: Masood Slams SP Over Seat-Sharing, Says Cong Will Decide If Talks Should Continue
Congress Uttar Pradesh working committee chief Imran Masood on Wednesday lashed out at the SP, saying, "We aren't begging," after the latter announced candidates for five seats ahead of the upcoming assembly polls even as the seat-sharing talks are underway.
His retort came as the Samajwadi Party (SP) has named a candidate in Saharanpur -- in Masood's Lok Sabha constituency. The Congress leader said he will discuss with the party leadership whether seat-sharing talks with the SP should continue. He said, "When you are holding talks on one hand and making announcements on the other, it shows that you are not serious."
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
"We will discuss within our party what needs to be done and whether we should sit for talks or not. The party will decide what course of action to take," he told PTI Videos. The first round of talks that ended on Tuesday at Congress veteran Pramod Tiwari's Delhi residence remained inconclusive, with SP revealing its initial offer of 26 seats, way lower than Congress's expectations.
Questioning the intention of their ally, Masood said, "I do not understand whether you want to fight me, the Congress or the BJP. It needs to be decided whether we want to fight the BJP or fight among ourselves." Of the five seats that the SP declared candidates for in a surprise move, four are held by its sitting MLAs -- Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana, Umar Ali Khan from Behat and Mehboob Ali from Amroha.
The four seats are in western Uttar Pradesh, where the SP expects a challenge from BJP, its ally RLD, as well as the recently floated Samajik Parivartan Morcha of AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi and Aazad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) chief Chandrashekar Aazad. Its fifth candidate is Jyoti Lodhi, who will contest from Lalitpur in Bundelkhand. On differences within the INDIA bloc, Masood said he could not comment on the internal matters of other parties. "Everyone has their own views. We are making honest efforts, but I cannot say what is going on in the minds of others," he said.
Later, he told PTI while talking about seat-sharing, "We aren't begging. The deal has to be mutually acceptable, respectable." On the Constitution Day rally scheduled to be held in Lucknow on Wednesday, he said Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge would attend the event.
"We have reached Lucknow to oversee the preparations for the rally," he added. SP chief Akhilesh Yadav, in a post on X, said that the best approach, which could yield the most positive results, would be to field candidates as "PDA candidates".
Reacting to queries on the controversy, SP veteran leader Shivpal Yadav said, "The alliance will remain; everything will be sorted out." SP leader Udai Veer Singh too played down the controversy, saying the party has declared names in seats held by SP in 2022 UP polls. "The practice is the same as it was during 2024 Lok Sabha polls when the party kept making gradual announcements amid seat-sharing talks. The arrangement was successful then, wasn't it?" he asked.

title: Centre Allots Lutyens' Delhi Bungalow To Dalai Lama's Office Following MEA Request
description: The Centre has allotted a three-year bungalow in Lutyens' Delhi to the Gaden Phodrang Trust, which manages the Dalai Lama's office. The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile has welcomed the move.
author: Madhuri Adnal
content:
Centre Allots Lutyens' Delhi Bungalow To Dalai Lama's Office Following MEA Request
The Central government has allotted a bungalow in Lutyens' Delhi to the Gaden Phodrang Trust, which manages the office of Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama and looks after his spiritual and humanitarian work.
The bungalow is located on Pandit Ravi Shankar Shukla Lane in New Delhi, PTI reported, quoting sources. The allotment was made following a request from the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). The Union Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry has not yet issued an official statement on the matter.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The accommodation will give the Dalai Lama's office a base in Lutyens' Delhi, an area known for its government buildings, official residences and prominent institutions.
Government sources said the bungalow has been allotted for an initial period of three years under the usual accommodation arrangement. The tenure can be extended, subject to the applicable rules.
The property has been allotted to the Gaden Phodrang Trust rather than directly to the Dalai Lama. The organisation handles the institutional responsibilities of his office and supports his various activities.
What is the Gaden Phodrang Trust?
The Gaden Phodrang Trust works to preserve the institution of the Dalai Lama and take forward his spiritual teachings and humanitarian work.
As outlined on its official website, the trust focuses on promoting human values, encouraging dialogue between different faiths and protecting Tibetan culture and identity. Its work also includes environmental protection and spreading awareness of India's ancient wisdom and traditions.
Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile thanks Indian government
The allotment has been welcomed by the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, whose members thanked the Indian government on Tuesday for providing a Type 7 bungalow for the Dalai Lama and his personal office.
Speaker Dolma Tsering described the decision as "very welcome news" and conveyed the Parliament's gratitude to the Indian government.
She said the accommodation would make the Dalai Lama's visits to New Delhi easier and offer him a more comfortable place to stay during his time in the capital.
The allotment is also expected to make it more convenient for his office to carry out its work during visits to Delhi.

title: Speed Limit on Yamuna Expressway to Be Reduced to 75 kmph During Foggy Conditions
description: Speed Limit on Yamuna Expressway to Be Reduced to 75 kmph During Foggy Conditions
author: PTI
content:
Speed Limit on Yamuna Expressway to Be Reduced to 75 kmph During Foggy Conditions
As part of measures to prevent road accidents caused by fog and mist during winter on the Yamuna Expressway, the maximum speed limit for vehicles on the expressway will be reduced from 100 kmph to 75 kmph for the period from November 25 to February 15, an official statement said on Tuesday.
Dense fog during winter reduces visibility, increasing the risk of accidents on expressways.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
In view of this, the authority has directed the concessionaire of the Yamuna Expressway, Jaypee Infratech Limited, to immediately implement additional safety measures alongside the reduction in the speed limit.
The objective is to alert motorists to exercise caution under low-visibility conditions and minimise the risk of road accidents, it said.
During the stipulated period, information regarding the revised speed limit will be prominently displayed at key locations along the expressway.
Information boards will be installed at various points, while motorists will also be informed through newspapers.
In addition, pamphlets detailing safe driving practices during foggy conditions will be distributed at entry and exit points, toll plazas and roadside facilities along the expressway.
Motorists will be informed about essential safety precautions through public announcement systems at toll plazas.
Radio FM channels will also broadcast advisories on safe driving during foggy conditions. Necessary instructions will further be displayed on large electronic display boards to keep commuters informed.
Emphasis has also been laid on strengthening technical safety measures to improve visibility during night travel and foggy conditions.
The authority has observed that the brightness and reflectivity of reflective tapes installed at several locations have deteriorated. This may result in inadequate visibility of road markings and warning signs, increasing the risk of accidents.
Accordingly, instructions have been issued for the immediate replacement of damaged reflective tapes. The installation of fog lights at the entry and exit points of the expressway has also been directed.
Traffic volume on the Yamuna Expressway generally increases on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. In view of this, instructions have been issued to ensure effective arrangements at toll plazas for smooth vehicular movement and passenger convenience.
The authority has directed the concerned agency to implement all the instructions and submit a compliance report.

title: Bombay HC restricts entry to building linked to Dawood Ibrahim, continues demolition stay
description: The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) Had On November 19 Begun Razing The Building After Classifying It As A 'dangerous And Dilapidated' Structure Requiring Demolition
author: PTI
content:
The Bombay High Court on Wednesday continued its stay to the demolition of a dilapidated South Mumbai building where fugitive gangster Dawood Ibrahim and his family once lived, and prohibited any person from entering it.
A bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna continued its stay to the demolition of the two-storey Haji Ismail Haji Habib Musafirkhana on Pakmodia Street till November 30.
The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) had on November 19 begun razing the building after classifying it as a "dangerous and dilapidated" structure requiring demolition.
However, Shaikh Abdul Razak and Amirali Vazirali Panjwani, who claimed to be interested parties and beneficiaries of Waqf institution Haji Ismail Haji Habib Musafirkhana Trust, moved the HC against the demolition notice on the same day.
Senior advocate Anil Sakhare, appearing for the BMC, on Wednesday told the bench that the severely dilapidated building posed a danger to the people in the vicinity.
"It is a building structure and not a mosque, as being claimed by the petitioners. Several small portions of the structure have been collapsing since 2007 and no one is occupying it," advocate Sakhare said.
The court noted that when the plea was mentioned last week and urgent hearing was sought, the petitioners had said that the structure was a mosque.
"If you (petitioners) have taken a status quo order by misleading us, then we will issue contempt of court (notice). Be prepared. Don't try to mislead the court. Today we are being told that it is not a mosque," the HC said.
The petitioners' advocates reiterated that the structure housed a mosque, and prayers were being offered five times a day there.
They sought permission from the HC to permit daily prayers, or at least Friday prayers.
The court, however, said in its order that nobody shall enter the premises till Monday (November 30) as it was in a dilapidated condition.
"What if some untoward incident happens, who will take responsibility?" the bench said.
According to the petitioners, there was a 148.79-sq mt ground-floor mosque belonging to the Sunni Hanafi sect inside the Musafirkhana building.
The property was permanently dedicated in October 1864 by Haji Miya Haji Ismail Haji Habib as a rest house for Haj pilgrims with a mosque, a fact recorded on an Arabic and Persian marble plaque embedded in the mosque wall, the plea said.
Asserting that the mosque is a public trust property "used by general public to offer Namaz, daily five times", the petitioners objected to the BMC notice pasted on the mosque's wall on November 17, referring to the shrine as a "prayer hall".
The plea alleged that this wording mirrored a disputed May 2016 sale agreement through which the trustees allegedly sold the property for Rs 1.10 crore to the Saifee Burhani Upliftment Trust (SBUT) for redevelopment.
"The mischief herein lies in calling a 'Masjid' as a 'prayer hall' by the Trustees and the developer, to circumvent the law of the land, that mandates that Masjid cannot be sold, since the ownership vests in the Almighty Allah," the petition stated.
The demolition notice was pasted on the building's walls on November 17, directing occupants to vacate by November 18, it said, arguing that giving less than 24 hours to vacate a property violated a government notification of April 25, 2025, which mandates a minimum 15-day notice.
The petitioners further alleged that the notice was issued at the behest of the developer and disregarded a State Waqf Tribunal order as well as Supreme Court directives that had granted status quo and permission for repairs.
The building figures prominently in the biography of gangster Dawood Ibrahim Kaskar, the mastermind of the 1993 Mumbai serial blasts, who lived there with his family in the 1970s during his rise in the city's criminal underworld before fleeing India in 1986.
After the Kaskar family moved from Temkar Mohalla to the Musafirkhana on Pakmodia Street, the building and its surrounding area not only served as the unofficial headquarters of Dawood's fledgling gang but also witnessed an assassination attempt on him when members of the rival Pathan gang opened fire at its entrance in a bid to eliminate him.
A March 2015 memorandum of understanding between the Musafirkhana Trust and SBUT, reproduced in a 2019 Bombay High Court judgment, noted that Dawood once occupied the entire 568.87-square-foot first floor of the building.

title: How big is too big? Anant Singh’s daughter’s wedding has horses, helipads and 50 lakh gulab jamuns
description: From A Thar For The Winner Of A Horse Race To A Land Rover Defender For The Groom, Mokama’s MLA Is Going Grand On The Wedding Spectacle
author: Our Web Desk
content:
Forget destination weddings in Udaipur or Phuket. Forget South Delhi's high-end lehengas, grand weddings with a celebrity sangeet and a guest appearance by the three Khans. Honey Singh performing at the reception? Indians have been there, done that.
Nadwan in Bihar's Barh may not be a tourist destination, but it has been drawing plenty of attention over the past few days. The reason? A wedding that could put even India's most extravagant celebrations to shame.
The bride is Shivangi Singh, younger daughter of Mokama MLA and Bihar strongman Anant Singh. Her November 25 wedding in the family's ancestral village is shaping up to be less shaadi and more of a full-scale Bihar spectacle.
Think five to six helipads for VIP guests, a 30-foot stage inspired by Jaipur's Hawa Mahal, eight sprawling pandals, a horse race with a Mahindra Thar as the top prize and a menu featuring 150 vegetarian dishes. There are also reportedly 30 lakh rasgullas and 50 lakh gulab jamuns being prepared for the celebrations.
Reports suggest that as many as four lakh guests are expected. To feed them, the wedding kitchen has reportedly been stocked with milk brought in tankers, while more than 300 stoves are said to be working.
And because a wedding this big apparently cannot end with pheras alone, there is a horse race.
More than 50 riders are expected to compete, with the winner taking home a Mahindra Thar, the runner-up a motorcycle and the third-place finisher a scooter. Horses named Barood, Lal Badshah, Khagaria, Babar, Rocket and Sikandar have reportedly been training for the race, reports say.
So, yes, a destination wedding might be on your cards, but at Anant Singh's daughter's shaadi, the whole of Bihar might just end up attending.
"Apne itihas raach diya" (You have created history) was one X user's verdict. Another asked: "Where's CBI and ED?"
Helipads, Hawa Mahal and a horse race
Eight huge pandals have been erected for the celebrations, while a 30-foot-high stage inspired by the Hawa Mahal has been built for the garland ceremony. Five to six helipads have reportedly been prepared for VIP guests.
More than 50 riders are expected to take part in the horse race, with the three winners set to receive a Thar, a motorcycle and a scooter respectively. The horses have reportedly been preparing for the contest for the past 15 days.
The arrangements suggest that the family has left little to chance when it comes to making the wedding an event to remember.
Enough sweets to feed a village
And then there is the food.
The menu is expected to feature 150 vegetarian dishes, with reports claiming that around 30 lakh rasgullas and 50 lakh gulab jamuns are being prepared. The kitchen has reportedly been supplied with milk tankers, while more than 300 stoves are being used to prepare the food.
At most Indian weddings, the family worries about whether the caterer has ordered enough gulab jamuns.
At Nadwan, the question appears to be whether Bihar has enough gulab jamuns.
The wedding guest who did not make the cut
With a wedding of this scale, the guest list was bound to attract almost as much attention as the arrangements.
Although the identities of the VIP guests expected to use the helipads have not been disclosed, several reports say politicians, actors, Bhojpuri stars and other prominent personalities are expected to attend.
But one conspicuous absence has already made headlines. JD(U) MLC Neeraj Kumar, Anant Singh's political rival, says he was not invited.
Kumar has questioned the scale of the expenditure and said investigative agencies should examine where the money is coming from.
"The investigative agencies may take note and look into it, from where the money is coming. But the public sees everything," he told ThePrint.
The strongman behind the spectacle
The extravagance is inseparable from the man hosting it.
Anant Singh, the Mokama MLA, has long been one of Bihar's most recognisable political strongmen. His name has featured in criminal cases for more than four decades. His 2020 election affidavit listed 39 criminal cases, while Patna High Court records have referred to as many as 52.
The cases include serious allegations involving murder, abduction and offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. His first recorded case dates to 1979, when he was booked in a murder case along with others, though no chargesheet was filed.
Yet Singh has remained a formidable political force in Mokama and won the Assembly election in 2025.
His political and legal troubles have also continued. Singh is expected to surrender about a week after the wedding in connection with the Dularchand Yadav murder case, according to reports. The case concerns the killing of 75-year-old Yadav during election campaigning in 2025.
For now, however, the wedding has taken centre stage.
A political wedding on another scale
The wedding gifts are reportedly as extravagant as the arrangements.
Singh is said to be gifting his son-in-law, Rishikesh Kumar, a Land Rover Defender reportedly worth between Rs 2.5 crore and Rs 3.5 crore, along with a 100-gram gold chain and an 80-gram gold bracelet.
Rishikesh is the son of CRPF commandant Ranvijay Kumar.
Bihar has seen its share of high-profile political weddings. When Lalu Prasad Yadav and Rabri Devi's eldest daughter Misa Bharti got married in December 1999, the couple told Income Tax officials that the wedding cost Rs 8 lakh. Of this, Rs 3 lakh to Rs 4 lakh reportedly came from their own pockets, with the rest said to have been covered by RJD workers.
The Income Tax Department later gave them a clean chit, finding no evidence of unaccounted extravagant spending. At the time, however, political chatter and media reports put the cost of the celebrations far higher, with some estimates reaching Rs 3 crore.
Anant Singh appears to have taken the political wedding spectacle to another level.
For now, criminal cases and political controversies can wait. The stage belongs to the bride, the horses, the Thar and the mountains of sweets.
Because in Bihar, the new question is no longer: destination wedding or home wedding? It is simply: how many bighas do you need to host one?

title: ‘People here don’t like Hyderabadi biryani’: AIMIM serves it in UP after Azam Khan’s dig
description: The Gathering Surrounding The Dish At An Aparty's Office In Bareilly On Tuesday Night Was Part Of A Campaign That They Say Would Continue Until The 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly Elections
author: PTI
content:
A biryani gathering at an AIMIM office in Bareilly on Tuesday night was part of a campaign that the party said would continue until the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. From Bareilly to Etawah, Asaduddin Owaisi’s party served Hyderabadi biryani to answer Samajwadi Party leader Azam Khan’s dig that people in the state did not like the dish.
“People here don't like Hyderabadi biryani. People here like pulao and mutton biryani,” Khan had told reporters in Rampur when asked about Owaisi. The AIMIM chief has teamed up with Chandrashekhar Azad’s Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) for the polls under the banner of the Samajik Parivartan Morcha.
AIMIM units began organising gatherings and distributing biryani days after Khan’s remarks, drawing crowds in Muslim-majority localities. In Bareilly, the party’s Uttar Pradesh general secretary, Nadeem Qureshi, hosted office-bearers, workers and supporters at his office.
“People have taken a liking to Hyderabadi biryani in the state and its popularity will only increase in coming days,” Qureshi said on Wednesday.
He said the party had held similar events in Rampur, Hathras, Bahraich, Etawah and Sambhal, among other districts, and would continue them across Uttar Pradesh until the Assembly elections.
In Etawah’s Nai Basti locality, the AIMIM district unit put up a poster featuring Owaisi at a biryani distribution event. District president Shamshad Hussain said the event was a response to Khan’s remarks. He claimed that “more than 85 per cent of Muslims now favoured Owaisi” and said the party would get their support in the 2027 polls.
The campaign comes as the AIMIM seeks to expand its presence beyond its Hyderabad base. Owaisi has pitched the alliance as an alternative to the BJP and accused the Samajwadi Party and Congress of failing to adequately represent Muslims.
At a recent rally in Meerut, Owaisi said the alliance would first remove chief minister Yogi Adityanath from power in Uttar Pradesh and then take on Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Delhi.
Owaisi has also repeatedly targeted the Samajwadi Party over the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, alleging that the government led by then chief minister Akhilesh Yadav failed to provide enough help to people displaced by the violence.

title: Kerala: Police investigate fairness cream's alleged link to kidney ailment in 17-year-old Indian girl
description: Doctors who treated the 17-year-old girl say that the cream allegedly contained toxic levels of mercury.
author: Ashraf Padanna , Cherylann Mollan
content:
Police investigate fairness cream's alleged link to Indian teen's kidney ailment
- Published
Police in India's southern Kerala state have registered a case against a fairness cream brand after a 17-year-old girl who used the cream allegedly developed a serious kidney ailment.
The girl's doctor told the media, external that she had developed a disease that impairs the kidney's ability to filter blood due to toxic levels of mercury allegedly found in the cream.
The girl - her name has been withheld to protect her identity - reportedly bought the cream to treat pimples and pigmentation after seeing an ad on social media.
India has an obsession with skin-lightening creams and this has led to a proliferation of brands selling fairness creams, though not all of them are regulated.
Experts say some of these creams may contain toxic metals like mercury and lead, but because they are sold via WhatsApp and other social media platforms, the brands often escape scrutiny of the authorities.
They also say that many of these brands use social media to market products to youngsters, even if they are uncertified and untested.
Laboratory tests revealed that the cream the girl used contained 12,500 parts per million of mercury, far exceeding the permissible limit of less than one part per million for skin-lightening products, Aster MIMS Mother Hospital in Malappuram district, where the teenager was treated, said in a statement.
Dr Satheesh, a nephrologist at the hospital, said that the girl had developed membranous nephropathy - a life-threatening kidney disorder where immune deposits thicken the filtering walls of the kidneys, causing large amounts of protein to leak into the urine.
She added that mercury absorbed through the skin could damage the kidneys' filtration units, leading to blood toxicity. If left untreated, such toxicity could cause kidney failure and severe neurological damage.
The girl said she started buying the fairness cream about a year ago through a social media app and had bought three bottles over the past year.
"The company claimed that continuous use [of the cream] every night would help remove pimples and pigmentation. It also promised visible results with consistent application," the teenager told Onmanorama newspaper.
But after using the cream for a couple of months, she began experiencing fatigue, headaches, dizziness, insomnia and her legs and face began to swell. The teenager told the newspaper that she even struggled to stand upright.
"The teenager was initially brought to the hospital by her parents with severe body swelling and acute physical distress," the hospital said.
"While primary treatment was initiated, the unusual progression of her symptoms prompted doctors to suspect an underlying toxin. Subsequent blood and clinical tests revealed dangerously elevated levels of mercury in her system," their statement added.
Doctors suspected that the mercury could have entered the girl's bloodstream through her skin. They sent a sample of the fairness cream to a laboratory for testing.
The test results confirmed that the cream contained mercury "drastically higher than" the permissible safety limits mandated by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) for cosmetics in India, the hospital said.
The doctors then treated the girl by administering medicines to eliminate toxins, while managing her kidney-related complications.
She was discharged from hospital after about a month and has been recovering at home.
On Monday, she told the BBC that she was still experiencing some health issues and was finding it difficult to study.
"Since starting treatment, she has shown gradual improvement. However, she is not back to normal yet and it may still take time for her to fully recover," Dr Satheesh said.
Meanwhile, the Kerala police have launched an investigation into the matter and the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has also registered a case against the fairness cream manufacturer.
The incident once again puts the spotlight on India's obsession with fair skin, and how people, especially women, are willing to buy creams that may not be regulated as long as they promise to make them fair.
This is because the cultural bias against dark skin runs deep in Indian society and those who aren't fair-skinned often face discrimination.
In recent years, social activists and even Bollywood actors have spoken out about this unhealthy preference for fair skin, challenging the widely-held notion that fairer is better.

title: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us
description: India will remain predominantly Hindu, though its Muslim population is projected to grow faster, according to a new survey.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
- Published
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.
The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.
Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.
The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.
It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.
The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.
Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.
If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.
Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.
Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.
Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.
"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.
"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.
"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)
The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.
"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.
"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.
Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".
The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.
Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.
There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.
By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.
Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.
But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.
Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.
The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.
The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.
One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.
In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.
Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.
China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.
By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.
The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.
And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.
Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.
There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.
"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.
India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed
Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.
South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.
Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

title: Lahori Zeera, Campa Jeera: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving the cola giants a tough fight in India
description: Cumin-laced sodas are capturing a bigger market share in India as demand for homegrown flavours goes up.
author: Nikhil Inamdar
content:
Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

title: India Top 3 country sending takedown requests to Google, up 61% in 6 months. Delhi Police sent 7 in 10
description: Amendments to the IT Rules that took effect on 20 February require platforms to remove content flagged through a court or government order within three hours, compared with 36 hours earlier.
author: Vrinda Tulsian
content:
New Delhi: Google’s Transparency Report showed that courts and government agencies in India sent it 4,006 requests to remove content between January and June 2026. Only Russia, with 21,240 requests, and South Korea, with 9,884, sent more during the period.
This marked a 61.3 percent increase from the 2,483 requests received in July-December 2025, and nearly double the 2,187 received in January-June 2025.
The requests flagged 65,091 items, including videos, links and posts, marking a 29.9 per cent increase from 50,097 in the previous six months.
Amendments to the IT Rules that took effect on 20 February require platforms to remove content flagged through a court or government order within three hours, compared with 36 hours earlier.
Who sent requests
Police accounted for 2,870, or 71.6 percent, of India’s 4,006 requests, naming 24,334 items. Courts sent another 695 orders, of which 353 were directed at Google and 342 at third parties. Together, these named 20,407 items.
The Information and Communications Authority sent 138 requests and government officials 66. The Consumer Protection Authority, the Data Protection Authority and the military together sent 20.
Since October 2024, the police and other agencies have been able to send notices through Sahyog, a portal provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs. Through it, state governments and central ministries send notices about unlawful content directly to platforms.
Google, Meta and ShareChat are among the companies that have joined the portal, while X has refused to comply.
The government released some figures on how the portal is used. According to PIB Fact Check, it flagged 2.98 lakh URLs for takedown between March and July 2026, and state governments accounted for over 82 percent of them. In November, an RTI reply showed that Gujarat Police had issued 5,358 takedown notices covering 1,90,633 URLs through the portal.
What they targeted
YouTube accounted for the bulk of the requests, receiving 3,399 of the 4,006 sent to Google. These named 59,779 items, or 91.8 percent of all items flagged in India’s requests. Web Search followed with 299 requests, Gmail with 83 and Play Apps with 77.
In 2,130 requests, defamation was cited as the reason, covering 33,420 items. 332 requests cited fraud and obscenity or nudity in 243. Authorities cited national security in 210 requests covering 2,781 items, and electoral law in 88. They cited government criticism in 74 requests, which named 160 items.
What Google did
Google removed 19,883 items for violating local laws and another 1,415 for breaching its own policies. It took no action on 19,402 items, while it said it lacked sufficient information to act on another 17,473.
The requests followed a change in the rules, with some of the government orders now facing legal challenges.
In March, YouTube blocked the channel of digital news outlet 4 PM, which had more than 84 lakh subscribers, along with 26 of its videos, following a government legal request. The Delhi High Court ordered the channel to be restored in May but allowed the 26 videos to remain blocked.
Separately, X has challenged a 2025 single-judge ruling of the Karnataka High Court that upheld the Sahyog portal. A division bench of the court has issued a notice to the Centre on the appeal.
YouTube’s own removals
The government requests are separate from content YouTube removes under its own Community Guidelines. Between April and June 2026, YouTube removed 34,41,973 videos uploaded from India out of the 1,11,59,676 videos it removed worldwide.
India ranked first, ahead of the United States (12,40,512), Indonesia (9,15,923) and Brazil (8,41,803).
Worldwide, child safety accounted for 68.2 percent of removed videos. Harassment and cyberbullying, violent or graphic content, and harmful or dangerous content followed.
YouTube removed 23,014 videos for misinformation. Automated systems first flagged 98.6 percent of removed videos, while government agencies flagged one.
YouTube also terminated 27,32,395 channels in the quarter for spam, deceptive practices and scams. It removed 155.2 crore comments.
YouTube assigns removed videos to a country based on the uploader’s IP address at the time of upload. The report does not break down removal reasons by country.
(Edited by Anupama Yadav)

title: Cabinet clears Rs 2,014 cr greenfield airport in Doloo, 2nd for Assam’s Barak Valley
description: Proposed airport at Doloo will be designed to handle 10.1 lakh passengers annually, with Centre citing operational and space constraints at Silchar’s existing airport as reason for the project.
author: Ananya Chaba
content:
New Delhi: The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the development of a greenfield airport at Doloo, near Silchar in Assam, at an estimated cost of Rs 2,014 crore.
The project, to be developed by the Airports Authority of India (AAI), will be funded entirely through its internal resources.
Located in Assam’s Cachar district, Doloo lies in the Barak Valley, a region known for its tea gardens and agro-based industries. The proposed airport will be located 30 km by road from the existing Silchar airport.
It will have a terminal building spread over 12,351 square metres, designed to handle 800 passengers during peak hour and 10.1 lakh passengers annually. It will feature a 2,705-metre-long and 45-metre-wide runway.
Why Silchar needs a new airport
Silchar, the headquarters of Cachar district, is an important commercial hub in southern Assam and serves as a gateway to Mizoram, Tripura and Manipur.
Built during the Second World War, the existing Silchar airport at Kumbhirgram is the only operational commercial airport in southern Assam’s Barak Valley. It operates as a civil enclave within an Indian Air Force (IAF) station, with air traffic control services provided by the IAF.
According to a 2018 Lok Sabha reply, the existing airport has a 2,286-metre-long and 45-metre-wide runway. Its terminal can accommodate 300 passengers at a time, according to IndiGo.
Announcing the Cabinet’s decision Wednesday, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said passenger traffic at Silchar airport’s terminal was already saturated. The existing airport also faces constraints on extending its runway, the minister said.
The government expects the new airport to cater to growing air traffic demand in southern Assam and adjoining areas of Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Meghalaya, thereby improving regional connectivity and reducing travel time.
Apart from boosting trade and tourism, the airport is expected to facilitate cargo movement, particularly of perishable goods and horticultural produce from the Northeast.
The project’s history
The AAI had identified Doloo Tea Estate as the preferred site for the greenfield airport following a pre-feasibility study in 2020. The project subsequently became embroiled in a controversy following the uprooting of more than 41 lakh tea bushes to make way for it in May 2022.
The Centre granted site clearance for the airport in February 2024. In May that year, the Supreme Court held that the clearance of vegetation without prior environmental approval violated environmental regulations.
The project received environmental clearance on 26 February this year, followed by in-principle approval from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 13 March.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
