title: Dwarka Expressway was sold as NCR’s Dubai. Buyers are flocking, roads & sewers missing
description: Thousands of families paid crores for homes along Dwarka Expressway, NCR's answer to Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road. They got broken roads, open drains — ‘residents have to cross open fields to reach homes.’
author: Sagrika Kissu
content:
Gurugram: Prakhar Sahay fought for almost a decade to get the Dwarka Expressway built. He protested at Jantar Mantar in 2016 and lobbied endlessly so that his distant corner of Gurugram would finally be connected to Delhi. The expressway is here now, but Sahay is still fighting. This time it’s for the basic amenities residents were promised but never got.
In premium towers and affordable projects alike, thousands of families who have invested crores in homes along the Dwarka Expressway are grappling with broken approach roads, open drains, incomplete sewage networks and unreliable electricity. They live in apartments with clubhouses and tennis courts beside a Rs 9,000-crore expressway, but some still have to cross open fields to get home.
“I would always say that I wanted to see the Dwarka Expressway completed while I was still a father and not a grandfather. Now that it’s finally there, the surrounding infrastructure is nowhere to be seen,” said Sahay, convener of the Dwarka Expressway Gurugram Development Association.
Announced in 2006, the 29-kilometre Dwarka Expressway was billed as Delhi-NCR’s answer to Dubai’s Sheikh Zayed Road. Not just India’s first eight-lane elevated expressway, but the centre of a new oasis of urban planning that could give central Gurugram and Noida a run for their money.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Gurugram stretch in March 2024 and the final Delhi section in August last year, though the building and buying boom had started well before that. Of the 42,816 units that were reportedly launched along the expressway between 2010 and 2024, 41,899 were sold in the same period. Today, about 115 housing projects are under construction. Sales of homes priced above Rs 10 crore have increased 22-fold in value to Rs 8,347 crore between 2024 and 2025. Real estate developers are marketing it as the new “power address”.
“Dwarka Expressway has been inspired by Dubai. Very soon, you will see towering skyscrapers lining the expressway just like Sheikh Zayed Road. The price rise after the launch of the expressway itself shows that it has become a power address,” said the sales manager of Roots Courtyard, which is selling plots starting at Rs 5 crore in a gated complex with amenities such as guards and EV chargers.
Connecting Mahipalpur in Delhi to Kherki Daula on the Manesar side of Gurugram, the road is an impressive sight, including its 3.6-km ‘musical’ underpass—a popular selfie spot with walls decorated with artwork representing different states. But the spectacle of the expressway ends where the neighbourhoods around it begin—whether it is luxury projects such as Tata La Vida or more modest developments such as ROF Alante.
The moment one turns off the Dwarka Expressway, the smooth, sweeping road gives way to broken access roads, clouds of dust and open drains. In newer sectors such as 99, 102, 104, 110 and 113, residents also contend with clogged stormwater lines and unreliable power. Many of the planned 24-metre and 30-metre internal roads remain unbuilt.
After repeated appeals to civic authorities went nowhere, the Dwarka Expressway Gurugram Development Association approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court last year over the missing roads. Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini promised a “permanent solution” in his March budget speech, but when the court asked for a timetable in September, the state still couldn’t say when it would finish acquiring the 1,157 acres needed for the 24-metre roads in Gurugram and Manesar.
Animals and drunkards enter the society at night. There was no STP until recently. My question is, how did the authorities issue the builder an occupancy certificate?
– Shivani Thusoo, ROF Alante resident
These sectors were meant to learn from the planning mistakes that have long plagued central Gurugram. Instead, they have inherited them in a more acute form.
“There are no internal roads, sewerage network or even drainage. Can you imagine, there are a few areas where residents have to cross open fields to reach their homes,” said Sahay. In his 40s now, he bought a 3BHK in Ansal Estella, Sector 103, in 2010, banking on the proposed expressway. A dispute with the builder has kept him in a rented flat nearby, at Rs 44,000 a month.
“It feels as though you must remain in complaint mode simply to secure the most basic amenities and necessities from the government,” he added.
Also Read: Inside Hyderabad’s housing glut. Unsold homes, skyscrapers without residents
A Rs 3-crore bubble
Tata La Vida in Sector 113 has all the trappings of a typical upscale Gurugram condominium: guarded gates, manicured gardens, a swimming pool, a well-equipped clubhouse, walking tracks and dedicated courts for tennis, badminton and basketball. Residents barely need to step out for daily necessities. Which is just as well, since they often don’t dare to.
Resident Kshitij Sharma paid Rs 3 crore for his apartment in 2024. The Dwarka Expressway was one of the clinchers. It promised easy access to Delhi and Gurugram, with IGI Airport just 15 minutes away. But the mess outside the gates has cast a pall, from piles of construction debris to the stagnant water lining both sides of the street all the way to the expressway.
“As soon as you step out of the society, the frustration really mounts. There is an open drain just 150 metres from our society. The approach road to the expressway is not built. And the sewage water lies stagnant on the roadside,” said 45-year-old Sharma, who works in the telecom sector. “I have everything inside my condominium, so unless it’s necessary, we don’t step out.”
As general secretary of the residents’ welfare association, Sharma spends much of his week shuttling between the offices of the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA) and the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram (MCG), repeating the same demands for roads, drainage, sanitation and basic services.
“Each time, I am told that they are working on it. And somebody will come soon to fix the problems. But nobody comes. And then I will visit their office again with the same request,” he said.
At least three couples have sold their apartments in the past year. They were unable to put up with the day-to-day infrastructural and civic shortcomings. Several other owners are also actively discussing leaving Dwarka Expressway
– Kshitij Sharma, Tata La Vida resident
In a letter to the GMDA chief executive officer on 22 May, the La Vida Residents Welfare Association (LVRWA) wrote: “The storm water drain project in the area being managed by GMDA has seen no progress for months. The lack of a proper drainage route causes rainwater to seep into the ground, leading to dangerous levels of water ingress and seepage into society apartments.”
The letter also blamed non-functional streetlights on a pending electricity connection from GMDA. “Street light infrastructure has been in place for over two years, yet the road remains dark at night,” it said. Six months on, it still hasn’t been fixed.
Expressway, then potholes & open fields
When Shivani Thusoo moved into her new apartment in Sector 108 in 2025, the first thing she looked for was a road. There wasn’t one. Residents of neighbouring Nanakheri wouldn’t let the apartment owners use the village road. They told them to use the “government road”.
“But there was no government road,” said Thusoo, who moved here primarily because it offered both connectivity and affordability. With six towers and over 700 apartments, her society ROF Alante never had premium pretensions. But living here has turned out to be much more harrowing than Thusoo had expected.
The daily commute is like an obstacle course. Getting home from the expressway means driving nearly two kilometres on a bumpy, unpaved road through the neighbouring village of Nanakheri. Then comes a dusty path between fields. Only the last 100 metres are paved—a stretch built by the developer. Even this is an improvement. It took months of visits to government offices and an intervention by the local MLA before residents could use the village road.
“Outside our society, we have roads up to 100 metres. After that, it is all soil and potholes. I am tired of visiting government offices now, they never listen,” Thusoo said.
Last year, ROF Alante residents staged a heated protest outside the builder’s office in Sector 44, asking how the project had got a licence and an occupancy certificate without a proper approach road. The builder, in turn, blamed local landowners for digging up the road and blocking access to the society.
The road problem is not limited to Sector 108. Across the Dwarka Expressway, residents have protested time and again for 24-metre approach roads. Fixing accountability on this front has been a challenge.
Under the Gurgaon-Manesar Master Plan 2031, developers are responsible for the 24-metre internal roads and government agencies for the 60-metre roads between sectors. One reason for the mess is that each builder is responsible only for the stretch within its licensed area. So a road can be built up to the edge of one project and stop at the next plot, where the land hasn’t been acquired or ownership is in dispute.
The government has repeatedly acknowledged the problem but a solution has been slow to come. In August last year, Haryana Industries and Commerce Minister Rao Narbir Singh directed town planning officials to withhold occupancy certificates in Gurugram until builders constructed the approach roads they had promised. “Public convenience is paramount,” he said.
Then in his Budget speech, CM Saini referred to the road issue in Gurugram’s Sectors 58 to 115. Blaming previous governments for leaving land acquisition out of the development charges paid by builders, he said the state would now acquire the land and that “the expenditure incurred will be recovered from builders.”
Some movement at least has started. In September, Haryana set up a joint site inspection committee led by the zonal administrator of the Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP), with officials from town planning, the city administration, land acquisition and urban estates. Of the roughly 1,157 acres needed for the missing roads, the state has zeroed in on about 38 acres in Sectors 58 to 67A and Sector 81 to acquire first. The committee will check land titles and submit a feasibility report to the HSVP’s chief administrator.
In Sector 109, Gaurav Prakash was among the early buyers along the corridor. He booked an apartment in 2010, when the expressway project was still getting repeatedly delayed by land acquisition, litigation and other issues. It was a leap of faith. According to him, the underlying issue is one of passing the buck. When residents asked officials for a proper approach road, he said, they were told it was the developer’s job.
I can’t lie to people and tell them that everything on the Dwarka Expressway is hunky-dory. I can only tell them the ground reality and let them make an informed decision
– Prakhar Sahay, real estate consultant
“But the developer had already built the stretch immediately outside their housing complex. The road beyond that is the government’s responsibility,” said Prakash.
The roads aren’t the only thing missing. Sewage tankers have become a familiar sight around societies along the Dwarka Expressway. With sewer lines incomplete or non-functional, they are the fallback for removing surplus treated effluent from in-house sewage treatment plants (STPs). But the solution is also a problem. Residents across societies say the tankers don’t take the waste to designated treatment plants, but instead dump it into open drains or vacant plots.
“Societies have their own STPs, but they cannot treat or reuse all the sewage. The surplus is meant to be taken to designated STPs, but it never reaches there,” said Prakash.
On 18 November, Municipal Corporation Manesar (MCM) Joint Commissioner Puneet Kumar caught two tankers dumping sewage in the open near the Holiday Inn by the expressway in Manesar and issued challans of Rs 50,000 each.
खुले में सीवरेज का गंदा पानी डालने वाले दो टैंकरों के 50-50 हजार रुपये के चालान
– संयुक्त आयुक्त @PuneetJ83054825 ने निरीक्षण के दौरान मौके पर किए चालान
– दोनों टैंकरों को जब्त करने के भी दिए आदेश@cmohry @ulbharyana @SwachhBharatGov @diprogurugram1 @DiprHaryana @DC_Gurugram pic.twitter.com/yPOxc3fH7N
— Municipal Corporation Manesar (@MCManesar) November 18, 2026
But many residents say they are yet to see their grievances addressed. Rajat Kumar, who lives in Sector 84, says he regularly files complaints on government portals with photographs of the tankers and the dumping.
“There is no answer or action,” he said.
Also Read: Gurugram, Noida are building for NRIs. Salaried class is trapped between dreams and means
Boom outside, bust inside
Soon after the Haryana stretch of the Dwarka Expressway opened in March 2024, prices along the corridor surged. A typical three-bedroom apartment went from around Rs 1.8 crore in 2022 to Rs 2.6 crore to Rs 4 crore by 2025.
The boom has attracted major developers, with new projects announced along the corridor, including Sobha City, M3M Capital, Adani The Marq and Roots Courtyard. But there are problems both outside and inside many of these complexes.
At ROF Alante, there is no proper boundary wall. A wire fence marks the edge, leaving the complex exposed to the fields beyond. Two massive diesel generators sit in the open beside the fence, their large exhaust pipes roaring. It would look like an industrial site were it not for the playground and small parking lot nearby.
Thusoo said the lack of a gate and boundary wall makes her worry for her family’s safety.
“Animals and drunkards enter the society at night. There was no STP until recently. My question is, how did the authorities issue the builder an occupancy certificate?” she said.
At Tata La Vida, about 600 apartments are occupied and only 70 are empty. But Kshitij Sharma says people are slowly trickling out and moving to Delhi and Noida.
“At least three couples have sold their apartments in the past year. They were unable to put up with the day-to-day infrastructural and civic shortcomings. Several other owners are also actively discussing leaving Dwarka Expressway,” said Sharma, with a sigh.
For Prakhar Sahay, the journey from fighting for the Dwarka Expressway to demanding basic amenities has reshaped his career. He moved from the corporate sector to real estate consultancy about five years ago.
“After a point, it feels like we should quit our jobs and spend all our time coordinating with the government to get the work done, simply because we bought a house here. That is why I decided to become a consultant,” said Sahay.
His conscience prevents him from endorsing his neighbourhood to would-be buyers.
“I can’t lie to people and tell them that everything on the Dwarka Expressway is hunky-dory. I can only tell them the ground reality and let them make an informed decision,” he said.
(Edited by Asavar Singh)

title: What Happens to Your Old Clothes? Inside a Mumbai Network Turning 17500 Kg Into Income for Traders & Artisans
description: What happens to your old clothes after you give them away? Inside a Mumbai network connecting discarded textiles with the workers who reuse and resell them.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
“Bhandiwala, bhandiwala.”
For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas, he collected old clothes, traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused.
He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them.
But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little.
That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi.
Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas.
“Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly,” he says. “We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages.”
Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence.
His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach.
According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas, whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation.
From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches
When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala. He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards.
Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three.
In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste.
He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO.
The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners?
In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use.
“Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved,” he tells The Better India.
The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead.
“At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system,” he says.
People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils.
Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them.
A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon
In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai.
They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection.
“I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends,” he recalls. “The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution.”
TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time.
He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material.
“We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it,” he explains.
What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them?
TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free.
A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles.
The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner.
The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally.
The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use.
That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product.
“Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place,” Vikram says. “We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be.”
Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners.
Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route.
TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders.
It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation.
Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use.
Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre.
For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations.
TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected.
‘Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work’
TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply.
Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households.
Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work.
Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers.
“We had to go and search for clothes ourselves,” he says. “Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular.”
For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar.
He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat.
Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes.
“The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect,” he says.
Now, he receives reusable garments from the team.
“Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular,” he adds.
He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine.
Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations.
Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping.
“Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work,” he says.
These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold.
What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them.
Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again?
Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations.
Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles.
Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients.
Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model.
“The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it,” Vikram says. “There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system.”
Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work.
According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline.
It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network.
17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next?
The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests.
Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month.
The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup.
Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them.
For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place.
There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested, the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply.
But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from.
For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning.
He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens.
What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to.
All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

title: Shot During Kasab’s Arrest on 26/11, This Retd Cop Now Helps Families With Last Rites & Legal Issues
description: Mumbai officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture Ajmal Kasab alive on 26/11. He survived, and now serves through books, an NGO and legal help for the vulnerable.
author: Vidya Gowri Venkatesh
content:
On the night of 26 November 2008, Mumbai Police officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture terrorist Ajmal Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty.
Across Mumbai, terrorists were attacking several locations. People across India followed the news from their homes, fearful of what might happen next. Police officers responded across the city, and many lost their lives in the process.
Sanjay survived the bullet injury. Years later, he continues to speak about that night, the colleagues he lost, and the work that has filled his life beyond the police force.
From writing books to helping families through an NGO he founded with friends, he has found different ways to serve people.
The Better India spoke to the former officer about the arrest of Kasab and the experiences that shaped his life afterwards.
‘Unfortunately, he never returned’
“I consider myself very lucky, as the bullet Kasab fired at me hit the left-hand side of my abdomen and not the right,” he smiles.
Around the time of the attacks, Sanjay had been excited about the release of his book, Stopwatch. He was going around his colleagues' desks to distribute copies to everyone.
Shortly before the attacks began in Mumbai, he visited his boss Hemant Karkare's cabin to give him a copy.
“Hemant sir was not there for some reason, so I left a copy for him on his desk. Unfortunately, he never returned,” Sanjay recalls.
The night he helped capture Kasab alive
“As the attack unfolded, we were tense, but we had only one goal: to serve our nation. The moment I heard that my boss, Hemant sir, had been attacked and lost his life, I was upset,” he shares.
Later that night, Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot.
“My colleague wanted to immediately shoot him down, but I convinced him to arrest him, as he was a key witness,” Sanjay shares.
Capturing Kasab alive became an important part of the investigation and trial that followed.
“After the arrest, I was immediately rushed to the hospital, where I received treatment for five to six days. I was asked to stay away from the news and was given counselling by a group of doctors. Finally, when I was discharged, I saw that all the noise was settling. My doctors and my family took great care of me,” he smiles.
The experience left Sanjay with a sense of pride in his service, though he is careful to share the credit with his colleagues.
When asked how it feels to have achieved something so significant, he says, “I am extremely proud of serving my country, and I would never want to take advantage of this.”
He goes on to credit his entire team for the recognition.
Why a police officer began writing about health
While Sanjay says that being a cop and serving the country was his duty, he was always driven by another passion away from work: writing.
Sanjay has so far written and published five books, all of them on health, mental health and relationships.
One of those was Stopwatch, the book he had just published when the 26/11 attacks took place.
“At one point in my career, I was posted as an immigration officer at the airport and had erratic shifts. This took a toll on my health and prompted me to write the book Stopwatch. It is a must-read for all people who work night shifts,” he shares.
Sanjay maintains clear boundaries between his profession and passion.
“I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing,” he says.
‘My biggest asset is my close friends’
His friendships have also shaped another important part of his life. Together with his close friends, Sanjay runs Jeevarang, an NGO inspired by a deeply personal experience.
“Twenty-five years ago, I lost my grandmother. She was very dear to me. We cremated her in my village, and the next day, when we visited the site to collect her ashes, we saw dogs feeding on the remains. I was heartbroken by what I saw,” he shares.
The memory stayed with him and became one of the reasons he wanted to help families give their loved ones a dignified farewell.
Through Jeevarang, Sanjay and his friends assist families who have lost their loved ones across 21 villages in Maharashtra. They provide support in cash or kind, depending on what the families need.
The NGO began operations in 2007 and also encourages writers by sponsoring the publication of their books.
A fraud case that inspired his next chapter
Sanjay retired from the police in July 2026. But his interest in helping people facing difficult situations has continued into his retirement.
He now runs his own legal and risk advisory firm.
The idea goes back to a case he encountered during his police career, involving a mother and daughter who lost their livelihood to online fraud.
“I came across a peculiar case in my career in 2009. Online fraudsters tricked a mother and daughter. They were told they had won a lottery and were asked to pay a huge sum of money. The women were innocent and, assuming they would receive a large amount, they sold their small pull-cart shop in Mumbai and lost all their money. The department, however, intervened and cracked the case. This incident stayed with me, and I decided that I wanted to help people who feel stuck in legal issues. That’s when I came up with this idea,” he shares.
The mother and daughter's experience stayed with Sanjay, much like what he had witnessed after his grandmother's cremation years earlier. Both experiences influenced the work he eventually chose to pursue outside policing.
When Sanjay speaks about 26/11, he credits his colleagues for what they achieved together. In the years since, he has continued to act on the concerns that have stayed with him, from helping families arrange a dignified farewell to supporting people facing legal difficulties.
Individuals seeking guidance or assistance with legal matters and risk-related concerns can find information about the services offered by Govilkar Legal & Risk Advisory on its official website. The firm aims to help people understand complex legal situations and consider their next steps.

title: Behind the Bisleri Scare: How Do Carcinogens End Up in Drinking Water?
description: From water treatment to packaging, understand how chemical contaminants can affect packaged drinking water and what safety standards are in place.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified.
Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging.
Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter.
FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs.
Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator.
Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it?
Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out.
What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant?
On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit.
Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs.
Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026. After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed.
FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies.
A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed.
How does bromate get into water?
Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe.
Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation, is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount.
How much forms depends on four things:
- how much bromide was in the water to begin with
- how much ozone is used
- the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is)
- how long treatment runs
Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water.
Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities.
So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching.
How much is too much?
Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans.
That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count.
The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested.
In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long.
Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking.
What are PAHs, and how do they get into water?
PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment.
PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO, one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff.
One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk.
Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from.
What about the plastic bottle?
Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water.
A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got.
Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here.
What checks are already in place?
Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order, packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means:
- manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration
- inspections happen once a year
- centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency
From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to:
- test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used
- test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter
- test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months
- test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass
The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection.
How does a failed sample end up in court?
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47):
- A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report.
- If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory.
- If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction.
In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process.
Should consumers be worried?
Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals.
But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe.
Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

title: How Tamil and Telugu Cinema Reduces Women Into Symbols
description: From The Paradise to Pushpa 2, women bear the violence of male ambition.
author: Prathyush Parasuraman
content:
A pregnant tribal woman is protesting in the Telugu film The Paradise, starring “natural star” Nani. Immediately, you know that she is going to be punished for her pregnancy. Like Chekhov’s flaming gun, a pregnant woman in Tamil and Telugu cinema is an invitation to imagine the worst—you know violence against her will ensue, just not how. In The Paradise, the woman’s protest is for her tribe to be recognised as a legitimate part of the state. The overlord, under whose clenched fist they live, does not want this.
As punishment, the woman is electrocuted, with her belly clamped to the engine of a revving car. The shock makes her twins slip out of the uterus—the boy survives, the girl dies. The boy will grow up wearing braids, a symbol of his lost, female twin; he will call himself Jadal, meaning braids. As a man, he will lead his tribe to victory.
But not before another pregnant tribeswoman is tortured. This time, the woman will tie up her feet and push until her child rips out of her body and she dies bleeding. This orphan will become the totemic symbol of the future around which the tribe will mobilise itself and finally emerge victorious. The mother’s final words to her child: “Think of this umbilical cord as your white ration card.”
Women are essential to The Paradise for the ways in which they are dispensable. Their presence is necessary. Their personhood, not so much. They provoke the plot and retreat. Or they hover over the narrative like a ghostly presence, exerting force on the events, like a wafting perfume, but without any pressure. Womanhood is stuck in ideas, unable to descend and occupy the body. There is a deep incuriosity built into the female characters; a deliberate effort is made to keep them from becoming compelling persons. It is not an unintentional lacuna, it is an enforced, strategic absence. You can watch the film dance around these characters, never embracing them, only poking at them, and then going back by two steps.
While women might be the object of male gaze, pregnant women quickly become symbols of male hope. Birthing a future generation, they are the object of something far more troubling than objectification—deification. Because, to objectify, you must at least consider the body. With deification, even that body—its marrow, a thing capable of exuding desire—becomes immaterial. Any violence committed on their bodies takes the shape of allegory. All of this is done in the garb of devotion.
To assault them is to threaten a future. To murder them is to wipe off this future. They become vessels, hollowed of presence, emblematic of a future often they will not get to inhabit.
At the cost of the feminine
Giving birth itself is a grisly affair, an original form of body horror. To look away from this, and turn the grisliness into something outside of the body—the electrocuted belly, the tied feet—is precisely the kind of perspective you adopt when you see the body not as something that inherently endures, but as something that must be given more to endure. What does it say about our cinema that it cannot show childbirth, but can make the audience watch a pregnant woman being tortured into childbirth?
This is not merely The Paradise’s cross to bear. In Jailer 2, too, it is a pregnant woman being flogged that revs its hero into action. In Ranabaali, a pregnant woman’s stomach must be ripped open to protect the child—another future buffering.
The woman’s body is a plaything for commercial Tamil and Telugu cinema—that much is incontestable. Women are arrayed, ready to be ravaged, hoping to be eventually saved, entirely instrumental. Mothers are essential to the plot in ways women are not. The violence exerted on these bodies is tactical, careful. There is a relish with which the scenes play out. Shorn of clothes, they are stripped down to sexual shimmer in songs; they pinprick the hero’s conscience by being raped and assaulted; they secrete fragile visions of the world that men will then murder and trample over.
What does it take to see a woman as a woman, and not the idea of a woman—the feminine not as means to an end, but as an end in itself?
For the longest time I thought that cinema’s obsession with rape, assault, and violence against women comes from society, where sexual and domestic violence is endemic—is an epidemic, in fact. It took a few films for me to recognise that rape is not what they care for, male power is. The proliferation of violence on the female body in cinema is entirely a product of directors—men, mostly—refusing to look the women they write in the eye. For how do you meet the gaze of a wispy idea? Of a burdensome ideal?
Given this apathy, it is impossible to see the hero with schoolgirl braids in The Paradise, or the hero donning a sari before ripping apart goons in Pushpa 2: The Rule, as masculinity that is comfortable with the feminine. Rather it is a masculinity that is expanding, not in tandem with but at the cost of the feminine, swallowing what it previously did not inhabit. The Paradise’s heroine, for example, is introduced in a rush, and her role is circumscribed into that of making B-grade films exposing her body, to earn money to pay off a debt. She makes her mother shoot these films.
The camera leers even as it claims that she is doing it under compulsion. This, perhaps, is the best that the film is capable of—to perform criticism as a shrug while revelling in the thing being critiqued. It is, after all, nice to know when being stabbed that the plunged knife felt bad about it.
Prathyush Parasuraman is a writer and critic who writes across publications, both print and online.

title: Fake Books in Tamil Nadu Libraries Point to a Deeper Institutional Rot
description: Tamil Nadu’s public library scam exposes deep-rooted corruption in book procurement, with thousands of AI-generated and fake books entering library shelves.
author: Ilangovan Rajasekaran
content:
Spurious books, fictitious authors, sham translations, and plagiarised content—the shelves of Tamil Nadu’s public libraries are flooded with AI slop, and the exposé of a massive procurement scam has led to widespread outrage in a State that takes pride in its rich literary, linguistic, and cultural heritage.
On November 6, the well-known Tamil writer Perumal Murugan flagged the issue first in an article on the Tamil online portal Sindhai, in which he expressed shock at the presence of hundreds of such fake books in the recently inaugurated Periyar Arivulagam Library in Coimbatore. Incidentally, Murugan served on a committee that was assigned the task of recommending books for the State’s special libraries in Tiruchi, Madurai, Cuddalore, Salem, and Tirunelveli. The writer, who has been writing on corruption in libraries for quite some time, in his latest article said that these crude AI-generated books had committed “an intellectual fraud” on Tamil society.
Murugan alleged that nearly 1,800 books had been procured from at least one single, and previously unknown, publishing house called Agal Vilakku Publishers, which was not part of the committee’s original list of recommended publishers.
It has also come to light that numerous other books from dubious publishers were procured at exorbitant prices, many of them with questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
DVAC probe
The government swung into action after Murugan’s exposé. The School Education Department referred the matter to the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) for investigation, while the Minister for School Education, A. Rajmohan, ordered an inquiry into the procurement process. IAS officer S. Jayanthi was relieved of her charge as Director of Public Libraries.
On the basis of a complaint filed by the School Education Department Secretary, the anti-corruption team held an enquiry and filed a first information report (FIR) before the designated court for anti-corruption on November 15. The Directorate of Public Libraries under the School Education Department has also reportedly ordered the removal of over 70,000 books by these publishers from more than 4,700 libraries across the State.
The police report largely agrees with what Murugan alleged in his article. For instance, he had pointed out that one dubious book claimed that “Naladiyar” was a poet-philosopher; “Naladiyar” is actually the name of an ancient Tamil literary work.
What Murugan exposed in his article is just the tip of the iceberg. The procurement process for books for public libraries has been a contentious issue for decades now. Several writers and publishers have expressed their displeasure on social media and complained about the endemic corruption that vitiates the process.
The publisher Kannan Sundaram of Kalachuvadu Publications, a prominent publishing house, said in a media report that libraries across the State were suffering from the problem of substandard and fake books. “An exhaustive investigation alone can eradicate this menace.”
A Tamil writer, who chose to remain anonymous, said: “It is an attack on the very idea of intellectual creativity and the lofty principles of a diverse democratic society it represents.”
2024 petition and court response
In 2024, the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court, while responding to a PIL petition by V. Ramasubbu of Tirunelveli on the procurement of books for state-run libraries, voiced concern and asked the government to revisit its policy.
Following this, the then Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government issued guidelines through a series of government orders (GOs), including GO No. 69 dated March 7, 2024, of the School Education Department, to ensure transparency in procurement.
It also launched a “Transparent Book Procurement Portal” on March 11, 2024, through the Directorate of Public Libraries. Later, the government issued a special GO No. 250 on November 5, 2025, to procure materials for special libraries in Coimbatore, Tiruchi, Madurai, Cuddalore, and Tirunelveli, and for new libraries in six newly formed districts. It also sanctioned Rs.50 crore each for the purchase of books, e-books, and other materials for its new special libraries through GO No. 198, dated September 3, 2024. Of this, a sum of Rs.30 crore was given as an advance.
The police investigation into the latest scandal, however, has found prima facie evidence of irregularities, illegalities, and procedural violations in book procurement for special libraries and other district libraries that violate these GOs issued to ensure transparent procurement. In other words, a syndicate of middlemen along with a few senior officials in the Directorate of Public Libraries were able to bypass the gatekeeping mechanism.
The police investigation has revealed that what was initially thought to be a scandal confined to the Periyar Arivulagam Library was actually a widespread malaise, involving a much bigger scandal in the bulk procurement process for all public libraries.
The police’s nine-page FIR states that from February 7, 2026, the Directorate of Public Libraries started placing purchase orders with publishers, including the two publishers under the scanner, Agal Vilakku and Phoenix. These two received purchase orders on February 13 and February 14, respectively, and are both owned by a Chennai-based individual named R. Mohan, who was subsequently arrested on November 16, on charges of criminal conspiracy, cheating, fabrication of documents, and criminal breach of trust.
The probe found that the books procured from these two publishing houses were AI-generated and spurious. The two publishers received purchase orders for a total of 1,857 books, and their books were received by the Librarian and Information Officer, Periyar Arivulagam, in two consignments, on February 25 and March 19, respectively. Payments were made before the end of the financial year in March 2026. There seems to have been a hurry to complete the whole exercise, with the State heading into the Assembly election.
The police report details how the two publishing houses cheated the public exchequer in connivance with a “few unknown” officials, whom the police have not named yet.
Phoenix Publications, which supplied spurious English language books, also followed the same modus operandi, with one of its titles a fake book in the name of the famous economist Jean Dreze, titled Democracy and People’s Rights in the Contemporary World. Dreze has categorically denied having written any such book.
A book titled Deepfakes: The Coming Infocalypse, was published under the author names of “Manisha Saravanan” for Agal Vilakku Publishers and “Charulatha Vivek” for Phoenix. However, the original author is Nina Schick, who published the book in 2020 with a unique ISBN number. In fact, some of these fake books received ISBNs only on February 7, the day the High Level Committee on book purchases finalised the list.
It is disturbing to note how easily these two publishing houses were able to procure ISBNs for spurious publications. A total of 94 books supplied to the library received ISBNs on February 4 and February 5. A perusal of the ISBN portal revealed that the publisher listed 418 authors, of whom six were credited with more than 100 books each on a total of 745 unrelated subjects, which was a clear indicator that the books were most likely plagiarised or AI-generated, but no flags were raised. A few books did not even carry an ISBN number.
Rigged procurement process
The entire procurement process appears to have been rigged to benefit two dubious publishing houses. The police have registered cases against Mohan and “unknown officials” under Sections 61 (2), 316(4), 316(5), 318 (2), 336 (1), 336 (3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or BNS, besides the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and the Copyright Act, 1957.
The investigation report points to “unknown public servants of the Directorate of Public Libraries of the Chennai Anna Centenary Library and the Coimbatore Periyar Arivulagam Library, and other unknown persons” as having colluded to commit the crime. However, Mohan is the only accused named in the FIR.
Although the police report is silent on the identities of these public servants, the government suspended five senior officers of the Directorate of Public Libraries on the day the FIR was filed. They are S. Kamatchi, Chief Librarian and Information Officer (in-charge), Anna Centenary Library, Chennai; Dinesh Kumar, Chief Librarian and Information Officer (in-charge), Kalaignar Centenary Library, Madurai; V. Santhanakrishnan, Librarian and Information Officer, Kalaignar Centenary Library, Madurai, and In-charge of Periyar Library, Coimbatore; S. Santhana Karthikeyan, Librarian and Information Officer, Anna Centenary Library, Chennai; and J. Juliet, Chief Accounts Officer, Directorate of Public Libraries.
Taken aback by the magnitude of the scam, the DVAC has said in its report that the investigation “is to be extended further to unearth whether other publishers supplied similar books to the public libraries”.
In 2024, when the DMK government decided to popularise the library movement, it took a series of initiatives to modernise and upgrade public libraries and construct new ones to provide the infrastructure and required materials for the modern age. To ensure transparency and address grievances that only a few publishers and authors were being favoured, the government set up a series of committees with domain experts, officials, librarians, scholars, journalists, authors, and publishers. The government issued GOs that laid down the rules and specific tasks of each committee.
The Book Recommendation Committee, with 137 members, was tasked with assessing lists of books and e-books, in English and Tamil, supplied by the Directorate of Public Libraries, and pick titles from these lists. A committee member said: “We were given 700 to 800 titles each and asked to pick the best in the shortest time possible. We had no option but to just browse and forward our lists.”
The lists from the Recommendation Committee was received and analysed by a 13-member Book Selection Committee, chaired by Prof. J. Jeyaranjan, Vice-Chairman, State Planning Commission. The committee also had to recommend academic books, Braille and audio books, and children’s books, both in Tamil and other languages.
The final list was sent to a five-member Book Procurement Negotiation Committee, whose main job was to shortlist the recommendations and negotiate with publishers on the number of copies to be purchased at the best prices. The Negotiation Committee was headed by the Joint Director of the Directorate of Public Libraries and included the Deputy Secretary (Education II), Department of Finance, the Deputy Director, Directorate of Public Libraries, the Principal Audit Officer, Directorate of Public Libraries, the Chief Librarian, Directorate of Public Libraries, and the Principal Librarian, Anna Centenary Library, Chennai.
The last link in the procurement process was a five-member High Level Committee, headed by the Principal Secretary of the School Education Department, with members from the Departments of Finance, Public Libraries, and Tamil Development, and the Tamil Nadu Textbook and Educational Services Corporation (TNTESC), and it took the final call.
The Books Recommendation Committee recommended some 26,000 books. Its members are unaware how fake books not recommended by them found a place in the final list. Many members told Frontline that they were not aware of these “unsolicited insertions”.
According to the DVAC report, apart from the above-mentioned committees, a Coordination Committee was officially formed by the then Director of Public Libraries on November 18, 2025, with officials from the Directorate of Public Libraries, and it had “added books that the Books Recommendation Committee had not recommended and placed them before the Books Selection Committee for consideration and approval”.
This was in clear violation of the procurement process. The police suspect the involvement of a few members of this Coordination Committee in accepting and adding lists from the two dubious publishers. The DVAC said that this gives reasonable grounds to believe that “unknown officials” of the Directorate of Public Libraries had colluded with Mohan and other “unknown publishers” to procure the fake books.
What is still a mystery, however, is how bulk orders from dubious publishers escaped the attention of the High Level Committee. While the new procurement system benefited a few new and small publishers, the two dubious publishing houses cornered a lion’s share of the orders, reportedly worth Rs.1.74 crore. Other deserving publishers were left out. Vasuki Baskar, editor of Neelam Publications, known for its Ambedkarite and Dalit perspectives, said: “We received orders for very few books and for a paltry sum.”
The issue has snowballed into a major controversy, with both the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) and the opposition DMK trading charges. The intervention of the higher judiciary has further amplified it.
A two-member bench of Justices G.R. Swaminathan and M.D. Sumathi asked the State government to file a status report on the total purchases made for all State libraries. The bench ordered the issuance of statutory notices to three senior IAS officers, namely B. Chandramohan, former School Education Secretary; S. Jayanthi, former Director of Public Libraries, and M. Aarthi, former Managing Director, TNTESC. “The people at the helm of affairs are bound to answer. Let them explain,” it said.
Clamour for transparency
The anti-corruption team’s initial probe was confined to Mohan, the owner of two of the errant publishing houses, and a few officials. The full extent of fake content that has infiltrated the State’s libraries is yet to be ascertained. To reveal the extent to which the procurement process may have been manipulated, the government must audit all taluk, village, district, and central libraries.
The renowned Tamil writer Cho. Dharman asked the government to “publish the list of all publishers from whom books were purchased and the money paid to them”. Sharing his views on social media, he said that there was no transparency in the procurement of books. He also urged the government to make public the details of the annual International Book Fair, such as its funding and its beneficiaries.
The publisher Badri Seshadri, who runs Kizhakku Pathippagam, told the High Court bench that a Recommendation Committee of eminent personalities would not have suggested books with fake content.
The writer and translator Marudhan said: “A publisher’s credentials must be stored in the procurement databases, which can deter the entry of an unknown publisher like Agal Vilakku.”
Tamil Nadu has 16,871 public libraries, including those run by the State government and local bodies. The Directorate of Public Libraries oversees a network of 4,661 public libraries across the State, which includes State public libraries, district central libraries, branch libraries, and village libraries. The Department of Rural Development and Panchayati Raj administers around 12,000 libraries.
Unless urgent measures are initiated to root out institutional corruption, this painstakingly built intellectual infrastructure of the State could become a symbol of collective shame.

title: E20 Petrol Row: Karnataka Seeks Transparency in Ethanol Blending
description: Karnataka flags excess ethanol in petrol, questions E20 fuel standards and demands greater transparency from the Centre and oil companies.
author: Sujay B.M.
content:
The ongoing tussle between the Karnataka government and oil marketing companies (OMCs) over the exact quantum of ethanol being blended in petrol is the latest chapter in the crucial debate over E20 fuel (a blended fuel containing 80 per cent petrol and 20 per cent ethanol).
A controversy erupted on November 6, when Karnataka’s Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs Minister Rizwan Arshad claimed that 11 of the 14 samples tested at a lab certified by National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) and the International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) exceeded the stipulated 20 per cent ethanol level, with one sample even containing as much as 31.2 per cent ethanol.
In response, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL), and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) brushed off the claims, saying they were “not supported by testing conducted in accordance with the prescribed statutory and technical procedures”.
The OMCs alleged that the testing had been conducted at a third-party laboratory, and not one specified under the Control Order. They also claimed that the certificates did not provide the complete technical details necessary to independently verify the reported ethanol content.
In a strong rebuttal on November 9, Arshad said that the State government had followed the IS 17021:2018 standard cited by the OMCs for testing ethanol content. He noted that the State government had provided 63 samples to the OMCs’ own laboratories and sought the percentage of ethanol blend in each sample.
In an exclusive interview with Frontline, published on November 13, Arshad said that the OMCs did not give a “clear answer” on the issue of the percentage of ethanol blended for any of the 63 samples.
He said: “That made us suspicious. What options were left with us? We had to collect more samples as per the law, [samples that were] also jointly collected by all three parties, duly signed in the proforma. The testing was conducted by an NABL-accredited third-party lab. The result was that ethanol up to 31.2 per cent was being blended.”
While Congress leader Rahul Gandhi picked up the issue and questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi about the quantity of ethanol in petrol, the Congress-led UDF government in Keralam followed in Karnataka’s footsteps, ordering a similar investigation to ascertain the quantity of ethanol in petrol.
Minister’s demands from Centre
In his latest move, Arshad wrote to Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on November 18, recollecting the recent developments, and placed five demands before him.
They include displaying the actual percentage of ethanol blend in every petrol pump and bill, providing an option to choose between pure petrol, E10, and E20 until vehicles are fully compatible with higher blends, establishing a third-party mechanism to randomly test fuel quantity, and creating a dedicated fund to compensate consumers whose vehicles undergo damage due to usage of petrol with ethanol levels above the prescribed limits.
Speaking to Frontline, Bhamy Shenoy, a petroleum industry veteran and founding-working president of Mysuru Grahakara Parishat, said that the ethanol level depended on the part of the tank from which the fuel was drawn.
He said: “Since water and ethanol are heavier than petrol, they sink to the bottom. So, ethanol quantity at the top will be much lower, while it will have to be higher at the bottom. Since the nozzle goes to the bottom of the tank, samples need to be taken from the top, middle, and bottom to test ethanol content.”
He added that the issue could be resolved only through neutral, third-party testing by reputed institutes such as the Indian Institute of Science or the Indian Institute of Technology.
While allegations of over-blending act as the tipping point, the larger controversy revolves around whether E20 petrol is needed in its current form. The controversy began in 2025 itself, when widespread blending of 20 per cent ethanol in fuel began. The government faced outrage for having advanced its earlier plan of implementing E20 by 2030 by five years.
Since vehicles compatible with E20 petrol were being produced only from 2023 onwards, concerns grew that earlier vehicles may face trouble, including mileage issues and increasing frequency of vehicular repair. (Vehicles produced from 2008 are E10 compliant, while those produced before 2008 are built for pure petrol.)
In a press release on August 12, 2025, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas defended the 20 per cent blending of ethanol, saying it benefited the rural economy, eliminating sugar cane arrears and improving the viability of maize cultivation. “More income to farmers has not only contributed to furthering their well-being but has also helped decisively tackle the challenge of suicides by farmers. It may be recalled that in areas like Vidarbha, farmer’ suicides were widespread a few years ago,” the release said.
In June 2026 there were complaints over a drop in vehicle efficiency that raised suspicions over the usage of E20 fuel. On July 28, the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) wrote to the Union Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, raising concerns over E20 fuel.
SIAM letter and retraction
In a letter, which Frontline accessed, SIAM said: “SIAM members are observing huge increases in the issues in customer vehicle parts and replacement (like fuel injectors, duel pump, EGR valve, exhaust and parts that are in direct contact with fuel or engine emission gases). Investigations of field failure vehicle parts reveal the failure is due to corrosion or wear caused by high chloride presence which is traced to the fuel used. Deposits in failed parts also have shown presence of chlorides (sic).”
Pointing out that chloride is “highly detrimental” to engine parts, SIAM explained that including chloride limits in fuel specifications and implementing quality control was imperative to avoid chloride-related failures in customer vehicles.
However, SIAM retracted this move within a week and withdrew its earlier communication on August 4.
In a public clarification, SIAM said: “The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has also instituted 3 ppm guidelines for chloride/sulphur as a precautionary measure for all ethanol being blended into the petrol supply chain. All of these steps fully meet the needs of the automobile industry. Further, we understand from OMCs that checks have been instituted, including water ingress testing about 8-12 times a day in over 87,000 outlets and after each instance of rain near petrol pumps.”
It added: “There is no cause for concern arising from the matter reported as these issues have been routinely addressed over the past several decades between the auto industry and OMCs.”
Critics accused the Central government of pressuring SIAM into withdrawing its earlier objections. On Instagram, the political analyst Tehseen Poonawalla accused the Central government of trying to “hide this letter” and attempting to take down everything from the Internet, including news reports about this letter.
A major concern about the entire controversy of implementing the E20 policy five years ahead of schedule has been the lack of discussions, either in Parliament or in public forums.
Industry opinion
An oil industry veteran, who spoke to Frontline on the condition of anonymity, said that a major push for ethanol could result in a clash between the sugar, alcohol, and automobile industries.
He said: “In principle, ethanol blending in petrol has been accepted, and Brazil is the global leader in this. While E20 has been mandated in India, there are allegations of extra mixing, resulting in the consumer getting a raw deal. We need a discussion between the affected parties on the pros and cons of this policy decision. If any side stands to suffer, they must be informed about it in advance.”
Stating that there are concerns on side effects, potential engine issues, and extra wear and tear, the veteran sought a white paper on the entire issue. It is widely considered that biofuels are necessary at a time when oil is becoming more expensive and there are geopolitical risks in gaining access to it.
The practice is also expected to lower emissions and support the agricultural sector. In fact, the ethanol blended petrol (EBP) programme that was initiated in 2002-2003 by the Atal Bihari Vajpayee-led NDA government was subsequently expanded by the UPA government that succeeded it.
The latest controversy revolves around the incompatibility of a majority of existing vehicles with E20 petrol and the need to develop physical infrastructure in petrol pumps to ensure proper supply of E20 fuel.
“We are not against blending ethanol with petrol. However, engines should be able to digest ethanol-inclusive petrol. Petrol pumps must possess the required infrastructure to disburse such fuel,” Rizwan told Frontline.
Shenoy argued that cellulosic ethanol, which is prepared from cornstalks, grasses, miscanthus, bamboo, or woodchips should be prioritised over corn ethanol.
Gadkari under scanner
Within the ruling NDA government, Union Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari of the BJP has arguably been the biggest ambassador of the current E20 policy. During the 14th Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) Bioenergy Summit held on November 17, Gadkari batted for ethanol blending in fuel.
In a post on X, the Minister said: “Addressed the 14th CII #Bioenergy Summit, highlighting how scaling bioenergy can drive cleaner energy, reduce fossil fuel dependence, boost farmer incomes, create rural jobs, and unlock value from agricultural waste.”
During the KPMG ENRich 2026 Conference at New Delhi in November, the Minister announced the commercial launch of the 100 per cent ethanol powered Toyota Innova Hycross and urged major automobile manufacturers to adopt flex-fuel engines. However, critics have slammed Gadkari’s push for ethanol from a seat of power as a “conflict of interest”, pointing out that his children are top executives and major shareholders in companies producing ethanol.
While his elder son Nikhil Gadkari is managing director of CIAN Agro Industries & Infrastructure Ltd, his younger son Sarang Gadkari is a director of Manas Agro Industries and Infrastructure Ltd.
“Nitin Gadkariji was promoting ethanol and speaks more about ethanol than the Petroleum Minister himself. Let him propagate ethanol and its advantages. However, his own children are running ethanol-producing factories, and he as a Minister is promoting it. There is some sort of a conflict of interest here,” Rizwan told Frontline.
Speaking to Frontline, Poonawalla said that ethanol is the “biggest scam” in India, adding that the huge number of ethanol distilleries in Karnataka and Maharashtra had contributed to the ongoing drought situation in both States.
On the Centre’s claim that sugarcane farmers benefit from increased ethanol blending, Poonawalla said: “Sugarcane farmers didn’t get any money from ethanol. In fact, Karnataka’s sugarcane farmers are on the streets. By growing water-intensive sugarcane, they have harmed India’s food security. We are now importing more oil and pulses and even sugar, a commodity which India used to export. So, we are not saving foreign reserves.”
Global ethanol blending trends
Across the world, ethanol blending has been in vogue for decades. As many as 19 European Union countries, including France, Germany, Belgium, Denmark, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Estonia, and non-EU countries like the United Kingdom and Norway, have rolled out the E10 policy.
However, the leading global practitioner of blending ethanol with fuel is Brazil. It began ethanol blending in 1931, mandating a minimum of 5 per cent blending, extendable up to 10 per cent.
Following the oil crisis in 1973 that exposed Brazil’s vulnerability in the energy sector, the Proalcool policy was rolled out in 1975, ramping up the ethanol blending percentage to 20-22 per cent. Currently, Brazil uses E32 petrol (blending 32 per cent anhydrous ethanol with 68 per cent petrol). Alongside, it also supplies E100 (95 per cent ethanol and 5 per cent water) fuel.
The policy has been successful as Brazil uses flex-fuel vehicles that can run on different types of fuel, which consumers decide based on a number of factors.
In his letter to Puri, Rizwan also highlighted the concerns surrounding the quantity of petrol being dispensed at fuel stations. Of the 5,946 retail outlets in Karnataka, 805 were inspected, and 768 required recalibration. Of the 3,071 nozzles tested, 2,618 showed deviation from their rated accuracy. A total of 101 outlets were found dispensing beyond the maximum permissible error and were booked, and fines totalling Rs.6.66 lakh were collected.
The Minister also took severe exception to Notification GSR 905(E) dated December 18, 2025, which doubles the mandatory verification interval for petrol and diesel dispensers from 12 months to 24 months, meaning that a faulty meter may now go unchecked for up to two full years. He said that the existing annual cycle itself was “barely adequate”.
