title: Vande Mataram played at Waqf Board function 'unacceptable': J&K group of Islamic institutions
description: Such Imposition Disregards Their Religious Convictions And Constitutional Rights, Deepens Distrust, Alienation Says A Statement By Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama
author: PTI
content:
In a statement, the Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU) on Wednesday has objected to the playing of Vande Mataram at the Waqf Day ceremony organised by the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board here by saying that the fundamental and non-negotiable principle of Tawheed in Islam prohibits associating any partner with Allah or attributing divinity to any person, object, land or creation.
The Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU) is an amalgam of religious organisations and institutions representing various schools of Islamic thought.
It said Islam encourages love for one's homeland but draws a clear distinction between loving one's country and worshipping or deifying it.
"Any expression or practice that attributes divinity to the motherland is contrary to the fundamental Islamic belief of Tawheed and is, therefore, un-Islamic and impermissible for Muslims," it said.
The MMU said the All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB) has also clarified the Islamic position on Vande Mataram and strongly opposed its compulsory rendition on both religious and constitutional grounds.
"It is highly regrettable and unacceptable that Vande Mataram was played at a function organised by the Waqf Board itself, an institution entrusted with safeguarding Muslim religious endowments and their sanctity," the MMU said.
"There was no legal obligation to play Vande Mataram simply because it was an official function, and playing it was optional. Yet the waqf board went ahead with it with utter disregard for the fundamental religious beliefs and sensitivities of Kashmiri Muslims, which has caused deep hurt and anguish among people," it added.
The MMU also expressed "grave concern" over the "increasingly routine inclusion of Vande Mataram" at official government functions across Muslim-majority Jammu and Kashmir, "despite the well-known religious reservations of Muslims".
Such imposition disregards their religious convictions and constitutional rights and deepens distrust and alienation, it added.
It said it was deliberating on seeking legal opinion on the issue and would submit a formal representation to the concerned authorities, seeking an end to what it termed the forcible imposition of Vande Mataram at government functions, educational institutions and other public events in Jammu and Kashmir.
The MMU further urged the authorities to respect the constitutionally guaranteed freedom of faith and conscience.

title: Chicken prices face Rs 50/kg hike threat as national poultry body seeks curbs on maize, soy hoarding
description: The Industry Is Facing One Of Its Worst Crises In 50 Years, The Association Said In A Statement, With Feed Prices Rising By About Rs 15,000 Per Tonne
author: PTI
content:
The All India Poultry Breeders Association (AIPBA) urged the government on Wednesday to impose stock limits on maize and soyabean, saying a sharp rise in feed prices was hurting farmers and could push up chicken and egg prices for consumers.
AIPBA also asked the government to release about 3 million tonne maize from state stocks to the poultry industry at concessional rates, similar to support given to ethanol manufacturers.
Poultry industry is facing one of its worst crises in 50 years, the association said in a statement, citing higher feed costs and concerns over the availability of maize and soyabean.
Poultry feed prices have risen by about Rs 15,000 per tonne, making production increasingly unviable and forcing some farmers to cut output or shut down, AIPBA President Bahadur Ali said.
Ali alleged that "artificial scarcity and hoarding" were putting unnecessary pressure on the market despite adequate production of both crops. He pointed to government and agricultural data showing sufficient output across states, suggesting that the shortage is not due to a real production deficit.
Production and demand at poultry feed plants have fallen by 15-20 per cent, while 20-25 per cent of poultry farms have shut or are facing closure, according to industry estimates cited by the association.
Major poultry-producing states, including Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, as well as in north India, have been affected, it said.
Farmers are losing about Rs 40-50 per kg on sales of chicken as prices have not kept pace with feed costs, the association said. Profits earned by integrated poultry companies between April and October were wiped out by November, it added, which could leave them with virtually no income-tax liability this financial year.
Chicken prices could rise by Rs 40-50 per kg and eggs by Rs 3-4 each, the association said. Higher maize prices have also forced several ethanol plants to halt operations, it added.
Some relief in maize and soyabean prices is expected by January, though the near-term outlook remains uncertain, the association said.
Ali warned that continued price increases and supply disruptions could threaten the livelihoods of millions of rural families dependent on poultry and dairy.

title: FSSAI launches pan-India drive to test packaged drinking water; results expected in 2 months
description: The Development Follows The Food Safety And Standards Authority Of India's Decision To Widen Its Scrutiny After A Bisleri Packaged Drinking Water Sample Failed Laboratory Tests
author: PTI
content:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has launched a nationwide enforcement drive to test packaged drinking water samples, with laboratory results expected to take one to two months, its Chief Executive Officer Rajit Punhani said on Wednesday.
The food regulator has also decided to expand its scrutiny to packaging materials used for food products, with inspections set to begin soon to ensure they meet food-grade standards.
The expanded scrutiny comes after a sample of Bisleri packaged drinking water failed laboratory tests, prompting FSSAI to sanction prosecution against Bisleri International.
Confirming the nationwide enforcement drive, Punhani said, " We are in the process. The process has started. We are doing all over the country."
On the timeline for completing the tests, he said, "It's a very big country. So I think it will take at least a month or two."
Punhani said the drive was not prompted by any specific incident but was part of the regulator's broader efforts to protect consumers by ensuring food safety.
"There is no particular reason. If you notice, in the last year, we have taken up, one by one, a lot of things. We have done dairy, meat, eggs, cereals, energy drinks, and sugary drinks. Water is also part of that process," he told reporters on the sidelines of a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event.
The FSSAI chief also highlighted the regulator's action against misleading advertisements and claims made on food product labels.
Asked about the timeline for initiating legal proceedings against Bisleri International, Punhani said it is a "normal routine thing and it will happen".
Earlier, sources had said FSSAI officials inspected the premises of all major food business operators (FBOs) engaged in the packaged water business and collected samples for laboratory testing.
Companies whose samples fail laboratory tests and are found violating applicable rules and regulations will face legal action, sources had said.
On Sunday, FSSAI announced through a social media post that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd over "unsafe packaged drinking water".
A regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from the company's premises for analysis.
"The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006," the regulator had said.
Following an appeal by the company, the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory, which also declared it "unsafe" after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the regulator added.
The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the law.
On Monday, Bisleri International maintained that its packaged drinking water is "safe" for consumption and said it would cooperate with the food regulator to address the issue.

title: Landeed, Fractal Analytics: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
description: From legal-tech to healthcare, dozens of Indian AI start-ups are solving uniquely Indian challenges.
author: Nikhil Inamdar
content:
The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

title: Sonia Gandhi's book 'Belonging' sheds light on her turbulent journey in Indian politics
description: Sonia Gandhi's memoir revisits love, loss and political inheritance, offering a deeply personal defence of her family and its legacy.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
'They will kill you too': Sonia Gandhi's turbulent journey in Indian politics
- Published
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.
Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.
The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.
Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.
"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.
The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.
Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.
It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.
The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.
The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.
For Sonia, the years that followed were marked by retreat.
At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.
After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.
When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".
But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.
Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.
She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".
Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.
Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".
Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."
The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita. Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.
"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."
The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory. Sonia had led the party's campaign.
Sonia goes with Manmohan Singh to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.
At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.
"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"
Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs "Theek hai" - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.
Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.
Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. "I've made up my mind. I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.
She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".
The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.
Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".
Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".
Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.
The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - "Theek hain, aap?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."
Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".
There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".
Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".
Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.
The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.
She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".
A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.
At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.
Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.
The 502-page memoir is less forthcoming about the less flattering aspects of Congress's own record. Sonia has much to say about political corruption, hypocrisy and the decline of public standards under her opponents, but largely sidesteps the culture of patronage, cronyism and corruption that dogged Congress during its years in power. There is little reckoning, either, with the party's own share of responsibility for the erosion of public trust.
She is at pains to defend the political inheritance of her husband and mother-in-law, even as the party they built has suffered a prolonged decline. The story she tells is as much about the costs of carrying that inheritance as it is about a woman who says she never wanted the life she ended up leading.
That gives the memoir's final pages an unmistakable melancholy. Sonia, 79, is now a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament. Rahul, 55, is a four-term MP and leader of the opposition; Priyanka, 53, is also a member of parliament.
Sonia says the challenge was to remain faithful to "a just and humane society", through pain and loss, victory and defeat, and the manoeuvring that politics demands. But she ends not with triumph, nor even with the assurance that history will vindicate her.
"At this moment it seems to me that, although I tried my best, I didn't succeed in beating back the forces I'd set out to fight."

title: Agniveer: Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
description: India has softened its recruitment scheme, giving young soldiers a longer military stint and another shot at permanent service.
author: Nikita Yadav
content:
Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
- Published
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.
The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

title: Taking aim at Atmanirbhar Bharat, US proposes 25% tariffs on Indian goods, 17% if trade deal is signed
description: The United States Trade Representative determined that under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, India has made several “unreasonable acts”.
author: Keshav Padmanabhan
content:
New Delhi: The US criticised India’s Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India) strategy and Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, citing market distortions, and proposed a 25 percent tariff rate on Wednesday.
The United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer determined that under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, India has made several “unreasonable acts” including industrial plans to expand manufacturing; inadequate labour protections; financial repression policies; sustained market access barriers; and failed to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies.
“These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in India and third-country markets…This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT),” the USTR said in its statement.
As a result of these investigations, the USTR proposed a 25 percent tariff rate on Indian imports, which could be reduced to 17 percent, in the event that a trade deal is signed, according to Reuters.
“The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods,” the USTR statement said.
The Section 301 investigation was launched in March 2026, after the US Supreme Court on 20 February struck down the previous tariff architecture put into place by the administration of President Donald Trump under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
The Trump administration had imposed a 25 percent tariff on Indian goods, accusing New Delhi of engaging in unfair trade practices that hurt American companies. After the IEEPA tariffs were deemed invalid, the White House moved to launch investigations under the Trade Act of 1974 against 16 economies over “excess capacity” and several other countries over their failure to prevent forced labour in supply chains.
The investigations into forced labour protections were completed a few months earlier, with the US imposing a 10 percent tariff rate on India. The new proposed tariff rate is unlikely to come into effect until January 2026.
If the first tranche of the India-US bilateral trade agreement is signed, the proposed tariff rate will be reduced to 17 percent. The new tariffs will not be levied over and above the existing 10 percent rate. Instead, they will replace it, becoming the final tariff rate applicable to Indian goods.
The lower proposed tariff rate on Indian merchandise is a result of the ongoing negotiations between New Delhi and Washington, D.C. Last week, ThePrint reported that the US had “assured” India of a comparative tariff advantage to its competitors. A total of 13 countries and the European Union (EU) face new proposed tariffs, while Mexico and Norway are currently outside the proposed levies, despite ongoing investigations.
The proposed rate of 17 percent in case of the trade deal is lower than several of India’s competitors, including Vietnam, which faces a proposed rate of 35 percent (or 20 percent tariff rate if they sign a trade deal with the US) and other countries including Thailand, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Indonesia, Malaysia and Cambodia, all of which face an 18 per cent rate, according to reports.
For India, the latest proposed 17 percent rate is lower than the 18 percent that was announced in February. The two governments had announced a joint framework for the trade deal in February, just about two weeks before the US Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
The first tranche of the bilateral trade deal has yet to be finalised and signed as New Delhi was waiting on the completion of the Section 301 investigations. Now that the US administration has completed the investigations and is set to carry forward the processes under law, which will take at least a couple of months, there remains a brief window for the two sides to potentially finalise the deal.
Prime Minister Modi is expected to travel to the US on 13 December to attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit, being hosted in Miami. Given that the US is hosting the summit, PM Modi is likely to have a bilateral meeting with President Trump, as is the norm when the Indian leader attends multilateral summits.
(Edited by Anupama Yadav)

title: Deepathoon Deepam row: Temple board cites traditional rules, shrine officials dispute their role
description: Temple board's 24 Nov resolution does not mention about SC interim order, but states that customary practice, Agama evidence, among others should be brought to court's attention.
author: Bhadra Sinha
content:
New Delhi: The Board of Trustees of Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple in Thiruparankundram, Madurai, relied on Agama (traditional) rules and established worship practices to deny lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon pillar on Tuesday.
“Based on the historical continuity and religiously significant documents, Agama evidence and the opinions of the sthanikars, the Deepam will be lit this year at the place where it is usually lit,” the resolution, signed by Trustee leader V Shanmugasundaram, noted.A sthanikar is a temple superintendent, chief administrator, or hereditary temple official.
The resolution is part of an intervention application filed before the Supreme Court, by a devotee, alleging the Tamil Nadu government flouted its order that permitted lighting of the Deepam at Deepathoon on the auspicious occasion of Karthik Purnima.
This, according to the 20 November interim order, was a one-time arrangement until the top court disposed of Tamil Nadu government’s appeal against a Madras High Court order that directed the state to facilitate the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon pillar and not the mandapam, which was the customary practice till then.
The High Court order came on a petition filed by a devotee who asked for this direction.
In compliance with the 20 November order, the district collector submitted a status report, which gave reasons for not being able to follow the court order. The collector referred to the resolution of the temple’s Board of Trustees.
The temple board resolution of 24 November, which ThePrint has seen, does not mention about the SC’s 20 November order. However, it states that the customary practice, Agama evidence, and opinions of the sthanikars should be brought to the court’s attention. The resolution is unanimous and in line with the established worship practices, it notes.
It also goes on to say how the age-old custom followed in the temple, which is that the lamp is lit in the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar Temple on the hill above the head of the deity, is a unique religious symbol of the temple, one of the ancient places of worship for the Tamils.
“The festivals, pujas, rituals and Karthigai Deepathi festival held at this temple are based on religious traditions, traditional customs and Agama rules that have been followed for many generations,” the resolution noted.
The application, however, countered the temple board’s resolution and claimed the sthanikars, who were quoted in it, had denied submitting their opinion.
It has annexed a letter which the sthanikars wrote to the temple’s administrative officer, soon after the board passed its resolution. According to this letter, the sthanikars did not submit any letter to the temple.
“We also inform you that we have no opinion regarding the lighting of the Deepam in the Deepathoon on the hill as per the Supreme Court order,” the letter stated, adding the sthanikars were in “deep sorrow” to learn that the board included their names in the letter published and circulated to the media, without letting them know about it.
According to the Madurai collector’s report, every effort was made to implement the Deepathoon lamp-lighting order. However, due to the temple board’s resolution, the lighting could not be completed. It said the temple authorities failed to authorise the designated team.
The collector denied any wilful or deliberate disobedience of the court’s directions, saying that he acted continuously and in good faith to ensure compliance. He also apologised for the lamp not being lit at the designated location on 24 November.
Between 20 November, when the court passed the order, and 24 November, a series of meetings, communications and security arrangements were undertaken by the district administration.
The collector said he convened meetings with revenue officials and subsequently with the police commissioner, officials of the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department, the temple’s Executive Officer and Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) representatives. The meetings finalised the composition of a team of not more than 10 persons authorised by the Devasthanam, the timing of the ceremony, access arrangements and security measures.
During the discussions, the temple administration proposed erecting temporary scaffolding near the pillar, using wet gunny bags and clay to protect its structure, and placing the ceremonial lamp on it. The ceremony was scheduled between 6 pm and 6.30 pm on 24 November.
Accordingly, the police prepared a comprehensive security plan, while involving 5,797 personnel to maintain law and order in the area. Executive magistrates were deployed at 20 locations.
Despite repeated reminders and requests, the collector did not receive any communication from the commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: Pakistan’s astronauts trade their tough image for a Mandarin friendship song
description: In a video released by the Pakistani Embassy in China a day before the Shenzhou 24 mission, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were seen singing in China’s flower gardens.
author: Soumya Pillai
content:
New Delhi: On Wednesday, Pakistani Air Force fighter pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first foreign national to step foot aboard China’s Tiangong space station. But before testing his mettle in zero gravity, this 40-year-old, 5-foot-6-inch-tall military man found himself in China’s flower gardens, with his arms spread open—invoking his inner Shah Rukh Khan—singing about China-Pakistan friendship in Mandarin.
In a video released by the Pakistani Embassy in China a day before the launch, Ali, along with his backup crew member Khurram Daud, also a Pakistan Air Force pilot, was seen singing a “friendship song” in Mandarin, ahead of Wednesday’s Shenzhou 24 mission.
The video, titled ‘Chinese and Pakistani astronauts sing the same song’, opens in a flower field with a lullaby-like melody reminiscent of school hymns. The scene continues to deliver on that promise, with young children lined up, rocking in sync as they sing, “Flowers once told me how you walked through days. The earth knows every corner inside your heart.”
But this children’s song quickly changes its protagonists. Two Pakistani fighter pilots, dressed in their astronaut overalls, take centre stage.
Fighter pilots turned singers
Daud starts off the song in the video. His hands first rest on his waist, then stay crossed and finally hang awkwardly by his sides as he hums, “We crossed a thousand seas and mountains tall.”
The lead astronaut joins in soon after. “Each meeting, each smile engraved in us all.” He seems much more aligned with his inner singer. He opens his arms and then tries to match his movements to the notes he is singing.
Ali and Daud’s Chinese astronaut colleagues join them, but the focus remains on the guests throughout the musical.
The Pakistan Embassy in China titled the video, “Pakistani astronauts sing in the language of their Chinese friends.”
The gesture was reciprocated by the Embassy of China in Pakistan, which called it, “One Song, One Dream!”
“From training side by side to journeying into space together, Chinese and Pakistani astronauts have come together with a shared dream,” the Embassy post said.
It added: “Shared feelings give us the same longing; shared happiness brings us together in one song. Across languages and mountains, this familiar melody celebrates the deep friendship between our two nations and our shared aspirations for peace, cooperation and a brighter future.”
Reception
Pakistani media coverage has called this performance a “special song”. To make it more accessible to local audiences, publications translated it as, “Sitaaron Se Aagay Jahan Aur Bhi Hain.”
“Its central theme reflects the message that Pakistan-China friendship has transcended geographical boundaries and is now reaching the vastness of space. The song features inspiring lyrics expressing determination, courage and the resolve to turn dreams into reality,” an article published by Radio Pakistan read.
But social media has not been very kind.
A handle on X, which goes by the name Surena Sokolov, said that Pakistan’s “bad boys” were reduced to “PG-rated entities”.
“ISPR (Inter-Services Public Relations) has always portrayed PAF pilots like untouchable bad boys but China has totally stripped them down into PG-rated entities,” the account said in a post.
Indian journalist Vishnu Som also posted the video.
“I’ve been fighting with people online for days. Then I watched Pakistani astronauts sing in Mandarin, in a field of flowers, and realised none of it ever mattered. One small step for man, one giant Bholari for mankind.”
(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

title: Viral Video of Chinese Helmets With Integrated Airbags Is AI-Generated
description: Fact-Check: Social media users and news organisations have shared an AI-generated video with the false claim that it shows a real video of innovative helmets in China, which have integrated airbags.
author: Aishwarya Varma
content:
A video showing an airbag opening up around a falling biker's helmet has gone viral on social media, where users have claimed that it shows innovation from China, which has introduced bike helmets featuring integrated airbags.
- Several news organisations, including Times Now, ET Now, and Moneycontrol, shared the video with the same information, noting that they did not independently verify the authenticity of the video.
- However, OneIndia News and Lokmat Times did not issue such a disclaimer.
But...?: The video is an AI-generated one and doesn't show real visuals of such a helmet.
How do we know?: While watching the video, we noticed some visual inconsistencies, such as one of the smartphone screens not showing the vehicle at the beginning of the clip.
Further along the video, the rider's jacket has a white stripe on the left forearm, which turns into a red stripe at the end of the video.
These errors are typically found in AI-generated videos.
We then ran a reverse image search on some parts of the video, which helped us trace it back to a Facebook page called 'Zero Gravity Gang'.
The page had shared the now-viral video on 2 October and regularly posts similar videos of futuristic tech.
To confirm whether the video was AI, we ran the video through Hive Moderation's AI-generated content detector, which showed a 99.9 percent likelihood of it being an AI-generated one.
We also ran it through the Buffalo University's Deepfake-o-Meter and two of their detectors showed 100 percent confidence in the video being an AI-generated one.
Conclusion: An AI-generated video is being shared to claim that it shows a real video of a Chinese helmet which has integrated airbags.
