title: How to Keep Your House Warm in Winter Without a Room Heater
description: Want to keep your home warm without a room heater? Try these 8 traditional Indian winter tips using quilts, rugs, sunlight, and reusable household materials.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Growing up, many of us watched our grandparents prepare for the season by bringing out thick cotton razais, spreading handwoven durries, and opening curtains to let the afternoon sun in.
These simple habits can still help us stay comfortable, reduce electricity bills, and make better use of things we already own. Here are eight traditional and sustainable ways to keep your home warmer this winter without constantly relying on a room heater.
1. Make the most of the winter sun
Open curtains and shutters in rooms that receive direct sunlight during the day. Let sunlight fall on floors, walls, and furniture. Once evening approaches, draw the curtains to reduce the chill coming through windows.
Thicker curtains can provide an additional layer between the room and cold window panes.
This is a humble form of passive solar heating. Traditional homes in our country were often designed around local climates, using natural light, ventilation, and locally available materials. Vernacular architecture in India offers useful examples of how traditional building designs work with natural conditions to create comfortable living spaces.
2. Bring out the traditional razais and quilts
A well-filled cotton razai, woollen blanket, or quilt can make a bed comfortable without consuming electricity. Layer a lighter blanket beneath a thicker quilt on particularly cold nights. Keep an additional throw near the sofa for chilly evenings.
Instead of replacing bedding every winter, air it on a dry, sunny day and repair loose seams or worn covers. Store it only when completely dry, preferably in a clean cotton bag.
Reusing and maintaining bedding helps extend its life and reduces unnecessary purchases.
3. Cover cold floors with durries and rugs
Stone and tiled floors can feel particularly cold during winter mornings. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas, such as beside the bed, near the sofa, and in a reading corner.
You do not need to cover the entire floor. A few strategically placed rugs can make everyday spaces more comfortable.
If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Shake it outdoors regularly and keep it dry to prevent dampness and unpleasant smells.
4. Layer clothing with natural fabrics
A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant.
Wear a few layers that can be added or removed as temperatures change. Woollen garments and hand-me-downs can last for several years when cared for properly. If you need something new, consider repairing an old garment or buying a durable piece from a local maker instead of choosing something that may only last one season.
5. Use old fabric to block cold air
Cold air can enter through gaps beneath doors and around windows. Instead of buying plastic draught stoppers, repurpose old household textiles.
Roll an old towel or stitch leftover cotton fabric into a long cushion and place it beneath doors to limit cold air entering from outside.
Check window frames for gaps and use suitable removable sealing strips where necessary. However, avoid blocking ventilation openings, particularly in kitchens and bathrooms, as homes need adequate airflow.
6. Spend more time in one sunny room
Rather than trying to keep every room equally warm, arrange your daily activities in the part of the house that receives the most sunlight.
Move a chair, work desk, or floor cushion closer to a sunny spot during the day. Close doors to rooms that are not being used, particularly those that remain noticeably colder.
This helps you make better use of naturally available warmth without needing additional appliances.
7. Take inspiration from traditional Himalayan homes
Traditional homes in colder parts of the country provide useful lessons in sustainable construction.
In Himachal Pradesh, Kath-Kuni houses use alternating layers of stone and timber, with thick walls and mud plaster. Their construction helps insulate interiors and retain warmth.
The revival of Kath-Kuni architecture in Himachal Pradesh shows how traditional building techniques and locally available materials can preserve architectural knowledge.
Similarly, homes in Ladakh have traditionally used mud, stone, willow, and poplar to respond to the region’s harsh winters. Traditional building techniques in Ladakh offer examples of how natural materials can be incorporated into contemporary homes.
While these construction techniques cannot directly be replicated in apartments, they demonstrate the importance of choosing materials and designs suited to local climates.
8. Keep your home dry and ventilated
Damp rooms can feel colder and may encourage mould growth. Dry wet clothes outdoors when the weather permits, wipe condensation from windows, and use kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans when cooking or bathing.
Open windows briefly when outdoor conditions are suitable to allow fresh air to circulate.
Keeping a home warm should not mean sealing it completely. Adequate ventilation is important for maintaining a healthy indoor environment.
A warmer home through mindful choices
Keeping your home comfortable during winter does not always require expensive appliances or renovations. Traditional architecture also offers lessons in building homes that respond to their surroundings. By combining these practices with mindful consumption, households can stay comfortable while reducing unnecessary energy use. These measures may not replace safe heating during severe cold, but they can reduce the need to rely on room heaters constantly.

title: Nana-Nani Park Tree Felling: Peepal Baba on Why Mature Trees Can’t Be Replaced
description: Mumbai’s Nana-Nani Park is losing 184 mature trees. Peepal Baba, who has planted over 2.5 crore trees, explains why old trees can’t be swapped for saplings.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
Last week, on 19th November, 2026, a video started doing the rounds on social media. You may have seen it.
A woman is standing in a park in Mumbai, crying. Around her, workers are cutting down trees. One of them is a big old banyan. The workers say it is about 35 years old. She shakes her head — it has been here much longer than that, she says. “This is our tree. This is not their tree to cut.”
The woman is Pooja Ruparel. If you have watched Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, you will remember her as the little girl in the film. The park is Nana-Nani Park in Versova. On 18 November, Mumbai’s civic body, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), started cutting trees there to make room for part of a new coastal road.
Pooja shared the clips on Instagram. Before long, news websites were writing about them. Actors like Dia Mirza and Richa Chadha spoke up too. People have not stopped talking about it since.
Not everyone sees it the same way. Some people felt her pain. Others asked: what will crying change? Doesn’t a crowded city like Mumbai need new roads? Pooja says the tree was protected and cutting it was illegal. The BMC says it had every permission it needed.
But set the arguments aside for a moment, and the video leaves you with a few simple questions. What do we really lose when a tree that has grown for 25 years is cut down? Can’t we just dig it up and plant it somewhere else? And does building a road always have to mean losing a park?
Scientists have actually tried to answer the first question. It takes roughly 400 saplings to do the work of one old tree.
That is the estimate of Andreas Roloff, a forestry scientist at TU Dresden in Germany. To match the shade, cooling, air filtration and carbon storage of a single mature tree with a 20-metre crown, he calculated, a city would need to plant around 400 young ones. Researchers at the Technical University of Munich arrived at a similar conclusion from another direction: when an old city tree is replaced with a young one, the tree count stays the same, but often more than 90 per cent of its benefits disappear.
India has tried to put a number on it, too. In 2021, an expert committee appointed by the Supreme Court valued a tree at ₹74,500 for every year it lives — counting the oxygen, biofertiliser, compost and micronutrients it gives away free — and observed that an old tree and a fresh sapling are simply not equivalent.
Those figures have been tested on the ground in Mumbai this past week.
Despite of many efforts by our community members to save Nana Nani Park, the trees there are being cut. Mumbai already lacks third places for people to hangout, Mumbai’s Air is unbreathable. Yet they want to make it worse! There seems no end to this destruction! https://t.co/61pIJNHNmw
— Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 18, 2026
On 18 November 2026, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) began felling trees at Nana-Nani Park in Versova to make way for an interchange on the Coastal Road North (Versova–Bhayandar) project. Under the approved plan, 184 trees in the park are to be cut and another 164 transplanted to Seven Bungalows nearby. Around 44 were reportedly brought down on the first day.
The park was built in 2001 on what had been a dumping ground. Residents planted and tended its trees for 25 years; many of them have spoken of raising those trees like children. Videos of the felling — including the loss of an old banyan — spread quickly, and protests followed. More than 3,200 objections had been filed with the civic body earlier in the year, and residents had proposed an alternative alignment. The BMC maintains that all permissions were obtained and that the felling and compensatory plantation plans were cleared by its Tree Authority.
There is one more detail worth knowing. Under Maharashtra’s 2021 amendment to its urban tree law, only trees estimated to be 50 years or older are classified as “heritage trees” and given special protection. Most of Nana-Nani Park’s trees, at around 25, fall well short of that line.
Swami Prem Parivartan thinks the line is drawn in the wrong place.
Better known as Peepal Baba, and often called India’s Tree Father, he planted his first sapling in 1977, at the age of 11, at the urging of a schoolteacher. Nearly five decades later, he and his Give Me Trees Trust have planted and preserved more than 2.5 crore trees across over 200 districts in India. He spoke to The Better Indiaabout what Mumbai stands to lose — and what it could still choose to do differently.
‘Any tree older than 20 years should be a protected living form’
Nana-Nani Park is losing 184 established trees, most of them mature. Ecologically, what does it mean for one neighbourhood to lose that many trees at once?
“Any tree that is more than 20 years old should, I believe, be recognised as a protected entity. It should be considered a protected living form.
“There are so many ecosystem services associated with a tree. This is not just about timber. Trees provide shelter and shade, help with carbon sequestration, and support pollinators such as bees, birds and butterflies. They provide nesting and roosting spaces, retain moisture, prevent soil erosion and support the microbial populations that live around their roots. They also help create microclimates wherever they grow.”
In other words, a neighbourhood that loses 184 trees does not lose 184 objects. It loses 184 small systems — each one sheltering, cooling, feeding and holding soil in place for everything around it.
‘You cannot protect yourselves if you destroy the elders of the natural world’
In a city as dense as Mumbai, surrounded by concrete, roads and buildings, how important are mature trees? And what happens to the birds and insects that have built their lives around them?
For Peepal Baba, a tree that has stood for two or three decades has become part of the community’s living fabric. Birds roost in it, insects feed on it, and a web of soil microbes depends on its roots. Remove it, he says, and those relationships do not simply relocate.
“Trees are a very important part of biodiversity. You cannot preserve your culture, or even protect yourselves, if you keep cutting down, chopping up, eliminating and destroying the elders of the natural world — while thinking that compensatory afforestation will somehow make up for it.”
The science on heat backs the urgency. A recent study from Northwestern University tracking Chicago’s tree canopy found that the near-term health benefits of tree cover come largely from big trees already standing, and that protecting existing canopy may do more good than planting alone. A sapling planted today will take decades to cast the shade that a 25-year-old tree casts now.
It is also why he is uneasy with replanting that happens far away. For the Coastal Road North project as a whole, the BMC’s compensatory plantation of more than 19,500 trees is planned in Panvel, citing a lack of space within Mumbai. His view is simple:
“If trees are cut down somewhere, the same species should be planted as close as possible to the location where they were removed.”
The work you don’t see in a park
When we look at a city park, we usually see trees and benches. What less visible ecological processes are going on inside an established green space?
Much of what an old tree does happens out of sight, Peepal Baba explains — in the soil around its roots, in the moisture it holds, and in the cooler pocket of air beneath its canopy. These are the processes that take years to establish and cannot be planted overnight.
“Wherever a tree grows, it creates a microclimate. It retains moisture. Its roots hold the soil together and support an entire microbial population. Bees, birds and butterflies come to it. So many forms of life depend on one tree.”
That matters in a city built on reclaimed land and battered by monsoon flooding and rising heat. Shade lowers surface temperatures. Roots slow run-off. Canopy catches rain before it hits the ground. In Nana-Nani Park, all of this was being done quietly, for free, by trees that residents had planted on a former garbage dump.
‘Transplanting sounds wonderful. In most cases, the tree does not survive.’
Under the plan, 164 trees will be transplanted. Residents had also suggested relocating mature trees rather than felling them. Is transplantation a real alternative?
This is where Peepal Baba is most emphatic.
“There is something people find very appealing to hear: that a tree has been uprooted from one place and planted somewhere else. It sounds like a wonderful solution. But scientifically, the success rate is extremely low.”
He points out that countries such as Japan, Germany, Switzerland, Italy and France have had better results — but with different climates, better technology and, crucially, years of committed aftercare.
“In India, when a tree is uprooted and moved to another location, nobody even goes back to check on it. Nobody ensures that it is watered. Even if you instruct a contractor to move a tree, once the two- or three-month tender period ends, the contractor will not return to maintain it. They will not make sure it gets water or manure, or that it is protected from cows, buffaloes, goats, nilgai — and human beings. In most cases, the tree simply does not survive.”
Mumbai’s own records suggest he has reason to be sceptical. In 2020, the city’s municipal commissioner admitted before the Bombay High Court that only about 36 per cent of trees transplanted for the Metro III line had survived after two years. A later RTI analysis by the Watchdog Foundation found that of 6,043 trees transplanted across the city’s wards, 4,444 had died.
Mumbaikars are speaking, are you listening. Today at Nana Nani Park people gathered to demand that @mybmc stop the cutting and where the 48 trees will be transplanted, if it will be an actual transplantation, not sapling-tokenism and independently review the alternative before causing irreversible damage. #savenanananipark
— Save Mumbai Mangroves (@MumbaiMangroves) November 21, 2026
Which is why, he says, the debate should shift altogether:
“At least in our country, uprooting a tree and planting it somewhere else should not even be considered a viable argument. The discussion should be about protecting the trees that already exist.”
If removal is truly unavoidable, he says, the replacement should be the same species, planted as close as possible, at the greatest height and maturity possible, with the largest root ball. And if anything must be moved, it should be the young.
“If it is a relatively new plantation — trees that are two, three, four or five years old — then perhaps those can be removed. That may still be manageable. But a large, old tree simply cannot adjust to being uprooted.”
‘Trees are not anti-development’
Nana-Nani Park has become shorthand for infrastructure versus ecology. How do you see that debate?
Peepal Baba rejects the framing entirely.
“The debate should not be about infrastructure versus ecology, or infrastructure versus old trees. If you want to build infrastructure, you must also acknowledge the life-giving features of the natural world, and the enormous role trees play in it.
“Trees are not anti-development. They are not anti-infrastructure. Build your infrastructure, by all means. But do it with a little sensitivity, compassion and empathy. Please do not touch the old trees.”
He argues the two are not just compatible but dependent on each other — and that the market already knows it.
“The beauty and value of a landscape, including its real estate value, rises when there are beautiful trees around, when there is water, when there are flowers, and when birds, bees and butterflies are present. Both can coexist. In fact, they are interdependent.”
Nana-Nani Park is not an isolated case. Similar disputes have surfaced in Nashik, around Bhimashankar, in Uttarakhand and across north India. Each time, he says, the same question returns: was every alternative examined before the oldest trees were marked?
The grandparents in the village
When asked why an old tree can’t simply start over somewhere new, Peepal Baba reaches for an image anyone can recognise.
“It is like saying we should uproot our grandparents, or our parents, who have spent their entire lives in one village. Their culture, their habits, their society, their friends and relatives — all of it is rooted in that one place. You cannot simply move them and settle them in another village. That is not how life works. They would die a slow death.
“The same thing happens to trees.”
Nana-Nani Park’s trees were planted by people who are now grandparents themselves. They watched the saplings grow into a canopy over 25 years. Whatever is built in their place, the residents of Versova will be waiting a long time for that shade to return.
“Trees are citizens of our planet, our country, our city, our landscape,” Peepal Baba says. “We need to recognise that.”

title: Kerala Orchid Conservation: 27,000 Orchids Rescued, 71% Survive
description: Kerala researchers rescued 27,324 native orchids threatened by road development and relocated them to three sites in Kozhikode. A 2026 study recorded 71.4% survival, highlighting how orchid rescue and relocation can support biodiversity conservation.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy.
For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat.
In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes.
A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort.
Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived.
Why roadside trees matter to orchids
Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants.
They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once.
The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala.
A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot, recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics.
The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support.
The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK.
More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme.
The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach.
Three sites, different survival outcomes
The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region.
Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas.
Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray.
The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment, while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive.
However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%.
It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively.
What the findings mean for conservation
The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%.
The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka.
This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions.
The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site.
Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc
— Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026
Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants, indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations.
However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided.
Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed.

title: Kerala Nursing Crisis: Low Pay and Long Hours Drive Nurses Abroad
description: Kerala's hospitals face a growing nursing crisis as low wages, unpaid overtime and poor working conditions push trained staff abroad, leaving public healthcare under strain.
author: Sumitra Nair
content:
It is past 9 am, and Jeeshma N.R., a staff nurse at Baby Memorial Hospital in Kozhikode, is waiting to hand over and call it a day. An emergency involving an elderly woman choking added hours to a shift that was to end at 7 am. Shibin Shivadas, who works with the National Health Service (NHS) in London, is sound asleep after a shift that began at 7 am and ended at 2:30 pm.
Jeeshma is working towards a job in Oman. Shibin moved to the UK in 2023.
Doctors and a former government medical official describe the problem in Keralam as a shortage of nurses with experience. Nurses and doctors cite pay that has not kept pace with living costs, overtime of two or three hours a day, and government hospitals where posts have not grown with patient numbers.
Keralam has a long history as a nursing hub. Between 1871 and 1888, British colonial rule and Christian mission hospitals established modern training; the first nursing school was started in Madras in 1871. The first missionary-led hospital, St. Joseph’s Hospital, was started in Manjummel in 1888 and was run with the help of Christian nuns and local women.
The Trained Nurses’ Association of India (TNAI) was established in 1908, and more nursing schools followed in the 1920s. Hindu and Muslim women were prevented from entering the profession on account of social taboos. British medical authorities relied heavily on Christian and Anglo-Indian women for nursing between 1890 and 1900. By the mid-20th century, Malayali Christian women made up a large share of the nursing workforce in India.
According to research by the anthropologist Urmila Goel, West Germany, facing a shortage of nursing staff, began recruiting young Malayali women through Catholic Church networks in the 1960s. Her research documents an early Malayali nursing community there.
Britain, since the inception of the NHS in 1948, has been drawing on overseas nursing labour. Initially, the UK recruited nursing personnel from the Caribbean, particularly Jamaica, as well as other Commonwealth countries. A new phase of international recruitment began in the late 1990s, gathering momentum around 2000–02, when India and the Philippines emerged as major source countries for the NHS. India remains the largest source of international joiners to the register of the UK’s Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC). The council recorded 4,215 joiners from India in 2025–26, which was 54.4 per cent fewer than the 9,249 of the previous year.
The number of Malayali nurses cleared to work abroad has fallen from 9,980 in 2023 to 8,572 in 2024, and 6,393 in 2025, Onmanorama reported, without naming the source of the data. Nurses’ associations attributed the fall to Gulf countries employing their own citizens and to tighter restrictions elsewhere. Malayali nurses still received more clearances than nurses from all other States combined.
Also Read | The tech gap
According to the 2023 Kerala Migration Survey, conducted by the International Institute of Migration and Development (IIMAD) and the Gulati Institute of Finance and Taxation, Keralam has 22 lakh emigrants. Women make up 19.1 per cent of them, and 51.6 per cent of the women worked as nurses or nursing assistants abroad.
“The COVID-19 pandemic was the watershed moment, world over,” says a former government medical official who does not wish to be named. According to him, the term “shortage” would be a misnomer, as trained nurses are being added to the existing pool of nurses. “However, there’s a crunch; difficulty in procuring nurses with experience. Because a lot of the nurses, after working in Keralam for a few years, go to other countries. And see, the situation warrants a study; what can be done about it is another matter because no one can be prevented from going and working abroad and having a better life.”
The intensivist Deepu R., who works at a private hospital in Kozhikode, describes the same gap. “I wouldn’t say that there’s a shortage of nurses but a shortage of experienced nurses,” he says, because many nurses go abroad after two or three years with a hospital.
Pay is not the only reason, the former official says. “Apart from the pay, I also feel that it is also about job satisfaction. It’s about the need to be exposed to the latest technology, job space, and ergonomics. Our nurses are not just a hardworking lot; they are also keen to learn. So when it becomes the combination of working for an unsatisfactory salary, plus working on dilapidated machinery, the prospect of working abroad, with the latest technology becomes very attractive.”
Europe’s shortage
European nations faced a shortage of nursing staff before the pandemic, according to a report by the Mediterranean Institute for Investigative Reporting (MIIR) that cites Eurostat figures. In 2017, Germany had nearly 13 nurses per thousand inhabitants, Luxembourg about 11.72, Belgium 10.96, Sweden 10.90, and Denmark 9.95. In the same year, Greece had 3.31, Spain 5.74, and Italy 5.80 per thousand. Italy and Spain also have lower-than-average ratios of nurses to doctors.
The gap extends beyond Europe. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated in its State of the World’s Nursing 2025 report that the world was short of 5.8 million nurses in 2023, down from 6.2 million in 2020, and projected a shortfall of 4.1 million by 2030. One in seven nurses worldwide, and 23 per cent in high-income countries, are foreign-born, the report found.
“The COVID-19 pandemic exposed deficiencies in the hollowed healthcare systems in Europe—it was exposed not just to the world, but to their citizens; this was no longer acceptable,” the former official says. European governments then brought in trained personnel, creating new opportunities in the nursing sector.
During COVID-19, skilled migrant workers, nurses, and medical practitioners among them, made up a significant portion of the frontline health workforce, according to a 2023 paper in the journal Social Sciences. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) says in its report “Health at a Glance: Europe 2024” that pre-existing shortages of nursing staff were exacerbated by the pandemic.
Pay and the strike
The last time nurses in Keralam went on strike was in March 2026. The United Nurses Association (UNA) began a protest on March 4 and an indefinite strike from March 9. The demand was that minimum monthly pay in private hospitals be increased to Rs.40,000. According to the UNA, wages had stayed stagnant since 2018, despite a rise in living costs. The strikers also demanded better working conditions.
The strike disrupted emergency care and neonatal care services in several private hospitals in Kozhikode, Kannur, and Kochi, to the point that some turned patients away. Aster DM Healthcare said it lost Rs.5.78 crore in additional revenue across its seven hospitals in Keralam.
On March 7, the State government issued a draft notification revising minimum wages for nurses in private hospitals based on the number of beds in the hospital. The UNA rejected it and said nurses would not withdraw from the strike unless pay reached Rs.40,000, according to Onmanorama.
On March 13, the Kerala High Court directed the UNA to defer the strike until March 19 and referred the nurses and the private hospitals’ management to mediation. The court asked both sides to avoid any action that might escalate the situation. Mediation failed, and on April 17 the court modified its March 13 order, allowing private hospital managements to initiate disciplinary proceedings against striking nurses.
The Kerala Private Hospitals Association (KPHA) has called the strike illegal because it began without notice, and has said minimum wages are set by the government through a formal process. The UNA said 422 hospitals had agreed to raise nurses’ salaries to Rs.40,000. Frontline reached out to the management of a private hospital for comment but did not get a response.
“Post the strike, minimum wages might have increased to Rs.30,000. But, if one were to consider student loans, rent, and other living costs, it really is a pittance. More so, if the person has a spouse and children or even parents as dependants. Sometimes, the spouse might not be earning either,” says D. Khan, an executive member of the UNA in Kochi.
The former official says the private sector has a part to play in keeping trained nurses. “Increasing wages and giving nurses a pittance each time they strike, and limiting the salary bracket of experienced nurses is going to hurt—that won’t bridge the gap. There needs to be a rational take on the issue and a largesse on the part of the private sector to maintain trained nursing talent.”
Deepu R. says the strike made it difficult to manage the inflow of patients at his hospital, which, at one point, he claims, had to turn away patients. “Almost no work was getting done,” he says. “Salary really is a problem. I think nurses aren’t afraid of hard work. But I feel that for the amount of work they put in, they really are underpaid.”
Keralam does not have a standard minimum wage for skilled labourers; it depends on the industry or sector. In England, a newly qualified nurse starts on Band 5 of the NHS pay scale, at £32,073 a year in 2026/27, according to NHS Employers.
“A lot of times, private hospitals curb hiring new nurses to maximise profits. Scrub technicians or surgical technologists are being hired instead of nurses and are being paid lower in comparison to someone who has studied BSc Nursing. They are also called GDA or general duty assistants. They are mainly used for surgery assists rather than patient care,” Khan says. Nurses also leave, he says, because “there’s a great demand for nurses from Keralam and they aren’t valued here”.
Shibin Shivadas, 34, studied BSc Nursing in Bengaluru and got his first job at a private hospital there in 2014, on Rs.6,000 a month. “And this is definitely not a salary on which one can survive,” he says. He worked at a private hospital in Farook in 2016 for a few months, returned to Bengaluru for two years, and in 2018 joined Meitra, a private hospital in Kozhikode, where he was paid Rs.22,000. “I realised that my pay won’t see much improvement in the foreseeable future,” he says. After a gap year to prepare, he moved to the UK in 2023. He and his father were the only earners in a family that included his parents, grandparents, and sister.
“We often take loans to study. It is difficult to repay the loan when we get paid as low as Rs.6,000 a month,” says Jeeshma, 29, recalling her pay when she started out as a nurse about seven years ago.
Wages have risen after strikes, but there is still no system of yearly increments. “Yearly increments are next to nil. Nurses are given increments of Rs.500 or 600,” Khan says.
Shibin says he understands that smaller hospitals with 50 or 100 beds probably cannot pay as much, but “the larger private hospitals need to step up”.
Overtime and leave
For Shibin, it was not just the money that made a difference—it was the working hours too. In Bengaluru, he says, “My hours were from 8 am to 6 pm—but, I would have to reach by 7:30 so that the nurse working in the shift before me could hand over.”
The standard working week in the NHS in England is 37.5 hours, and staff in Bands 1 to 7 are eligible for overtime pay at 1.5 times the standard rate beyond that, according to the Royal College of Nursing. UK law sets an average weekly limit of 48 hours, which workers can opt out of. “Whether or not to take on overtime is up to the nurse,” Shibin says. Back home, this was not the case, he says.
“Here, I get insurance coverage under National Insurance. Something I didn’t get back in Keralam. Back home, the government says they will ensure work-life balance and regulate hours, but nothing of that sort happens. Here, in the UK, everything takes place as per NHS regulations,” he says.
Jeeshma, who works in the ICU, is working towards going to Oman. “There’s certainly a shortage. Most nurses end up going abroad. And I don’t blame them. The hours are better; there’s a sense of work-life balance. Almost every day I end up doing overtime for two or three hours. And there’s no overtime pay. And we get a day off once a week,” she says.
Shifts at a hospital are usually divided into three time blocks—a morning six-hour shift from 7:30 am to 1:30 pm, an afternoon shift from 1:30 pm to 7:30 pm, then a night shift lasting 12 hours from 7:30 pm to 7:30 am.
“Night shifts are always 12 hours,” says Titto Xavier, a nursing officer at the government hospital in Mananthavady, Wayanad. “But almost always, nurses go into overtime. For example, I work as an OT (operation theatre nurse). On certain days, six surgeries get scheduled for one shift. However, only four surgeries are completed during the said six hours. Staying back for the two remaining surgeries, puts me in overtime.”
Deepu R. says nurses’ shifts “almost always go into overtime—at least for 2–3 hours each day. He adds: “Lack of a work-life balance is what most nurses have lamented to me about—a nurse’s job isn’t done after a handover. They need to do indentation of the medicines used throughout the day at the pharmacy, add it to the billing of the patient and so on before they leave. Nurses in the private sector don’t really have job security either.”
The gynaecologist Anjitha Pillai, who previously worked at Indo-American Hospital in Vaikom, says pay, working hours, leave, and opportunities for professional development all need to improve. When there is a shortage of experienced nurses, “the workload on existing staff increases, thereby affecting patient monitoring, documentation, giving medication and timely communication with doctors,” she says.
“It is difficult for nurses to get leave—they are asked to ensure another person fills in for them before they’re sanctioned leave. This is something a manager should do,” Khan says.
Government hospitals
In government hospitals, the gap is in posts. As of 2023, the latest figures in the report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) on public health infrastructure and government hospitals across Keralam were short of 978 nurses. The audit found that none of the district and general hospitals it test-checked met the national norm of one nurse for six beds. Records for February 2020 showed ratios as adverse as one nurse for 60 beds at the General Hospital in Neyyattinkara and one for 51 at the District Hospital in Nedumangad.
“As far as I know, openings for doctors and nurses alike in the government sector are less,” says the general physician Mohammed Ali, who works at a government hospital in Malappuram. “We, at government hospitals, get quite a bit of footfall; nurses do get fairly paid. But I still feel that funding in the government sector is less. Moreover, I feel, a lot of the [times], nurses don’t opt to work in a government hospital, because they don’t want to be transferred to different hospitals.”
Xavier says out-patient numbers are not taken into consideration in government hospitals. The out-patient department mostly goes into overtime, he says, because emergency patients are also taken there, and an emergency patient placed under observation is not counted as an in-patient. On some days the number of out-patients is as high as 200. Staff or roles are also not created for day-care patients, such as those who come in for dialysis. The shortage in nursing staff has become acute in the last three to four years, he says.
“New departments have been added in government hospitals. But the recruitment pattern remains the same as it was 40 years ago,” Xavier says. Hiring has not increased in proportion to the population or the footfall, he says, and new posts are created “here and there”, but the transition is “extremely slow.” Forty years ago, a ward with about 70 beds had two nurses. Logging medicines and recording procedures and lab tests have since become more cumbersome, and “even if there were to be 6 nurses for a ward with 60 or 70 beds, the situation would be difficult to manage.”
What the State has done
On pay, the State has acted through the Labour Department. In December, after talks in the Minimum Wages Committee failed, Labour Minister V. Sivankutty directed that a draft notification be issued within a month. He said that since the High Court struck down the 2018 notification, most private hospitals had been paying wages based on the 2013 one, according to Onmanorama.
The draft proposes minimum pay for staff nurses of Rs.25,450 to Rs.30,800, depending on bed strength, against Rs.20,000–24,200 under the 2018 notification, according to Deshabhimani. It is to take effect retrospectively from October 1, 2022, once final. Complaints could be filed within two months, after which a final notification is to follow.
On posts in government hospitals, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan ordered in June that vacancies in the Health, Medical Education, and AYUSH departments be reported to the Public Service Commission (PSC) without delay, after PSC rank holders petitioned that several had not been reported. The government also sanctioned 152 posts for Family Health Centres, including 47 for nursing officers, Onmanorama reported.
On September 23, Muraleedharan said the government would revise a hospital staffing pattern that “dates back to the 1960s” to ease the workload on staff, creating additional posts with the Finance Department while filling existing vacancies, according to Medical Dialogues. The report gave no figures or timeline and did not mention nurses. In October, he announced plans for 1,800 doctor posts.
Also Read | Care over cure
On migration, the State has worked on facilitation and regulation. NORKA Roots, the recruitment agency of the Department of Non-Resident Keralites Affairs, has agreements with Germany, the UK, Saudi Arabia, and Austria for nurse recruitment, and more than 1,400 nurses from Keralam have been recruited under its 2021 agreement with Germany, Eastern Eye reported in March 2025. A stakeholder dialogue by the International Labour Organization and NORKA Roots on decent work for migrant care workers from Keralam was scheduled for April 21.
‘Thank you, Geethu’
In his recent budget speech, Malta’s Prime Minister, Robert Abela, thanked a nurse from Keralam by name, according to Onmanorama and Deccan Herald. Abela told Malta’s parliament that a foreign nurse had come to the aid of his parents when they fell ill and of his daughter when she needed care. “Her name is Geethu. Thank you, Geethu, we are indebted to your service,” he said.
Geethu Louis, 35, is from Meloor near Chalakudy in Thrissur district. She worked as an operation theatre nurse in Keralam before moving to Malta in 2018. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when authorities sought healthcare workers to screen incoming passengers at the airport, she volunteered. She went on to lead COVID-19 testing across the country, managing about 300 healthcare personnel at 32 hospital facilities, the reports said.
When George Abela, the former President of Malta and the Prime Minister’s father, was injured in an accident, she was asked to provide specialised care at the official residence, where she lived with the Abela family for nearly a year. She lives in Malta with her daughter, Tiana. Like Shibin, she worked as a nurse in Keralam before she left.
Sumitra Nair is an independent journalist based in Kochi, Keralam, who writes on culture, gender, and social issues.
With inputs from Frontline News Desk.

title: Tamil Nadu Defies Supreme Court Order in Thirupparankundram Row
description: Tamil Nadu skips the Thirupparankundram Deepam despite a Supreme Court order, raising the prospect of contempt proceedings.
author: R.K. Radhakrishnan
content:
Just past 6 p.m. on November 24, the traditional jothi (flame) was lit atop the Uchipillayar Koil in the Thirupparankundram hill, marking the celebration of the Karthigai Deepam festival of lights in the State. Soon afterwards, Hindu homes across the temple town lit lamps, even as a tense atmosphere prevailed all over town.
“This is how we celebrate Karthigai Deepam,” said the senior journalist Tharasu Shyam, who hails from Thirupparankundram. “As soon as the lamp is lit on the Uchipillayar Koil, which we can all see, we light the lamp in our homes,” he said, adding that the story of a deepathoon (pillar for lighting a lamp) had no relevance for the people of the temple town.
The Supreme Court, in its interim order of November 20, allowed the lighting of the lamp on the deepathoon, which was a demand of the BJP and right-wing organisations. Despite agreeing to all the stipulations made by the Supreme Court and the Madras High Court, the temple administration did not light the lamp on the deepathoon.
And in doing so, the TVK government followed in the footsteps of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which did not comply with a court order in 2025. All TVK allies, including the Congress, the Left parties, the Indian Union Muslim League, and the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi, welcomed its stand.
While there was a clear Supreme Court order on the lighting of the jothi, the Madurai bench of the Madras High Court intervened on November 24, in one part of the issue, and summoned the authorities. The Madurai District Collector was summoned and the court insisted that he show up. He was questioned on why prohibitory orders (Section 144) were in place in the temple town. The Collector placed before the court that his intention of invoking Section 144 was aimed at stopping unauthorised people from climbing the Thirupparankundram hill.
“It won’t apply to anything done to comply with or give effect to the Supreme Court’s order,” he said. He was advised by the court that he was a civilian authority and a public servant answerable only to the Supreme Court in this matter. He was also told that he should ignore any contrary advice from other authorities. The court noted that officials had defied judicial orders on the issue in 2025, when the DMK was in power.
State contention and court stance
The State’s main contention was that it had filed a review petition against the Supreme Court order dated November 20, but no order had been passed on this petition. The court relied on Israr Ahmed Khan versus Ahmednagar Prasad (2026, SC) and other rulings; it said that a review petition can be filed, but the order must be complied with first. Pending review is not a ground for non-compliance, the court said.
The court also made it clear that none of the officials—the Collector, the Commissioner of Police, the DC/Executive Officer, or the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the temple—can plead that they could not comply because of the review petition, which was filed on November 21.
It held that the prohibitory order must not be applied in a way that affects the petitioners’ rights. The court repeatedly told the officers that judicial orders can be criticised, even strongly, but no one can demand with impunity that the Supreme Court’s order not be implemented.
The court agreed with a counsel that it should come down heavily on those openly calling for defiance. Subsequently, in an unprecedented manner, it passed an injunction in the nature of a “John Doe” order, restraining members of the general public from calling for the violation of the Supreme Court’s order dated November 20.
With such stringent orders in place, the authorities went to work. But it was not clear what the government intended to do, as ahead of the November 20 order of the Supreme Court, the State government did not file two crucial pieces of evidence: one, a Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology (TNSDA) report on survey stones across Tamil Nadu, and two, a police intelligence report on the same subject.
But a day after the November 20 order, the State government hurriedly released the survey report the next day, and filed a review petition. But given the intervening holidays, the matter could not be taken up for hearing ahead of the Karthigai Deepam festival.
GTS stations report
The report, titled Documentation of the Great Trigonometrical Survey Stations in Tamil Nadu, was prepared by the Tamil Nadu Department of Survey and Settlement (DOSS) and the TNSDA, documenting physically verified GTS stations across the State.
It noted that more than 800 stations were identified in the first phase of the survey, of which 484 stations, comprising 210 primary and 274 secondary stations, were physically documented. “We have identified around 450 survey stones in Tamil Nadu which were placed in several hills. Based on this report, the Supreme Court special leave petition is filed,” a government spokesperson said.
The GTS of India stands out as one of the most significant feats of scientific and technological endeavour undertaken during the colonial era, and its legacy continues to influence modern geospatial sciences.
Initiated in 1802 under the leadership of Colonel William Lambton, the survey was driven by a vision to create a precise and comprehensive geodetic framework for the Indian subcontinent. It involved the meticulous triangulation of vast terrains, spanning from the southern tip at Cape Comorin to the Himalayan peaks, including the mapping of Everest, which was named in honour of Sir George Everest, a pivotal figure in the survey’s progression.
This monumental project employed advanced instruments such as massive theodolites weighing over 1 tonne and involved constructing durable survey stations ranging from solid masonry pillars in hilly regions to brick and stone structures in plains, each carefully marked with control points for accurate positioning, M. Venkadesan, Additional Director, DOSS, said in the foreword to the report.
“The preserved data and physical markers serve as invaluable links to India’s rich heritage of scientific exploration, highlighting the enduring importance of integrating historical knowledge with contemporary technology,” he added.
With the results of the survey in place, Tamil Nadu hopes to convince the apex court that the structure atop the hill is only a survey stone, with nothing sacred about it. But, for now, there is more trouble for the State and its officials. On November 25, the Tamil Nadu government informed the Supreme Court that its order on lighting the jothi atop the survey stone could not be complied with. In a move that raised several eyebrows, the Madurai Collector filed a compliance report, in which he blamed the temple authorities for not carrying out the instructions.
A petitioner named Rama Ravikumar has claimed that the State government and all its organs lied to both the Supreme Court and the Madras High Court. The Supreme Court has granted liberty to the original parties to file a contempt petition against the Tamil Nadu government.

title: India’s Healthcare Crisis: Why Quality and Accountability Fail
description: India’s healthcare system boasts world-class hospitals, yet diagnostic errors, unsafe medicines and commercial interests expose deep inequalities. Who protects patients? Demand accountability.
author: Ameer  Shahul
content:
In his review of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi’s Belonging: A Journey of Love in a Malayalam newspaper, A.K. Antony, former Defence Minister, recounted a personal experience. A prolonged spell of weight loss had led him to consult four premier hospitals, including the prestigious All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. He was diagnosed with cancer in 2014. Before starting treatment, he informed Sonia about it. She advised him to wait and facilitated an urgent medical consultation in the US. The subsequent assessment attributed his weight loss to protein deficiency rather than cancer. In the review, Antony thanked Sonia for helping him avoid what could have been an expensive, painful, and entirely unnecessary course of cancer treatment.
Sonia herself had chosen to undergo surgery to remove a precancerous growth in her pancreas at the University Medical Centre in Rotterdam, even though, she asserts in the book, she had complete confidence in the doctors who treated her breast cancer at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital in New Delhi in 2010.
Their narratives raise deeply uncomfortable questions about the reliability of medical diagnosis in India. Four hospitals, including one of the country’s foremost tertiary-care institutions, and two superspeciality private hospitals, apparently failed to identify the underlying problem in Antony’s case. Remember this was not an ordinary citizen struggling to navigate an unfamiliar healthcare system. Antony was Defence Minister at the time, with access to the country’s most distinguished medical professionals and institutions.
What, then, is the experience of the millions of ordinary Indians who have neither the resources nor the connections to seek a second opinion abroad?
The above anecdotes are not proof of Indian healthcare being poor overall. But they are an invitation to examine a much larger malice: the quality of healthcare delivered by institutions that millions of Indians trust with their lives.
India has invested considerably in building hospitals, medical colleges, specialist institutions, and diagnostic infrastructure. It is true that we have some extraordinarily accomplished doctors and world-class medical facilities. But Antony’s experience proves that such capacity and infrastructure need not translate into clinical excellence always. A hospital can have the most sophisticated equipment, an impressive building, and internationally trained specialists and still fail patients in the most crucial step: correct diagnosis.
Diagnosis is the foundation of medical treatment. An incorrect diagnosis can send patients down an entirely wrong treatment pathway, exposing them to unnecessary procedures or medication, financial expenditure, and psychological trauma. In some cases, it can delay the treatment of the actual condition until it becomes much more difficult to manage. Therapies administered for a non-existent disease can also have far-reaching implications on the person’s health.
The problem can partly be attributed to the growing commercialisation of diagnostics. Investigations which should be guided by clinical necessity can become part of a revenue-generating chain. Patients are often asked to undergo multiple tests, sometimes at different facilities, without being adequately informed about its necessity or the interpretation of results.
The proliferation of diagnostic centres without proper accreditation and external quality assessment is further cause for extreme concern. We need stronger standardised reporting and accountability for diagnostic errors. A test result is only as useful as the quality of the laboratory, the interpretation of findings, and the clinical judgement that follows.
There is also a fundamental distinction between technological sophistication and medical competence. A hospital possessing an advanced MRI scanner or sophisticated laboratory facilities does not automatically possess the clinical judgment required to use them appropriately.
These scenarios force us to ask a difficult question. Are we measuring the success of healthcare institutions by the buildings they construct, the number of beds they add, and the revenue they generate, or by their diagnostic accuracy, treatment outcomes, and patient safety?
The quality crisis does not end at the diagnostic centre or the hospital pharmacy. It extends to the pharmaceutical industry.
The reputation of Indian pharmaceuticals cannot become a shield against scrutiny of manufacturing quality, regulatory enforcement, and access to medicines.
The pharmaceutical market is characterised by considerable information asymmetry. Patients generally have little ability to assess the quality of a medicine, its manufacturing standards, bioequivalence, or the reliability of its supply chain. They depend on doctors, pharmacists, and regulators to protect them.
Substandard and spurious medicines, manufacturing deficiencies, and failures in quality control raise questions about the effectiveness of regulatory oversight. The problem is not confined to small manufacturers. Quality assurance must cover the entire manufacturing ecosystem, including large companies, contract manufacturers, and suppliers of active pharmaceutical ingredients.
India needs stronger risk-based inspections, transparent publication of inspection findings, independent testing, and swift action against repeat offenders. Drug recalls must be timely, traceable, and publicly accessible.
There is one more concern worth flagging: the growing commercial influence over prescribing practices. Pharmaceutical marketing tactics like doctor engagement and incentives influence the relationship between the prescriber and the manufacturer. The patient, who ultimately pays for the treatment, is often the least informed participant in this transaction. A medicine is not merely a commercial product. Its quality can determine whether a patient recovers, remains ill, or suffers additional harm.
Inadequacy of life-saving medical devices
Medical devices are an under-examined dimension of India’s healthcare quality crisis. From cardiac stents and orthopaedic implants to diagnostic equipment, surgical instruments, and intensive-care devices, modern medicine increasingly depends on sophisticated technologies. These devices can save lives, restore mobility, and improve the quality of treatment. But they also introduce risks when manufacturing standards, clinical validation, procurement practices, and post-market surveillance are inadequate.
The issue is particularly important because a substantial part of the medical device market in our country depends on imports, even while domestic manufacturing is expanding. A device approved for use is not necessarily a device that will perform identically across every clinical setting. Its safety depends on manufacturing consistency, proper installation, calibration, maintenance, and the competence of the medical professional fixing it.
Implantable devices present an additional challenge. Once a cardiac stent, artificial joint, or another implant is placed inside a patient, identifying a defect or adverse outcome can be difficult. Patients may not even know the manufacturer, model, or batch number of the device implanted in their bodies to address possible complications caused by the device later.
India needs a much stronger system of device traceability, mandatory adverse-event reporting, independent performance testing, and transparent disclosure of device-related complications.
The regulation of medical devices cannot stop at granting market approval. It must follow the device throughout its life cycle, from manufacturing and importation to clinical use and post-market surveillance.
Across hospitals, in diagnostics, in pharmaceuticals, and with medical devices, the one problem that recurs is accountability. Issues are fragmented and nobody wants to own up to them. The hospital blames the diagnostic laboratory. The laboratory points to the limitations of the test. The doctor may attribute the outcome to the patient’s underlying condition. The device manufacturer will question the manner in which his product was used. The pharmaceutical company will insist that its medicine met the prescribed specifications. Meanwhile, the patient is left to bear the consequences.
India’s regulatory architecture must therefore move beyond licensing and procedural compliance towards measurable healthcare outcomes. We need publicly accessible information on hospital-acquired infections, diagnostic accuracy, surgical complications, readmissions, medication errors, device failures, and treatment outcomes. Equally important is the need for independent mechanisms through which patients can seek redressal.
We must also strengthen public healthcare. Institutions such as AIIMS, Christian Medical College Vellore, Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences, and the Cancer Institute (Adyar) demonstrate that India has the institutional and professional capabilities to deliver high-quality medicine. Public and trust-run hospitals must be strengthened, not displaced by an increasingly commercialised healthcare ecosystem.
A healthcare system should be capable of identifying disease correctly, treating it safely, and accepting responsibility when it fails. For the patient, the difference between these capabilities is not academic. It can be the difference between recovery and suffering, financial security and ruin, or even life and death.
Ameer Shahul is the author of the best-selling books Heavy Metal, Vaccine Nation, and The Silent Syndicate: How Global Finance is Destroying India’s Healthcare.

title: Prevented court-ordered lighting of Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, challenged Madras HC order to remove Periyar statue from temple land: How TVK has outperformed DMK in being anti-Hindu in just six months
description: The TVK government has not only filed review petition against Supreme Court order allowing one-time lighting of Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, it has also moved a petition before the Supreme Court, challenging the October 2026 Madras High Court order directing the removal of a statue of anti-Hindu ‘activist’ E. V. Ramasamy Naicker, better known as Periyar. | OpIndia News
category: Editor's picks, Featured, Opinions, Political History of India, Politics
author: Shraddha Pandey
content:
Tamil Nadu is arguably the only state in India where mainstream political parties compete with each other to prove that they are more anti-Hindu than their opponents. For years, the DMK government and leaders openly suppressed Hindu, and even declared intentions to eradicate Sanatan Dharma. Now the over six-month-old TVK government led by CM C Joseph Vijay appears to be aiming to outperform DMK in taking anti-Hindu measures. The TVK demonstrated its anti-Hindu stance through its defiance of the Supreme Court order to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill on 24th November.
TVK government opposed Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, filed review petition, arrested Hindus and defied court order: How TVK crushed Hindus to appease Muslims
On 20th November, the Supreme Court allowed the lighting of ‘Karthigai Deepam’ atop the Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai, during the Karthigai Deepam festival on November 24, 2026.
A Bench comprising Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi passed the order with the condition that only authorised persons from the Devasthanam (temple administration) and government officials will be able to conduct the lamp lighting ceremony.
The court granted the interim relief considering the present circumstances. It noted that if the lighting of the lamp was not allowed on the festival, no subsequent relief would be able to make up for that.
This was strictly a one-time measure. Yet since Muslims are against the lighting of Karthigai Deepam merely because the Deepathoon is situated near a Dargah on the same hill, the Muslim-appeasing TVK government blatantly defied the court order.
First, the TVK government, through the HR&CE Commissioner, filed a review petition against the Supreme Court order.
It contended that granting one-time permission amounts to granting final relief at the interlocutory stage itself.
The petition asks whether the Supreme Court should have issued a mandatory interim direction without the petitioners establishing a strong prima facie case and demonstrating that the balance of convenience favoured them.
The petition invoked provisions of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
It highlighted that under Section 28(1), trustees are responsible for administering the affairs of religious institutions. Section 63(e) empowers the Joint Commissioner to inquire into and decide questions concerning established usage in a religious institution.
The TVK government’s review petition says that the question of where the Hindu temple’s traditional lamp should be lit must be addressed through the appropriate statutory and institutional process instead of determining it through an interim judicial direction.
It also argued that there is no established customary or legal right to light the lamp at the stone pillar atop the hill.
Know Your Rights
The review petition also claims that the Hindu petitioners have not presented documentary evidence establishing that the location was historically used for the ceremony.
The TVK government expressed its apprehension that granting even one-time permission for lighting the traditional lamp, Karthigai Deepam, would set a precedent for future claims.
The review petition is worried about the Deepathoon’s proximity to a nearby Islamic shrine named Sikandar Badhusha Dargah.
The CM C Joseph Vijay-led government is concerned that lighting a traditional Hindu lamp at this spot close to a Dargah could pose a risk of disturbing communal harmony.
The Vijay government’s opposition to the Supreme Court order didn’t remain confined to a review petition.
The TVK government mobilised the state machinery to defy the Supreme Court order and ensured that the Karthigai Deepam could not be lit at the Deepathoon.
Heavy police deployment, promulgation of Section 144 in Madurai and other obstructive acts by the TVK government showed that it is just as anti-Hindu as the DMK, in fact, even more desperate for appeasing Muslims.
In the process, hundreds of Hindus, including several BJP leaders, were arrested or detained.
As the TVK government stopped the lighting of the Deepam at Deepathoon on the Thiruparankundram Hill, Hindu Munnani State president Kadeshwara Subramaniam said that the “anti-Hindu” TVK regime will collapse.
On 25th November, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government apologised in the Supreme Court after it lit the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the traditional Uchipillayar Deepa Mandapam rather than the Deepathoon stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill, in violation of its order.
The state claimed that the order was not executed because of the Board of Trustees.
However, the legal representatives of the Hindu petitioners exposed the deceptive tactics.
“This is like anticipatory breach, anticipatory mentioning. Most unfortunate, My Lords. State tells the High Court some prohibitory orders were. They use the Board of Trustees, and I say this, to say the custom does not permit it, and the sthanikars have said it cannot be done,” they said, adding that the government and the devasthanam joined hands to defend the contravention of the verdict.
Clearly, from legal routes, mobilisation of administrative machinery to deceptive rhetoric, the CM Vijay-led TVK government played every tactic in the book to ensure that the Hindus could not light the Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, Muslims remain content, and TVK could dodge contempt charges while also coming across as an upholder of ‘secularism’.
TVK’s anti-Hindu actions are not confined to the Thiruparankundram controversy.
Vijay government filed plea challenging Madras High Court order to remove Periyar statue from Hindu temple land
On one hand, the TVK government filed a review petition against the Supreme Court order in the Karthigai Deepam case.
On the other hand, it moved a petition before the Supreme Court, challenging the October 2026 Madras High Court order directing the removal of a statue of anti-Hindu ‘activist’ E. V. Ramasamy Naicker, better known as Periyar, installed on land belonging to an ancient Shiva temple in Tamil Nadu’s Thanjavur district.
The Vijay government filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) through the District Collector of Thanjavur on 22nd November 2026.
The High Court order concerns the statue installed on land belonging to the Brahma Sirakandeeswarar Temple at Kandiyur, an ancient Hindu shrine revered by devotees of Lord Shiva.
A bench comprising Justices Velmurugan and Ramakrishnan passed the order while hearing a petition filed by Rama Ravikumar, a resident of Ezhumalai in Madurai district. He had approached the court challenging the installation of the statue on temple-owned property.
The case raises questions about how a statue of a notorious Hinduphobe came to be installed on land belonging to a Hindu temple, particularly when the petitioner claims that the installation never received the necessary approval from the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department.
The petitioner had filed an inquiry under the Right to Information Act (RTI).
The May 2025 RTI response stated that the HR&CE Department had not granted any permission or approval for installing the statue of EV Ramasamy on the temple property.
The Hindu petitioner’s objection was not limited to the alleged absence of official permission.
He also questioned the presence of an inscription beneath the statue that openly rejects the existence of God and uses derogatory language against those who believe in and worship God.
The inscription reads:
“There is no God, there is no God, there is no God at all. He who created God is a fool. He who propagates God is a scoundrel. He who worships God is a barbarian.”
This is not an isolated case. Similar inscriptions were installed near prominent Hindu temples during the tenure of Dravidian governments.
Despite knowing that these inscriptions are blatantly Hinduphobic and that Periyar was an outright Hindu hater, the TVK government has challenged the Madras High Court order which directed removal of the statue.
This is when TVK and C Joseph Vijay publicly declared earlier that he and his party have accepted Periyar’s broader principles, but they do not accept his atheism or rejection of God.
And yet, the TVK government has an issue with the removal of Periyar’s statue.
Reason? Tamil Nadu’s political landscape.
In Tamil Nadu, the supposed liberal and progressive political parties compete with each to prove that they are more secular, tolerant, inclusive, rational and progressive than others.
However, these are all high-sounding words for opposing, crushing and humiliating Hindus, their beliefs, sentiments and rights.
DMK prevented the lighting of Karthigai Deepam when it was in power; now TVK has done the same.
DMK leader and former Deputy CM Udhayanidhi Stalin gave calls for eradication of Sanatan Dharma, so did TVK MLA VMS Mustafa.
In the Indian Islamo-leftist understanding of secularism and rationality, Hinduism alone is the dogmatic, divisive and dehumanising religion.
Islam, Christianity and other religions are not subjected to such ‘rational’ scrutiny perhaps because of the electoral usefulness of their adherents as a votebank.
From Periyar and Annadurai to DMK and TVK, rationality, social justice, freedom from superstition and smashing patriarchy have always been about scrutinising and mocking Hindus, Hindu Gods, rituals, vilifying Brahmins and appeasing Muslims and Christians.
Periyar’s anti-Hindu activism and how Nehru described him as a lunatic
Born in 1879, Periyar was a vehement anti-Hindu and anti-Brahmin activist.
While contemporary EVR apologists argue that he never advocated racial hatred against Brahmins. Periyar was quite explicit in his expression of his hatred against Hindus.
The magazine Periyar edited published articles praising the ascendancy of Adolf Hitler and warned Brahmins in Tamil Nadu that they should learn from the plight of Jews in Nazi Germany and opt for course correction.
He reportedly used to tell his followers that if they ever encountered a Brahmin and a snake on the road, they should kill the Brahmin first.
Periyar, in his lifetime, spread numerous canards about the Ramayana. All his lies were directed towards slandering the God who is considered Maryada Purushottam by Hindus. His lies ranged from accusing Shri Rama of being casteist to claiming that he killed and mutilated women.
Periyar not only claimed that no ‘North Indian Brahmin’ died in the war against Ravana but further propagated that Lord Rama had married women other than Sita for his sexual pleasure. He had also claimed that Lankan King Ravana was, in fact, a Dravidian King from South India.
Periyar had also burnt pictures of Lord Rama, who is one of the most revered Hindu gods. This is not all; Periyar is notorious for organising a procession in Salem in Tamil Nadu with big cutouts of “Ram”, “Sita” and “Hanuman” garlanded with slippers.
Periyar also broke statues of Lord Ganesha. From rhetoric to action, Periyar exploited every opportunity at hand to express his visceral hatred against Hindus and Brahmins.
Interestingly, India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru had on many occasions called out Periyar’s Hindu hate. Nehru had gone to the extent of suggesting that Periyar should be sent to a lunatic asylum.
In a letter [pdf] to Madras Chief Minister Kumaraswami Kamaraj on November 5, 1957, PM Nehru stated, “I am much distressed by the anti-Brahmin campaign continuously carried on by E.V. Ramaswami Naicker… I find that Ramaswami Naicker is going on saying the same thing again and calling upon people at the right time to start stabbing and killing. What he says can only be said by a criminal or a lunatic.”
PM Nehru was of the view that anti-Brahmin ‘activists’ such as Periyar should be placed in a mental asylum, meant for the treatment of ‘perverted minds’.
In a November 1957 letter to Tamil Nadu CM Kamaraj, Nehru urged the CM to stop Periyar’s hate campaign against Hindus.
A book on Madras State’s fourth CM, C. N. Annadurai, written by PC Ganesan, also makes reference to PM Nehru dubbing Periyar as an ‘old and senile’ man who deserved to be in a lunatic asylum.
“The Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru considered it a sacrilegious act and in an outburst of anger remarked that “old and senile men like Periyar deserved a place more in a lunatic asylum than in public life,” it quoted PM Nehru as saying.
TVK’s Muslim and Christian appeasement policies
Coming back to the current TVK government in Tamil Nadu, it has been accused of squandering state funds on freebies and Muslim appeasement-driven schemes even as the state’s financial health is deteriorating.
Recently, the TVK government announced that the state government will cover the full undergraduate tuition fees for Muslim female students admitted under the government quota in government, government-aided, and self-financing colleges. For this, the government allocated ₹20 crore.
Minister A M Shahjahan also announced the expansion of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board scholarship for Muslim girls, from Classes 1-8 to Classes 9-10 at ₹2,000 per year. The scheme is expected to benefit 41,384 Muslim schoolgirls for Rs 8.28 crore.
An announcement was also made about a ‘minorities’ women’s college in Chennai through the Waqf Board, with an initial grant of ₹2.45 crore.
Moreover, the Vijay government has also announced a ₹100 crore interest-free revolving fund for loans to develop income-generating assets like marriage halls, commercial complexes, etc. on Muslim and Christian properties.
The state government will also construct a new headquarters for the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board at an estimated cost of ₹40 crore. The administrative grant for the state Waqf Board will also be raised to ₹5 crore.
In November 2026, the Joseph Vijay-led government in Tamil Nadu decided to regularise encroachments by issuing pattas to thousands of mosques, churches and dargahs.
According to A M Shah Jahan, Minister for Minorities Welfare, the government was working to regularise religious institutions that lack ownership documentation. He informed that minority groups petitioned the government for pattas for unlawful houses of worship that had been on government property for 25-50 years.
Conclusion
Tamil Nadu Hindus are on their own. DMK or TVK, the names change, but their disdain and bias against Hindus remain constant. This disdain finds an outlet in their conduct in matters like the Karthigai Deepam issue and the Periyar statue case.
For them, no length is too far when it comes to appeasing Muslims at the cost of suppressing Hindu rights. It’s not even a cost; they enjoy it.
The BJP, though, is standing firmly and unapologetically with Hindus in the Thiruparankundram issue, and otherwise, they have just one MLA in the state assembly.
While it remains to be seen whether the courts hold the TVK accountable or tell Hindus to accommodate, until a political-ideological turnaround unfolds in Tamil Nadu in view of the civilisational stakes, this mockery of Hindu rights under the pretext of secularism will continue.

title: Assam: Union Cabinet Clears Rs 2,014 Crore Greenfield Airport Project At Doloo In Silchar's Barak Valley
description: The Union Cabinet approved the development of a new greenfield airport at Doloo in Silchar, Assam, at an estimated cost of ₹2
author: Arjun Brij
content:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 07:56 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Union Cabinet approved the development of a new greenfield airport at Doloo in Silchar, Assam, at an estimated cost of Rs 2,014 crore today.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, cleared the proposal for the Airports Authority of India to construct the facility.
The project will overcome the severe operational and spatial constraints of the existing defence landlocked civil enclave at Silchar Airport and accommodate sustained passenger growth.
Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw stated that the airport will have the capacity to handle 800 passengers during peak hours and an annual passenger handling capacity of 1.01 million.
The proposed terminal building will span 12,351 square metres with modern passenger amenities, sustainable green building principles, and modular expansion capability. The project will be funded entirely from the Airports Authority of India's own internal resources.
The infrastructure includes a 2,705-metre-long, 45-metre-wide Code-4C compliant runway suitable for A-320 aircraft operations, along with construction of a new apron capable of parking six A-320 aircraft and a dedicated isolation bay.
The current Silchar airport operates only as a civil enclave inside a defence-controlled airfield, which restricts its space and operations at a time when passenger numbers are rising steadily.
Doloo, situated in the Cachar District of Assam, serves as the strategic heart of the Barak Valley.
