title: ‘Where is the accountability?’: Modi govt’s focus on ‘mild’ anaemia cannot obscure scale of crisis, says Cong
description: Citing ICMR-SAMPADA Data, The Opposition Party Flags Anaemia Among 55.9% Of Women Of Reproductive Age And Nearly Two-thirds Of Adolescents, While Questioning Unutilised Nutrition Funds And Shrinking Budget Allocations
author: Our Web Desk
content:
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Wednesday questioned the Modi government’s record on tackling malnutrition, asking how the country can reap its demographic dividend when millions of women and children continue to suffer from anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies despite years of welfare schemes and supplementation programmes.
In a post on X, Kharge cited findings from the Centre’s own ICMR-SAMPADA survey, pointing to the high prevalence of anaemia among women and children and widespread vitamin B12 deficiency among adolescents. He also questioned the government’s spending priorities and sought accountability for what he described as gaps in implementing its nutrition programmes.
"How can India realise its demographic dividend when millions of its women and children continue to suffer from malnutrition?" Kharge asked.
According to the figures cited by the Congress chief, 55.9 per cent of women of reproductive age in the country are anaemic, while nearly two-thirds of adolescent girls and boys suffer from Vitamin B12 deficiency. As many as 42 per cent of children aged one to four years are also anaemic.
Kharge singled out Gujarat, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state, where the corresponding anaemia estimates were 66.2 per cent for women and 56.5 per cent for young children.
He also questioned the Centre’s emphasis on the share of cases classified as mild. The Union health ministry said most cases nationally were mild. For the group of women Kharge cited, the survey estimated that 26.9 per cent had moderate anaemia and 2.9 per cent had severe anaemia.
“Modi Govt’s emphasis on ‘mild’ anaemia cannot obscure the fact that nearly 30% of women of reproductive age suffer from MODERATE or SEVERE anaemia,” he wrote.
Citing the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), the Congress leader pointed out that nearly one-third of children under five were underweight. The national estimates were 31.8 per cent and 19 per cent, respectively.
Beyond the health indicators, Kharge questioned whether the money allocated to nutrition programmes was translating into meaningful outcomes.
Citing government financial records, he said more than Rs 1.13 lakh crore had been released under Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 and their predecessor schemes over six financial years. He flagged a gap of more than Rs 2,500 crore between funds released and utilised under POSHAN 2.0 in four years. Nearly 44 per cent of the funds released under the original POSHAN Abhiyaan also remained unutilised, according to the figures he cited.
Kharge also pointed to a decline in the Ministry of Women and Child Development's share in the Union Budget, from 0.96 per cent in 2015–16 to 0.50 per cent in 2025–26.
“After 12 years of the Modi Govt, multiple nutrition schemes, fortified rice and iron supplementation programmes, where is the ACCOUNTABILITY?” he asked.
The criticism comes amid a separate intervention by Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh, who on Tuesday, in a post on X, flagged findings from a Union health ministry report titled *Anaemia and Micronutrient Deficiencies Across Life Stages in India*.
Comparing Gujarat and Kerala, Ramesh questioned the gap in nutritional outcomes between the two states, particularly as the BJP has frequently projected Gujarat as a model of development.
According to figures Ramesh shared, 61.4 per cent of adolescent girls aged 10-19, 63.8 per cent of adult women aged 20-59 and 66.2 per cent of women of reproductive age in Gujarat were found to be anaemic during 2023-25. Chhattisgarh was the only state with a worse situation, he said.
In Kerala, the corresponding figures stood at 21.4 per cent, 28 per cent and 29.1 per cent.
Ramesh also pointed to the sharp contrast in anaemia levels among young children. Gujarat recorded the country's highest prevalence among children aged 12-59 months, at 56.5 per cent, while Kerala had the lowest, at 14.5 per cent.
"Of course, these figures should be even better, but Kerala is far ahead of Gujarat in this respect, even though the Prime Minister and his cheerleaders have spent the past few years promoting Gujarat as a model state," Ramesh said.

title: ‘Only PM Modi being promoted’: Abhijeet Dipke mocks BJP over social media censorship
description: CJP Founder Dipke Says We Thought That If We Keep Modiji's Photo During Media Interaction, Instagram May Not Remove This Press Conference From Its Platform
author: PTI
content:
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Wednesday mocked the ruling BJP over what he described as "Meta and Instagram censorship" and the purported removal of more than "five million" posts by playing a "Modi Chalisa" song at his press conference and placing the PM's photo.
"Censorship in the country is so rampant that excluding PM Modi's photo, any other political content is being suppressed on Instagram and Meta. Taking this into account, we have kept the PM's photo and 'Modi Chalisa' for Instagram and Meta," he said while addressing the press conference in Nagpur.
The Cockroach Janta Party founder claimed that more than "five million” posts with political content were removed from Instagram between January and June.
"Hence, we thought that if we keep Modiji's photo during media interaction, Instagram may not remove this press conference from its platform.
"I and CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka are addressing you in the presence of "Aadarniya, Sanmanniya and Mahamanav Prime Minister,” he said with Modi’s photo placed in the background.
When asked about whether this "Modi Chalisa" audio would hurt the sentiments of Hindus, Dipke said an FIR should be immediately registered against the singer of the concerned song and against the BJP social media platform from where they have picked up the audio.
Speaking on the contribution of Gen Z, Dipke said the young people have brought accountability back in the country, citing the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan amid protests against the NEET paper leak.
"The country has been afraid of raising questions for the last 12 years; however, Gen Z has given courage and voice to the people, which is the most important contribution," he added.
Dipke said the CJP has no plans to form a political party.
"We are not here to side with any party. We are not inclined towards any party; our commitment is towards the youth of this country," he added.
He said the CJP will not side with any party in the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.
"The CJP is not here to side with any party. We want the elections to be contested on issues concerning young people. Gen Z wants good opportunities, education, and infrastructure. They don't want caste and religious issues, which are often raked up during polls. We will talk about education, employment, healthcare, and public infrastructure," Dipke added.
Addressing the media, Ranka rejected allegations that CJP’s recent tour in poll-bound Goa was a pressure tactic ahead of the elections.
"The CJP’s intention is not to topple any government or replace it with another. We want elections, including in Goa, to be contested on real issues concerning the people. The CJP will draft a citizen manifesto in the coming weeks in association with the local civil society organisations, activists and people of Goa and will make every political party agree with that manifesto," he said.

title: Delhi SIR: Only 3.5 lakh Form 6 applications filed, 44 lakh excluded voters at risk
description: The Low Number Of Applications Comes Even As The Election Commission Launched A Fresh Exercise To Reach The Electors Excluded From The Draft Roll Under The Absent, Shifted, Dead And Duplicate (ASDD) Categories
author: PTI
content:
The claims and objections phase of the SIR exercise in Delhi ended on Wednesday, with only around 3.5 lakh Form 6 applications received since the draft roll was published, implying that nearly 44 lakh of the 47.5 lakh excluded voters may be left out of the final roll.
A total of 3,31,540 Form 6 applications had been received between August 31 and November 24, officials said.
The number was expected to reach around 3.5 lakh by Wednesday, they said, adding that several applications received so far were from first-time and new voters.
The numbers show that nearly 44 lakh of the 47.5 lakh voters excluded from the draft roll have not applied for inclusion through Form 6.
The draft roll published on August 31 excluded around 47.5 lakh names from Delhi's previous electoral roll of 1.45 crore voters. Of these, 43.32 lakh were categorised as shifted, 2.82 lakh as deceased and 1.45 lakh as duplicate entries.
The low number of applications comes even as the Election Commission launched a fresh exercise to reach the electors excluded from the draft roll under the absent, shifted, dead and duplicate (ASDD) categories.
These electors, who were issued enumeration forms during the earlier exercise between June 30 and August 17, were given another opportunity to establish their eligibility and get their names included in the final roll to be published on December 22.
However, the exercise has made little progress so far. Officials said the distribution of enumeration forms began last week, but only a few hundred had been distributed, while a few electors had submitted them online.
Booth-level officers (BLOs) have also struggled to trace the voters marked as shifted, particularly those who moved out of rented accommodation without leaving behind their new addresses or contact details.
As reported by PTI earlier, a BLO from Babarpur's unauthorised colony said nearly 300 voters in his polling booth had been marked under the ASDD category, mostly tenants who had vacated their rented accommodations.
“Most of the people marked under the ASDD category were tenants. They have moved out, but nobody is willing to tell us where they have gone. Even their landlords are unwilling to give anything in writing confirming that the tenants have shifted as they are unaware of their whereabouts,” he said.
Form 6 is used by citizens, including first-time voters and those whose names are missing from the electoral roll, to apply for inclusion.
Before the draft roll was published, the CEO's office received 2,12,400 Form 6 applications up to August 30.
During the same period, it also received 51,471 Form 7 applications, used to raise objections to the inclusion of names or seek deletion of entries, and 2,60,768 Form 8 applications, used for corrections in electoral roll details, including changes in residence.
Between August 31 and November 24, another 35,592 Form 7 and 1,24,554 Form 8 applications were received.
Among the districts, West recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications during this period at 40,029, followed by North-East at 32,673, South-East at 31,771, North-West at 31,660 and East at 31,619.
The distribution and collection of enumeration forms will continue until November 30, while their disposal is scheduled for December 10.
The final electoral roll is scheduled to be published on December 22.

title: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory
description: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.
author: Azadeh Moshiri
content:
After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
- Published
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

title: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
description: BBC Verify analysis indicates missing data led official Diwali pollution figures to be lower than they should be.
author: Shruti Menon and Barbara Metzler
content:
Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
- Published
BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem.
As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems.
But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was excluded from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), even though these higher readings were present in the data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC).
Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality, so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data. Firecrackers are not the only cause of pollution, which is also attributed to a mix of reasons including vehicle emissions, construction dust, farm fires and atmospheric factors. But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter.
Government critics and opposition parties have accused the government of deliberately under-reporting the pollution data. The CPCB rejected this in a statement, which said the body was "committed to transparent, scientific and reliable reporting".
The CPCB, whose figures are generally cited by Indian media, said readings above 1,000 micrograms are treated as "outside" the range for detection its equipment has been calibrated for and are excluded from calculations.
"During extreme episodes which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the statement added.
Dr Manoj Kumar, a researcher at Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told BBC Verify that excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures.
Our analysis found that, across the same 30 stations over 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre - less than half the average of 551 in DPCC's data.
What does the pollution data show?
On the night of Diwali from Sunday into Monday, Delhi's already high pollution levels rose sharply as the celebrations peaked.
Three different pollution monitoring stations recorded PM2.5 hourly concentrations above 3,000 micrograms, DPCC data examined by BBC Verify shows.
Dr Kumar said that even a short-term exposure to extreme levels of particulate matter can have adverse health impacts.
The World Health Organization's air quality guidelines state that annual average concentrations should not exceed five micrograms per cubic metre.
Between 21:00 local time (15:30 GMT) on 8 November and 07:00 on 9 November, during the peak of Diwali celebrations, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 16 stations reported complete data during this period, while 43 had at least one missing observation.
None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records they feed data into.
This matters because stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average, according to CPCB's methodology. So a station with too many missing or invalid readings will not contribute to official pollution calculations.
One example of a station with several hours of missing data was at RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms.
Using hourly PM2.5 readings from this station, BBC Verify calculated an average concentration of about 945 micrograms over the 24-hour period after 17:00 on 8 November.
But similar averages of CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours produced a much lower figure of 299 micrograms. The missing 10 hours also meant this data was not included in daily average calculations.
The missing data across the city means that, despite a sharp overnight rise in pollution at some monitoring stations, CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on 9 November, down from 376 at the same time the day before.
Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist from City St George's, University in London, warned classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out days which "contribute the most to short-term health events, such as asthma attacks and heart attacks".
She told BBC Verify "for transparency", Delhi's pollution reporting could show two scenarios including and excluding extreme pollution episodes.
"The latter would give a sense of typical pollution levels that are more representative of people's day-to-day experience. But it is also important to show the impact of those few days and what they contribute," Dr Clark added.
Pollution in Delhi is not limited to PM2.5 and satellite imagery shows a thick haze over the city on 8 and 9 November.
Satellite measurements of other pollutants like nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO) and fire activity in the atmosphere, rather than at ground level, showed increases on 8 November.
But their overall average for Diwali week was not very high compared with 2024 and 2025.
Graphics by Jess Carr and Tom Shiel.

title: Tamil Nadu: India investigates alleged 'AI scam' involving public library books
description: The Tamil Nadu government has ordered an internal audit of library collections across the state.
author: Xavier Selvakumar and Yazhiniyan
content:
New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
- Published
An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI.
The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city.
The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books.
The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations.
Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state.
The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references.
It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread.
The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; £26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month.
Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam.
He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages.
It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics.
Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books.
Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author.
The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House.
Drèze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission.
BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business.
A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts.
The controversy has prompted writers, academics and publishers to question how the books were selected for public libraries.
More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have signed a joint statement calling for an independent inquiry, the release of procurement records and an audit of library collections across Tamil Nadu.
They have also called for the recovery of public money if the investigation finds that funds were misused.
The group questioned how the disputed books could have passed through a selection process involving expert committees, price negotiations and several levels of review.
The state government has ordered an internal audit of public library collections.
Rajmohan said 523 books had already been removed from the historic Connemara Public Library in Chennai city after preliminary checks raised concerns about their authenticity and quality.
Disputed books have also been removed from Periyar Arivulagam, while anti-corruption officials examine procurement records and inspect other libraries, he added.
The controversy also sparked a political row in Tamil Nadu. Rajmohan accused the previous DMK government of ordering the disputed books and said the state would seek to recover public money if the investigation found wrongdoing.
The DMK has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and has called for an investigation into the purchases.
Additional reporting by Rachita Prasad

title: Uncovering Hate: Investigations, Ground Reports & Deep Dives into Hate Speech, Hate Crimes and Discrimination in India
description: Uncover the hidden truths of hate speech in India. Join us on a journey to expose the dark underbelly of society as we delve into investigations, ground reports, and deep dives into the multifaceted issue of hate. From hate speech to hate crimes, we shed light on the real-world impact and explore potential solutions
content:
Uncovering Hate: Investigations, Ground Reports & Deep Dives
In the last decade, India has seen a steep rise in incidents of hate crimes, discrimination, and communal violence. This doesn't mean mob lynchings alone but also targeted violence, arbitrary laws, and everyday forms of discrimination and hate.
The Quint has consistently been the leading news organisation breaking stories on communal violence and hate crimes and carrying out in-depth investigations on communal issues – be it our documentary on the hijab ban in Karnataka and our investigations on the 2020 Northeast Delhi violence, the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Conversion laws and the violence being carried out by cow-protection vigilantes.
These investigations involve a lot of work and often come at great personal risk to our reporters who are on the ground. We need your support as we continue to bring out more such investigations and voices from the ground.

title: Time Out Market Delhi introduces Khatai by Chef Manish Mehrotra
description: Time Out Market Delhi unveils Khatai, a vegetarian restaurant by Chef Manish Mehrotra. Opening December 2026, explore India's diverse plant-based cuisine with innovative dishes and cultural experiences in Aerocity.
author: The Quint
content:
Note: Quint Digital Limited (QDL) is bringing the first Time Out Market to India, with a flagship location at Worldmark Aerocity, Delhi. The launch is part of QDL’s franchise agreement with Time Out Group plc.
Opening in December 2026 at 5 Worldmark, Aerocity, Time Out Market Delhi will bring together a curated selection of chefs, restaurants and bars, alongside cultural experiences that reflect the city's diverse food scene. The Market will have 11 kitchens, two full-service bars, a live performance stage and seating for around 500 guests. It will also feature Time Out Studio, a dedicated space for cultural programming and events.
Among its offerings is Khatai, an all-vegetarian new concept created exclusively for Time Out Market by Manish Mehrotra Culinary Arts (MMCA), which will be the Market’s only full service restaurant. 
Conceived around the idea of Khatta Meetha India, the menu explores the interplay of sweet, sour, spicy and savoury flavours that characterise the country's regional cooking. From street-side preparations to everyday home-style favourites in a premium setting, the selection brings together dishes reimagined through Chef Manish's approach to ingredients, technique and presentation.
Growing up in a vegetarian household gave Chef Manish Mehrotra an early appreciation for the depth of India's plant-based cooking. His travels across the country have since introduced him to local ingredients, regional specialities and traditions that continue to influence his work. With this concept, he turns his attention to dishes that are often overlooked on restaurant menus, while retaining the flavours and character that make them familiar.
The menu brings together a selection of small plates, substantial dishes and Indian desserts, celebrating the diversity of the country's vegetarian cuisine.
Highlights include Patna Sev Puri with Arbi Fry and Green Chilli Chutney, Kanpur Batasha with Kala Chana and Hing Khatai Pani, and Haridwar Dal Ki Chaat with Baby Hing Tadka. The larger plates feature Bihari Sattu Hing Kachori with Kala Chana Ghugni, Meetha Kaddu and Jimikand Chokha, Tawa Paneer Keema with Ajwain Paratha, and OG Khichadi. The experience concludes with Indian desserts, including Daulat Ki Chaat with Rose Chikki and Mishti Doi Soft Serve.
Speaking about the concept, Chef Manish Mehrotra, Founder Chef, Manish Mehrotra Culinary Arts (MMCA), says:
“India has an extraordinary vegetarian food culture, and I have always believed there is much more to explore beyond the dishes we commonly see on restaurant menus. Some of the most memorable food I have eaten has been simple, everyday cooking, where the balance of flavours and the smallest details make all the difference. With Khatai, I wanted to bring some of these favourites together and give them a new perspective without losing the flavours that make them special. For me, the most important thing is that the food tastes wonderful and that people want to come back for it. I am delighted to introduce Khatai at Time Out Market Delhi and share this new restaurant with diners.”
This marks another addition to MMCA's restaurant portfolio, following Nisaba, Manish's first independent restaurant, which opened in New Delhi in January 2026.
Ritu Kapur, Co-founder and Managing Director, Quint Digital Limited, says:
“At Time Out Market Delhi, our vision is to create a destination that celebrates the diversity and evolving character of Delhi’s food and cultural landscape. Khatai is a wonderful expression of this vision, bringing together the culinary expertise of Chef Manish Mehrotra and the richness of India’s street food in a format that is both distinctive and accessible. We are particularly excited to introduce a concept that has been created exclusively for the Market, adding a unique dimension to the dining experience we hope to offer our guests.”
About Time Out Market Delhi
Time Out Market Delhi is a food and cultural destination at 5 Worldmark, Aerocity, New Delhi, opening in December 2026. Across approximately 25,000 sq. ft., it will have 11 kitchens, two full-service bars, a private events space, Time Out Studio, a live performance stage and seating for around 500 guests. It is brought to India by Quint Digital Limited (QDL), a digital and media-tech company focused on AI, which is the master franchise partner for Time Out Market and Time Out Media in India.
Time Out Market brings a city together under one roof: chefs, restaurateurs, drinks and cultural experiences, from live music to installations by local artists. The first opened in Lisbon in 2014, and there are now 13 Markets in cities including New York, Montréal, Dubai, Cape Town and Osaka. It is part of Time Out Group PLC (AIM: TMO), a global brand that connects people with city life through Time Out Media and Time Out Market. Time Out launched in London in 1968, and local experts now create and curate content on what to do, see and eat across more than 350 cities in over 50 countries.
For more information, please visit our website at https://www.timeout.com/time-out-market-delhi, and for the latest company news, visit our Press Office. In addition, connect with us on Instagram at @timeoutmarketdelhi.

title: 'We Will Take Back What is Ours': Hindutva is Moving Out of the Fringe in Bengal
description: Hindutva groups in Bengal: After a somewhat stymied stint under the three decades of the Left rule, the Sangh started proliferating in the state soon after Mamata’s tenure in 2011 and intensified following Modi's arrival as PM in 2014.
author: Rakhi Bose
content:
Six months into Suvendu Adhikari's tenure, West Bengal is witnessing shifts across its political, social, and cultural landscape. Follow The Quint's Bengal's Saffron Turn for in-depth coverage of these shifts. Become a member to power our ground reports.
"Wherever there is injustice, the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) and the Bajrang Dal will be present,” Raja Pramanik, a resident of Kulpi in West Bengal's South 24 Parganas district wrote while posting a video on Facebook on 9 September.
The video shows Pramanik, along with a group of men—some wearing saffron sashes—marching towards a home in Patkelberiya village and accosting the people inside over allegations of forced conversion. They are seen threatening the women inside, accusing them of conducting an illegal prayer meet.
“Some jihadis of the Christian religion were trying to convert our Hindu religion to the Christian religion. Members of Kulpi VHP and Bajrang Dal stopped it," he writes in the caption. In the video, he and the others can be heard saying, “We will not tolerate such filth in Hindu samaj. If you want to pray to Jesus, you can do so in private. If anyone else comes to join the prayers, we will not tolerate it...“

title: Eurasian Otters in Kashmir: New Study Documents Their Return After Decades
description: Eurasian otters are reappearing in Kashmir after decades. A new 2026 study documents sightings across the Lidder, Rambiara and Sindh rivers and examines the conservation challenges facing the species.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
This story is part of The Better India’s new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India’s wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India’s rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status.
For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare.
Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution.
Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways.
A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge, documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley.
Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction.
The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline.
Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply.
The return was first noticed in 2025
According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral.
Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile.
The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents.
Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025.
Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area.
Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley.
The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district.
The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river.
The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs.
The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights.
However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley.
Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems
The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health.
A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation.
More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats.
What could threaten their return?
The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported.
Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals.
The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats.
Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival.
We are into the middle stage of our ’13 Weeks of Otters’ series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv
— International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022
Climate change presents another challenge.
Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms, which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley.
What conservation efforts need to focus on
The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations.
This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations.
It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters.
The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour.
The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral.
Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people.
For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population.
Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley.

title: Delhi Teens Make Rs 140 Classroom Air Purifier
description: Discover how Project Vayu is helping Delhi schools tackle indoor air pollution, with classroom tests reporting a 60% drop in harmful PM2.5 levels in an hour.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
A classroom fan spins above a group of children bent over their notebooks. As the teacher moves between desks and lessons continue, the fan keeps the air circulating. But in a city like Delhi, where pollution often makes its way indoors, circulating air does not necessarily mean breathing clean air.
For thousands of children studying in schools that cannot afford expensive air purifiers, this is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day inside classrooms, often with little protection from fine particulate matter suspended in the air.
Two Delhi teenagers, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle, decided to look at this problem differently. Instead of asking schools to invest in expensive purification systems, they wondered if the fans already fitted in classrooms could be made to do more.
Their idea took shape as Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed an affordable filter that fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping turn them into air purifiers. At approximately Rs 140 per filter, the innovation offers schools a way to tackle indoor air pollution without having to invest in entirely new equipment.
"Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo say. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection."
What if a classroom fan could also clean the air?
Rather than building a new appliance from scratch, Krish and Samarth decided to work with the infrastructure schools already had.
The biggest technical challenge was developing a filter that could trap fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, without restricting the airflow of an ordinary fan.
"We experimented with different designs before arriving at our balloon-shaped filter, made from electret media with electrostatically charged fibres," they explain.
The filter uses electrostatically charged fibres that attract and capture tiny airborne particles. It fits over an existing table or wall fan with the help of an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates the filter into a balloon-like shape, increasing its surface area for filtration.
There is no need for additional motors, electrical modifications or specialised installation. The filter can be fitted in under a minute, without tools.
To develop and test the technology, the teenagers approached Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. They initially emailed the company's India team with their idea and were surprised by its willingness to support them.
The company provided filtration media free of cost and collaborated with the team on research and development.
"The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it. By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure," they say.
This support has helped keep the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter.
What difference can a Rs 140 filter make?
For the young innovators, developing an affordable product was only half the task. They also needed to establish whether it could make a measurable difference to indoor air quality.
According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research and development with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results.
In a closed room measuring approximately 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly dropped from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour of using the filter, a reduction of over 90%.
The results, however, depend on the room's size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 levels over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use.
There is also a visible reminder of the particles being trapped.
"One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use. It's a visible reminder of just how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms," they say.
From 295 classrooms to thousands of students
Getting schools to trust an unfamiliar technology developed by high school students was not easy.
Initially, many institutions were understandably hesitant. Demonstrations and explanations of the testing behind the filters, however, helped the team build confidence.
Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and approximately 8,000 students. The initiative has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics.
Their work has not been without challenges. Identifying schools, securing permissions and navigating institutional processes have often slowed installations.
"Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging. A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals," they say.
The effort has also brought recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his work with Project Vayu. For him, the recognition belongs to everyone who helped build the initiative, including Samarth and their collaborators.
"Project Vayu has taught me that innovation doesn't always require inventing something entirely new. Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible," Samarth adds.
What's next for Project Vayu?
The duo now hopes to expand Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and eventually other parts of India. They are keen to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help take the filters to children who need them.
Their ambition is rooted in a simple belief: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend.
For Krish and Samarth, the idea was never just about making a fan work differently. It was about looking at something already available in classrooms and asking how it could serve children better.
And sometimes, making a difference does not require an entirely new machine. It begins with finding a new purpose for something that is already there.
All images courtesy of Krish Aggarwal

title: Dharwad Women Farmers Preserve 250+ Indigenous Seeds, Win Rs 10 Lakh Award
description: Meet the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group in Dharwad, Karnataka, which has conserved 250+ indigenous seed varieties, supported 5,000 farmers across 30 villages and won the Rs 10 lakh Plant Genome Saviour Community Award in 2026.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
A handful of seeds can carry generations of farming knowledge.
In Karnataka's Dharwad district, a group of women has been collecting, preserving, and sharing these seeds, helping farmers continue cultivating indigenous crops suited to the region's rainfed conditions.
On November 12, 2026, the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group (SHG) from Teertha village in Kundgol taluk received the Plant Genome Saviour Community Award, along with a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh, a citation, and a memento.
The recognition acknowledges the collective's efforts to conserve more than 250 indigenous seed varieties and revive traditional millet-based mixed cropping systems across 30 villages in Dharwad's rainfed farming areas.
The initiative began in 2018, when farmer Bibijaan Maulasaab Halemani brought together 14 other women to establish the collective.
According to Bibijaan, her interest in seed conservation came from her father, who also preserved seeds.
Speaking to The New Indian Express in a report published on November 5, 2026, she said, “My father used to conserve seeds, and I too developed an interest and took to seed conservation.”
She established the SHG and its seed bank in 2018, with the aim of making good-quality indigenous seeds accessible to farmers and encouraging traditional crop cultivation.
A seed bank with more than 250 varieties
The group's community seed bank preserves a wide range of indigenous crops, including:
- - Jawari (sorghum)
- - 70 varieties of finger millet
- - 25 varieties of little millet
- - Two varieties of browntop millet
- - 10 varieties of foxtail millet
- - 25 varieties of horse gram
- - 10 varieties of chickpea
- - 25 varieties of paddy
- - Three varieties of green gram
- - Around a dozen oilseed varieties
- - Several varieties of vegetables
These varieties form part of the region's traditional agricultural diversity. The indigenous millet varieties, in particular, are adapted to local agro-climatic conditions and can withstand variations in weather.
The collective has also worked to revive millet-based mixed cropping, in which farmers cultivate multiple crops together rather than depending on a single crop.
According to the United Nations Development Programme's Equator Initiative, the group now supports more than 5,000 farmers across 30 villages. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices.
Beyond seed conservation, the collective has expanded into agricultural processing and livelihood activities.
It operates a solar-powered millet processing unit, which helps women produce value-added millet products. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security.
Recognition for community-led seed conservation
The national award is not the group's first recognition for its work.
In August 2025, the United Nations Development Programme announced Bibifathima Swa Sahaya Sangha as one of the 10 winners of the Equator Prize 2025. The award recognised community-led initiatives working on nature-based solutions under the theme 'Nature for Climate Action', with a focus on women's and young people's leadership.
According to the UNDP's August 20, 2025 announcement, the collective received recognition for its work combining traditional agricultural knowledge, seed conservation, renewable energy and climate-resilient farming. Each winning initiative was awarded $10,000.
For the women of Dharwad, their work continues to centre on collecting indigenous seeds, keeping traditional crop varieties in cultivation and helping farming communities access planting material suited to their local conditions.

title: COP31 and the climate crisis: Why the focus must shift to solutions
description: COP31 exposed divisions over fossil fuel phaseout and climate finance. Why global climate policy must prioritise adaptation, innovation and just transitions.
author: Raghu Murtugudde
content:
The Conference of the Parties 31 or COP31 that just concluded in Antalya, Türkiye, was the longest and was also the first one to be organised by two countries. Türkiye was the host, while Australia played a special role as the President of Negotiations. Negotiations were extended by two days but were accused of doing backroom negotiations without involving all parties or being open about the secret dealings. It is now also branded as the worst COP by some countries and NGOs.
The sticking point was the same as the one in Brazil at COP30. And that was to explicitly mention the phasing out of fossil fuels in the cover text as a major outcome of COP31 negotiations. With the absence of the US, other major oil-producing countries blocked any statements on phasing out of fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are now being called the “F” word, and many countries continue to invest heavily in producing fossil fuels. Major fossil fuel producers tried to push electrification (35 by 35, i.e., 35 per cent renewables by 2035) and carbon capture as effective steps towards eventually reaching fossil fuel phaseout. The knee-jerk reactions to such suggestions only underscore the tunnel vision on emissions without acknowledging the lack of pathways to phasing out fossil fuels right now.
The European Union broke the consensus that is required to approve the cover text at COPs. Roadmaps for phasing out fossil fuels are being put out by several countries now with their own strategies for accomplishing this goal. The tyranny of consensus has once again led to failure at a COP. Climate finance and other issues continue to struggle as well. The overall process is doing better on climate mitigation, albeit progressing much more slowly than desirable. Adaptation struggles as always since it is neither ideal for global leadership nor attractive as an investment option for banks and financiers. Even the development banks conflate economic development projects with adaptation programmes.
What is clear as daylight is that all the headlines are about the impacts of global warming, the threat of crossing the warming thresholds, the lack of political will for climate actions, the unwillingness to phase out fossil fuels, or the insufficiency of climate finance for developing countries. It is impossible to find any significant attention on investing in innovations and training the design engineers, doctors, and social scientists for all the solutions and adaptations needed. Where will the solutions for climate mitigation, carbon capture, phasing out fossil fuels, and adaptations in critical sectors such as agriculture and food, water, energy, transportation, buildings, health, etc., emerge from if nobody is paying attention to them? Will grand statements about phasing out fossil fuels drive innovations for solutions? Or is it better to start producing cover statements on solutions and finances to drive just and equitable innovations and designs to transition to a safe and sustainable world?
Mitigation is all political now
Climate change and global warming narratives always scream implicitly and explicitly about the need for mitigation. The agreed-upon warming target for 2100 in the Paris Agreement of 2 degrees Celsius and then reduced to 1.5 degrees Celsius is now the rallying cry for accelerating mitigation efforts and updating national commitments to reducing emissions. Countries continue to struggle internally and on international stages with the socioeconomics, geopolitics, climate justice, and just transition issues that come with the tunnel vision on the warming targets. The relentless push for mitigation despite all other pocketbook and economic development issues is leading to election outcomes in some countries that indicate how disconnected the climate negotiations may have become from everyday lives of common people and the political realities. One tunnel vision always brings an opposing tunnel vision. Even the most progressive countries are struggling with their commitments to climate actions.
The side effects of these rather unscientific global warming targets are also the cacophony about natural climate variability such as the noise about the “super” El Niño and the alarm about crossing the 1.5 degree Celcius threshold. Super El Niño is another unscientific concept with no clear science to explain what special impacts it may bring at local scales. Especially since global warming patterns are now confounding the El Niño impacts and the models continue to struggle to predict the impacts at hyperlocal scales. No clear guidance is available to help anticipate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from disasters and risks. The same goes for this magical global warming threshold as to the impacts in one’s backyard. How are adaptation projects and programmes to be designed and financed with so much noise then?
Adaptations avoid losses and benefit economies
Adaptation programmes and projects are critical to blunt the impacts of global warming. But they are very contextual, location- and sector-specific. They are also about avoiding losses and inducing economic and ecological co-benefits rather than about making profits. The more successful adaptations are in mitigating the risks, the less willing societies may become in sustaining finances for continuing those projects and programmes.
The local nature of adaptations with only co-benefits for economies makes adaptation an unclear investment option for banks and private financiers. Insurance companies may underwrite risks, but pitching adaptation as purely risk mitigation or risk avoidance programmes may limit their long-term goal of building resilience. Resilience is the foundation for ensuring that the risks from global warming and other natural and human-made disturbances do not disrupt economic development and the steady progress towards sustained climate actions for sustainability and net zero.
As long as climate finances are seen as charitable work and not a collective choice for investing in global economic development, COPs will always struggle to line up new financial commitments. The narratives may have to shift from insisting on unrealistic texts on what can be phased out to being more explicit on how and if anything can be phased out. Whether it is the fossil fuels or the emissions. We should not totally dismiss optimal use of fossil fuels with effective carbon capture if that brings consensus on making real progress.
Can COPs focus on climate solutions rather than just aspirational and unrealistic statements?
Global warming is here, and impacts are seen every day in every corner of the world. No country, rich or poor, and no species in the natural-human earth system is spared now. And yet the drive at COPs has been on addressing the symptoms and not the disease. Human lifestyles are energy-intensive, and energy is carbon-intensive. The narratives have to focus on optimistic visions for the future that provide rich standards of living for all without devouring the environment and without emitting or capturing greenhouse gases.
It is highly unlikely, if not impossible, to find our way out of our energy-intensive lifestyles, but it can be a feasible goal to decarbonise energy. All rich countries have achieved high standards of living with high environmental impacts. The remaining countries are striving to achieve higher standards of living, and they have no option right now but to increase their environmental footprints to get there. Instead of the tunnel visions on emissions reductions which have struggled, the paradigm can be at least to transform the narrative to climate solutions in all sectors with just transitions.
The pathways to climate solutions and investments to drive the science, technology and carbon-free living may be a way to get us away from the survival-level street fights at COPs and the relentless lobbying for status quo. Without a clear path and an obvious destination, humans are incapable of changing paths, neither at individual levels nor at group, national or global levels.
The destination of staying under a certain warming threshold may seem sufficient as a cover text, but it does not come with any clear vision of who gets what by achieving this target. The tyranny of consensus may need to end to make progress with a majority rule.
Raghu Murtugudde is Emeritus Professor, University of Maryland; Visiting Professor, Kotak School of Sustainability, IIT Kanpur.
